{"new_message": "Campaign brief: Wickhold Leashgate general availability
From: Ilse Varga-Holm, VP Marketing
Date: October 20, 2026
Status: Approved to plan. Internal until launch day
Reviewers: Noor Eskelund (audience, goal, voice), Priit Salonen (claims), Dov Achterberg (technical read), Kofi Anselm (developer content, X)
What is happening
Wickhold Leashgate reaches general availability on Tuesday, January 26, 2027. Product and Legal have confirmed the status change, and this brief is Product Marketing's announcement of it for everyone working on the campaign.
Two things follow from that.
The early access label comes off for this campaign. Every asset below publishes on or after January 26, so it says "Wickhold Leashgate" on first mention and "Leashgate" after that, with no early access label. On launch day it is correct to say Wickhold Leashgate is generally available. The label rule in the 2026 release notes, the early access wording in the messaging house and the Leashgate section of the approved claims all stay in force for everything else until January 26. Those documents get updated for launch. Where one of them conflicts with this brief on Leashgate's status alone, this brief wins for these assets. On anything else, they stand.
Nothing external mentions general availability or the date before January 26. No teasers, no "coming soon", no countdown. Early access copy already in market stays as it is until launch day.
General availability changes the status of the product and not its scope. Leashgate at launch is what the product overview and the 2026 release notes describe: agent identity, tool-call policy, and the blast radius report, with a gateway running as a sidecar or as a shared Deployment, for agents that make tool calls over HTTP or MCP. Approvals can be answered from Slack. The tie-in that lets Leashgate ask Wickhold Quenchline for a containment action is optional, off by default, and needs Quenchline on the node.
Goals
The numbers here are internal and do not go in copy.
Customers hear it from us first, on launch day, with enough detail for a platform team to judge whether it applies to them.
60 demo requests by March 31, 2027 from teams with an agent running against real tools, in staging or production.
Get the blast radius report into security reviews. We want platform leads to bring it to their next one, as the answer to "what is the worst this agent could do on a bad day?" Sales will track how often it comes up on calls.
Audience
Primary: platform leads who have been asked to get an agent into production and have a security review standing in their way. They already have the concern, and the budget conversation has started. They read docs first, want the failure behavior early, and trust a config snippet over a paragraph.
Secondary: security leaders and security architects writing internal rules for agent use. They need something more enforceable than a policy document. Lead with the decision they have to make. No humor for this group.
Existing customers get the news first, through the technical customer list. Several asked about agents at Slow Burn Summit, and most were not running any in production yet, so do not write as if they all are.
Keep these audiences apart. Platform and security leadership are separate email lists, and they stay separate here. The landing page is written for platform leads. Security leaders get their own email and the launch post.
Key messages
Treat an agent as a workload with credentials, and give it a boundary. This is pillar 3 of the messaging house and the argument under everything else. Talk about tool calls in a cluster. Leave the future of work to other people.
What it does. Leashgate gives each agent an identity, checks every tool call against a tool-call policy, writes a decision record, and reports the blast radius of an agent, including any route around the gateway.
The outcome statement. Leashgate "limits what a compromised agent can do". Use those words exactly.
For platform leads. defaultAction: deny. Your agent framework stays the same. Leashgate fails closed, so an outage of the gateway stops the agent's tools, and teams need to plan for that. Say so plainly.
For security leaders. Before an agent goes live, know its blast radius. Every decision leaves a record your team can read in a security review.
What it does not do. Leashgate sees tool calls, and it does not read or judge prompts. It runs on Kubernetes only, and frameworks that call tools in-process, with no network hop, are out of scope. Being plain about this is part of the pitch.
Channels and assets
Eleven assets, on owned channels only. This is my starting list, so if the mix is wrong, say so when you bring the plan on November 6. The release note, press and sales enablement run separately and are not part of this brief.

Pricing. Pricing after early access is not settled, and I am handling the pricing page separately before launch. Do not state a price or a tier for Leashgate in any asset. Link to the pricing page where a reader needs it, and send buying questions to sales.
Support terms. Say nothing about SLAs or support levels. Those live in the order form.
Roadmap. Describe what the product does on launch day. No future features, no adapter lists, no dates beyond the launch itself.
Competitors. Leashgate stays out of competitive positioning. No comparisons and no comparison blog in this campaign.
Code in copy. Excerpts of ToolCallPolicy rules are welcome. Leave out the apiVersion line, build numbers and the install command. The early access versions do not carry over, and Kofi adds the final block at the paste test.
Images. Use the library. Design's console screens for launch will not be ready in time, and the Leashgate console screens in the library carry the early access pill, which is not to be cropped off. Keep them off every asset in this campaign. The landing page hero is a working room.
Maren's post. It is a draft for her to rewrite. Do not schedule it, and do not assume a yes.

What is happening
Wickhold Leashgate reaches general availability on Tuesday, January 26, 2027. Product and Legal have confirmed the status change, and this brief is Product Marketing's announcement of it for everyone working on the campaign.
Two things follow from that.
The early access label comes off for this campaign. Every asset below publishes on or after January 26, so it says "Wickhold Leashgate" on first mention and "Leashgate" after that, with no early access label. On launch day it is correct to say Wickhold Leashgate is generally available. The label rule in the 2026 release notes, the early access wording in the messaging house and the Leashgate section of the approved claims all stay in force for everything else until January 26. Nothing external mentions general availability or the date before January 26. No teasers, no "coming soon", no countdown. Early access copy already in market stays as it is until launch day.
General availability changes the status of the product and not its scope. Leashgate at launch is what the product overview and the 2026 release notes describe: agent identity, tool-call policy, and the blast radius report, with a gateway running as a sidecar or as a shared Deployment, for agents that make tool calls over HTTP or MCP. Goals
The numbers here are internal and do not go in copy.
Customers hear it from us first, on launch day, with enough detail for a platform team to judge whether it applies to them.
60 demo requests by March 31, 2027 from teams with an agent running against real tools, in staging or production.
Get the blast radius report into security reviews. We want platform leads to bring it to their next one, as the answer to "what is the worst this agent could do on a bad day?" Sales will track how often it comes up on calls.

Treat an agent as a workload with credentials, and give it a boundary. This is pillar 3 of the messaging house and the argument under everything else. Talk about tool calls in a cluster. Leave the future of work to other people.

Ilse", "conversation": [{"role": "user", "text": "Campaign brief: Wickhold Leashgate general availability
From: Ilse Varga-Holm, VP Marketing
Date: October 20, 2026
Status: Approved to plan. Internal until launch day
Reviewers: Noor Eskelund (audience, goal, voice), Priit Salonen (claims), Dov Achterberg (technical read), Kofi Anselm (developer content, X)
What is happening
Wickhold Leashgate reaches general availability on Tuesday, January 26, 2027. Product and Legal have confirmed the status change, and this brief is Product Marketing's announcement of it for everyone working on the campaign.
Two things follow from that.
The early access label comes off for this campaign. Every asset below publishes on or after January 26, so it says "Wickhold Leashgate" on first mention and "Leashgate" after that, with no early access label. On launch day it is correct to say Wickhold Leashgate is generally available. The label rule in the 2026 release notes, the early access wording in the messaging house and the Leashgate section of the approved claims all stay in force for everything else until January 26. Those documents get updated for launch. Where one of them conflicts with this brief on Leashgate's status alone, this brief wins for these assets. On anything else, they stand.
Nothing external mentions general availability or the date before January 26. No teasers, no "coming soon", no countdown. Early access copy already in market stays as it is until launch day.
General availability changes the status of the product and not its scope. Leashgate at launch is what the product overview and the 2026 release notes describe: agent identity, tool-call policy, and the blast radius report, with a gateway running as a sidecar or as a shared Deployment, for agents that make tool calls over HTTP or MCP. Approvals can be answered from Slack. The tie-in that lets Leashgate ask Wickhold Quenchline for a containment action is optional, off by default, and needs Quenchline on the node.
Goals
The numbers here are internal and do not go in copy.
Customers hear it from us first, on launch day, with enough detail for a platform team to judge whether it applies to them.
60 demo requests by March 31, 2027 from teams with an agent running against real tools, in staging or production.
Get the blast radius report into security reviews. We want platform leads to bring it to their next one, as the answer to "what is the worst this agent could do on a bad day?" Sales will track how often it comes up on calls.
Audience
Primary: platform leads who have been asked to get an agent into production and have a security review standing in their way. They already have the concern, and the budget conversation has started. They read docs first, want the failure behavior early, and trust a config snippet over a paragraph.
Secondary: security leaders and security architects writing internal rules for agent use. They need something more enforceable than a policy document. Lead with the decision they have to make. No humor for this group.
Existing customers get the news first, through the technical customer list. Several asked about agents at Slow Burn Summit, and most were not running any in production yet, so do not write as if they all are.
Keep these audiences apart. Platform and security leadership are separate email lists, and they stay separate here. The landing page is written for platform leads. Security leaders get their own email and the launch post.
Key messages
Treat an agent as a workload with credentials, and give it a boundary. This is pillar 3 of the messaging house and the argument under everything else. Talk about tool calls in a cluster. Leave the future of work to other people.
What it does. Leashgate gives each agent an identity, checks every tool call against a tool-call policy, writes a decision record, and reports the blast radius of an agent, including any route around the gateway.
The outcome statement. Leashgate "limits what a compromised agent can do". Use those words exactly.
For platform leads. defaultAction: deny. Your agent framework stays the same. Leashgate fails closed, so an outage of the gateway stops the agent's tools, and teams need to plan for that. Say so plainly.
For security leaders. Before an agent goes live, know its blast radius. Every decision leaves a record your team can read in a security review.
What it does not do. Leashgate sees tool calls, and it does not read or judge prompts. It runs on Kubernetes only, and frameworks that call tools in-process, with no network hop, are out of scope. Being plain about this is part of the pitch.
Channels and assets
Eleven assets, on owned channels only. This is my starting list, so if the mix is wrong, say so when you bring the plan on November 6. The release note, press and sales enablement run separately and are not part of this brief.

response.instructions: Supported deliverables are LinkedIn posts, X posts, emails, blog articles and landing pages. We do not produce videos, animations, audio or podcasts. Never offer these as deliverables, including in clarification questions or mixed-format choices. If explicitly requested, explain the limitation and offer supported alternatives; never silently convert formats. When the brief delegates channel mix or asks for a recommendation, propose a reasonable mix of supported formats. Unspecified formats and counts in such a brief are not blockers: choose a modest scope and record assumptions. Model-selected counts, audience and timing are recommendations, not explicit user requirements. Never describe them as specified by the user. Preserve the stated goals and priorities. Ask only for essential missing constraints. Records with origin reviewed_rule are verified source-grounded treatments from the campaign review. Apply them to claim wording over contradictory historical brief text and extracted requirements. They do not grant publication permission or override explicit user decisions. Records with origin confirmed_authority are source-backed automatic resolutions, not user answers; apply their factual resolution without changing user intent. Other current decisions are explicit user answers to saved questions. Apply them as updates to the original brief; the original request is historical where an answer supersedes it. Never report a conflict solely because the original brief differs from an accepted answer. Do not require the campaign goal to narrate the correction or its legal justification. An answer is campaign intent, not proof of a factual claim. If a new evidence conflict still needs a decision, ask it explicitly rather than silently overriding the answer. Do not reopen the same question unless relevant evidence or user intent changed, or the answer was ambiguous. Explain the specific change when reopening. You manage a brand campaign using tools. For removals or individual outline edits to an existing ungenerated plan, use revise_plan directly: do not extract, retrieve, or propose again. Preserve all unspecified fields. Resolve numbered assets by latest saved plan order; read_campaign if needed. Format changes and additions require planning. Before proposing a plan call extract_requirements. Inspect structured issues and ask one essential clarification using ask_question if required information is missing. Optional details need not block planning. After a saved conflict choice, reuse current requirements and retrieved evidence; apply current decisions when proposing the plan. Extract again only for new instructions or incomplete requirements. Once brief issues are resolved, call retrieve_context, inspect its topic and channel tracks and empty_tracks, then propose_plan. Compacted context preserves sources but does not establish claim approval. Ask if essential evidence is absent; do not invent facts. Perform requested actions, never merely describe them. Edits apply immediately; new assets (social posts, emails, blogs and landing pages) require a plan and explicit UI approval. Never approve or generate new drafts yourself. For compound requests execute edits first then propose additions. Resolve numbered posts by saved order. Ask when ambiguous. Preserve the full user request, especially publication dates and required statistics, in tool instructions. Use propose_plan for requests to create any campaign assets, including emails, not answer_brand_question. When adding assets to an existing generated campaign, set addition=true and preserve existing drafts. Resolve requests such as an email for it using the current campaign topic and audience. Resolve brief issues before planning. After a plan reports a question, use ask_question and wait; never answer it yourself. Never write unsaved campaign copy. Finish only after tool results confirm success. For automatic library image selection use add_images, preserving existing attachments unless replacement is requested. Inspect per-asset results and report gaps honestly. Never generate images. Exact image edits require list_brand_images then change_image; revise_draft edits text only and preserves the attachment. For compound requests perform both tools. A change_image result must confirm the saved image ID before you claim it changed. Never claim scheduling is available or offer to schedule; requested dates are draft planning dates only. When a plan needs clarification, relay its one essential question concisely without introducing alternative evidence or reports that the plan has not verified as eligible. Use finish_turn to finish.

# The Wickhold Field Report 2023 Is Here!

The wait is over! Today we are thrilled to release the Wickhold Field Report 2023, our annual, deep-dive look at what is really happening inside production Kubernetes environments. If you run containers at any scale, this is the one report you can't afford to skip.

Attackers aren't waiting for your next sprint planning session. Every minute a risky container runs unwatched is a minute they can use against you. Our researchers spent months talking to the teams on the front lines, and the headline finding should make every security leader sit up:

**68% of runtime incidents began with a misconfigured workload.**

Read that again. Before anyone wrote a clever exploit, somebody shipped a container running as root, a service account with cluster-admin, or a hostPath mount nobody remembered approving. The call was coming from inside the house!

## Three takeaways from this year's report

**1. Misconfiguration is the new perimeter.** With 68% of runtime incidents began with a misconfigured workload, config review can no longer be a once-a-quarter activity. It has to run all the time.

**2. Visibility gaps are everywhere.** Most teams we spoke with could not say with confidence what was running in their clusters last Tuesday, much less right now. Spreadsheets and quarterly audits will not save you.

**3. Security and platform teams still speak different languages.** Security teams file tickets. Platform teams close them without reading them. Everyone is frustrated, and the attacker doesn't care.

## Why we run this research

Maren Tolliver, our CEO and co-founder, puts it this way: "Dov and I spent years on call before we started this company, and the thing that always surprised us was how ordinary the root cause turned out to be. We wanted hard data on that, so teams could stop chasing movie-plot attacks and fix what's really hurting them."

We publish the Field Report every year, and it keeps getting bigger. We spoke with platform engineers, security leaders and SREs at companies of every size, from startups with a single cluster to global enterprises with hundreds. We asked what broke, how they found out, and what they wish they had done differently. Many of the answers were painful to read!

# Tallowatch is now Wickhold Evenburn

As of today, Wickhold Tallowatch has a new name: Wickhold Evenburn. It's the same cloud and cluster posture management product you already use, with a name that fits what it does.

## Why rename it

"Tallowatch" was all about watching. Customers kept telling us that watching wasn't the problem. Their queues were full of things they had already seen. What they wanted was help deciding what to fix first and an honest picture of how a mistake could actually be reached from outside.

An even burn is what you want from a candle: steady, predictable, nothing flaring up. That's the goal for your clusters.

The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report], and that figure comes from incidents involving ordinary workloads with ordinary service accounts. Wickhold Leashgate, our runtime policy product for AI agents and their tool calls, is now in early access. This post explains what early access includes, how the product works, and what it does not do.

## The problem with agents in production

An agent in a production cluster is a workload that makes its own decisions about what to call next. Platform teams are being asked to run these agents, often with credentials that were copied from a developer's laptop during a pilot. The agent can reach a database, a ticketing system and a deployment pipeline, because during the pilot that was convenient.

Most of the time this works fine. When it does not, the failure is hard to reason about. A model may be manipulated by content it read, or it may simply make a poor decision. Either way, the question for the on-call engineer is the same as for any other incident: how far can this get?

The term we use for that is the blast radius of an agent. It is set by what the agent is allowed to do at runtime, and that is what Leashgate controls.

## What Leashgate does

Leashgate sits between an agent and the tools it calls. It works with three concepts.

**Agent identity.** Each agent gets its own identity, separate from the human who launched it and from the service account of the pod it runs in. Logs and policies refer to that identity, so "which agent did this" has an answer.

**Tool-call policy.** A team writes down which tools an agent may call, with which arguments, on which targets. A support agent may read a customer record but may not export a table. A deployment agent may restart a service in staging but may not touch production. Calls outside the policy are blocked and logged.

# Runtime containment for Kubernetes, decided before the incident

Wickhold Quenchline detects bad behavior at runtime and takes the containment action your team chose in advance. Small fires stay small.

**[Start a trial]** **[See it contain]**

## Most incident hours are waiting

41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. Those hours rarely go to detection. They go to finding an owner, getting approval and pulling the second team onto the call.

Quenchline takes that decision out of the worst hour of the night.

## How it works

**Observe first.** The eBPF agent starts in observe mode and logs what it would have done. Most teams spend two to four weeks here, reading decision records.

**Write the policy.** Start from the default containment policy and decide which detection leads to which containment action. Policies go through your repo like any other change. Every exemption has an expiry date.

**Turn on contain mode where you are ready.** Mode is set per policy. Going back is one line.

## Containment actions

| Action | What happens | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| Isolate a pod's network | The pod can no longer reach anything outside it | A workload is talking to something it never has |

## A fleet that had drifted

A grocery chain's infrastructure doesn't get quiet weeks to clean up. Over time the team had built a standard cluster template for stores and rolled it out widely. ## Why Evenburn

The team wanted to answer two questions it couldn't answer before: what had changed from what we meant to deploy, and which problems can actually be reached?

Evenburn's three concepts mapped onto that directly.

## 1. Where we sit

Wickhold is the runtime security company for teams that run Kubernetes. The buyer's question we answer is what happens in the minutes after something goes wrong in a cluster, and how far it gets before a person is awake.

Most of the market answers a different question. Posture tools tell a team what could go wrong. Detection tools tell a team what is going wrong. Broad platforms promise to do all of it from one console. We meet each of those in deals, and each has honest strengths.

Our position in one line, for internal use: **Wickhold contains runtime failures early, on the node, with an agent a platform team will accept.**

Three parts of that line carry the weight.

- *Contains.* Containment actions are what we sell: isolate a pod's network, freeze a process, drain a node. Everyone can raise an alert.
- *On the node.* Wickhold Quenchline acts where the workload runs, through an eBPF agent, without waiting for a ticket to cross two org charts.
- *An agent a platform team will accept.* The platform lead has a veto, and overhead, removal and failure behavior decide that vote.

Wickhold Evenburn supports the same position from the other side: it works out which exposure paths to close first so there are fewer things to contain. We sell the pair on Team because the two share workload context. We don't pretend Evenburn is the widest posture product available.

Wickhold Leashgate is in early access and stays out of competitive positioning for now. None of the three has been a factor in an early access account so far, and we don't want a roadmap conversation dressed up as a comparison. If a buyer brings up AI agents in a competitive deal, label it early access and hand the question to product.

What we don't claim: to be a platform, to cover endpoint, identity or email, or to have the most detections. A competitive argument built on any of those loses, and it costs us with the platform lead when it does.

## 1. The idea

A wick is where a fire is allowed to exist. The flame burns there, at a size someone chose, and it stops being an emergency. That's the company. Runtime failures in Kubernetes are going to happen. A pod gets compromised, a process does something it shouldn't, a policy drifts. What decides the outcome is how far the failure gets before someone or something contains it.

Mission: keep small failures from becoming big ones.

The old house was built around watching things. It made sense when customers mostly bought a dashboard, and it stopped making sense once the question from every serious buyer became "and then what happens?" The 2026 house answers that question.

## 2. Core message

**Wickhold contains runtime failures in Kubernetes early, tells you plainly what happened, and leaves your on-call team with a smaller problem.**

Short version for tight spaces: small fires stay small.

## Who this is

The CISO at a company with 200 to 5,000 nodes in production Kubernetes. She reports to the CEO or the CIO, presents to the audit committee or the full board once a quarter, and inherited most of the cluster estate from a platform team that built it before anyone asked her opinion. She has a team of analysts who are strong on identity and endpoint and thin on containers. The person who actually understands the clusters reports to somebody else.

She rarely buys on a first conversation and she rarely evaluates the product herself. She sponsors, she signs, and she kills deals that will embarrass her. Her platform lead does the proof of concept. Her job in the deal is to decide whether the risk reduction is worth a change to production, and to be able to defend that decision in one sentence to people who do not know what a pod is.

Typical titles: CISO, VP Security, Head of Information Security. At smaller customers the title may be Director of Security with the same duties and a smaller budget.

## What she is trying to get done

- Give the board a credible answer to "how long would it take us to contain something in production?" Most can't give one today, and they know it.
- Close the gap between detection and action. Her SOC can see an alert from a cluster, but it can't do anything about it without paging an engineer in another org.
- Get through audits without pulling platform engineers off roadmap work for weeks.
- Decide what to do about AI agents. Engineering wants to run them with real credentials. She needs a position before the next board meeting.

## What keeps the deal from moving

She has been burned by agents that took down a production node, so "runs in the kernel" is a concern before it is a selling point. She will ask who controls containment actions, who gets paged when one fires, and how to turn it off. She also has too many tools. Adding one means explaining why, and she would prefer to retire something.

Her platform lead has a veto in practice. A CISO who forces an agent onto a cluster over the platform team's objection tends to regret it, and she knows that. Treat the two conversations as linked: anything we tell her about contain mode has to match what the platform lead hears.

# The platform lead

Staff or principal engineer, or the manager of a platform team of 4 to 15 people. Title might be Platform Lead, Head of Infrastructure, SRE Manager, or Principal Engineer. They run the Kubernetes clusters everyone else deploys to, and they carry the pager or manage the people who do. Both of our founders held this job, which helps, and it's also why we get lazy here. They got burned by something. Usually it was a security agent that OOM-killed a node, or a DaemonSet from a vendor that rolled out with no resource limits on a Friday. So they start the conversation with a no. They're the ones who'll run `kubectl top` on our pods during the POC.

## What they want

- Nothing on a node that they can't explain, limit and remove with one Helm command.
- Fewer pages at 3am, and when the page comes, a clear statement of what fired and why.
- Their security team off their back. They don't mind security. They mind tickets with no reproduction steps.
- Control over anything that can drain one of their nodes. This is the sticking point on contain mode.

## How to talk to them

Lead with commands, flags and failure modes. The first thing they read should be something they could paste into a terminal, or a description of how the thing breaks. Concepts come after, if anyone's still reading.

Dry humor is allowed, and they'd rather have it. A straight-faced line about a Friday deploy does more for us than an adjective. It has to come from having been on-call. Puns about fires got old in about March.

No outcomes language. Nothing about "transforming" operations, "peace of mind", "improved security posture" or "business value". If a sentence would also work in a deck for their CFO, cut it. Tell them what the agent does to the node and what it costs in CPU and memory.

The order that works in docs, posts and talks:

1. The command or config.
2. What happens when it runs.
3. How it fails, and what you'll see when it does.
4. How to back it out.

**Install and removal.** They'll read the Helm chart before they read our site. Show the values file. Say what privileges the agent needs and why. Show the uninstall in the same post as the install, because they'll look for it.

Nearly every Evenburn conversation comes down to three concepts. Use these exact terms in copy, docs and demos, since they are also the names in the console.

### Drift

Drift is any difference between what a team declared and what is running. Declared state comes from Helm releases, manifests in a connected Git repo, and infrastructure baselines you approve in the console. Running state comes from the Kubernetes API and cloud provider APIs.

A typical example: the chart for `checkout-api` sets `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`, somebody ran `kubectl patch` during an incident in June to get a debug tool working, and the patch never came out. DRIFT  apps/v1 Deployment shop/checkout-api
```text
  field     spec.template.spec.containers[0].securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem
  declared  true    (helm release shop/checkout, rev 41)
  live      false
  first seen 2026-02-11T03:42:18Z
  changed by svc-oncall-breakglass (audit log)
```

Not all drift is a problem. Autoscalers change replica counts, and mutating webhooks add sidecars. Every ignore rule keeps its author and a reason, so a reviewer can tell a deliberate choice from a forgotten one.

### Exposure path

An exposure path is a chain of real, currently valid connections from somewhere an outsider can reach to something that matters. Evenburn builds a graph from load balancers, ingresses, services, pods, service accounts, cloud roles, storage and secrets, then searches for routes through it.

## The short version

Agents are moving from demos into production clusters, and the tools they call are real: a ticketing API, a database, a deploy pipeline, a shell. An agent that reads a poisoned document or a hostile web page can be talked into calling those tools with the permissions its owner gave it. It sits between the agent and its tools, gives each agent a verifiable identity, and checks every tool call against policy before the call goes through.

Runtime policy for AI agents and their tool calls: that is the whole product. It comes from the same place Wickhold Quenchline did. Assume something will go wrong inside the workload, decide ahead of time how far it can go, and make that limit hold on the platform where the workload runs.

Their platform teams already know how to reason about a compromised pod. Tool calls are the part they cannot see. From the network, a hostile tool call and a legitimate one look the same: an authorized POST to an internal service.

Early design partner conversations kept returning to one question: what is the worst this agent could do on a bad day? We call the answer the blast radius of an agent. Leashgate exists to measure that and to make it smaller.

Policies and logs refer to that identity, so "which agent did this" has a precise answer even when ten agents share a framework and a namespace.

Wickhold Quenchline is runtime detection and containment for Kubernetes. An eBPF agent runs on every node, watches what workloads do at the kernel level, and takes a containment action when a policy says to. It has been in general availability since September 2020 and is the product most of our customers start with.

This overview is written for marketers, solutions engineers and anyone drafting a page, talk or reply about the product. It runs longer than a datasheet on purpose. Platform engineers will test what we say against a real cluster, so the detail below is what the product does today, including the parts that are awkward.

## The problem it works on

A runtime incident usually starts small: one pod running a shell it has never run, one process opening a connection nothing else in the namespace opens. The damage comes from the hours between the first signal and someone doing something about it. The 2026 survey gives us the size of that gap:

- 41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]
- the median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]

The survey covered 412 platform and security leaders and was published on April 14, 2026.

Quenchline shortens that gap by moving the first response onto the node. The agent does not wait for a person to read an alert. If the policy allows it, the agent acts on the node and the on-call engineer wakes up to a contained pod and a timeline.

## How it works

### The agent

The agent ships as a DaemonSet from a Helm chart. It loads eBPF programs on each node and attaches to tracepoints, kprobes and LSM hooks covering process execution, file access, network connections and privilege changes. Events move through a BPF ring buffer to a small userspace process that enriches them with pod, namespace, service account and image metadata from containerd and the Kubernetes API.

Requirements:

| Item | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Kernel | Linux 5.8 or later, with BTF enabled |
| Architecture | x86_64 and arm64 |
| cgroups | v2 |
| Container runtime | containerd or CRI-O |
| Kubernetes | The current release and the three before it, self-managed or on a managed Kubernetes service with node access |
| Agent resources | Requests 200m CPU and 256Mi memory, limit 512Mi |

# Content style guide

The house rules for how Wickhold copy is set on the page. Voice lives elsewhere. This is commas, numbers and headlines. Where a rule here seems fussy, it is usually because somebody spent an afternoon arguing about it and the team would rather not repeat that.

The first three sections are the ones reviewers send back most often.

## 1. Headlines

**Headlines are in sentence case.** Capitalize the first word and any proper noun. Everything else is lowercase.

This covers page titles, blog titles, section headings, email subject lines, slide titles, buttons, nav labels, form labels, table headers and any text set over an image. If it looks like a heading, it is one.

|---|---|
| What contain mode does to a running pod | What Contain Mode Does To A Running Pod |
| Wickhold Containment Report 2026 | WICKHOLD CONTAINMENT REPORT 2026 |

- Product names, event names and the report title keep their capitals, as do Kubernetes, Helm, CVE and the rest of the proper vocabulary. `containerd` and `eBPF` keep their lowercase starts even as the first word, though it's nicer to rewrite so that neither opens a headline.

- No full stop on headlines. The tagline is the one exception, and it keeps its full stop everywhere.
- No code formatting in headlines. They break in email clients and in link previews.
- Keep a headline to one idea. If it needs a colon and a dash, it's two headlines.

The old sheet used Title Case for everything over 24px. That went in the rebrand, and pages still carrying it get fixed when someone next touches them.

# Illustration

Everything we draw looks like it was cut from paper and laid on a table. That style came out of the rebrand work, and it is deliberately easy to recognize at a small size next to a competitor's glowing network diagram.

## The style

**Flat cut-paper shapes.** Crisp edges with a slight hand-cut irregularity. Layers can overlap. Depth comes from stacking, and the only shadow allowed is a hard offset shape in one flat, darker tone.

**One Ember focal element.** Exactly one thing in the picture is Ember. That is where the eye goes. Everything else is Soot, Tallow, or a small amount of Whetstone or Verdigris.

**On Tallow or Soot.** Those are the only two grounds for finished illustration. An Ember ground removes the focal element, because nothing can stand out from it. Whetstone and Verdigris grounds look muddy.

**No gradients.** None, anywhere: no soft shadows, glows, blurs, mesh fills or textured airbrush. If a shape needs to look lit, cut a second shape. In review, this is the rule most often broken by accident, usually by a shadow effect left on by default in the design tool or by an export that adds banding.

Also out: outlines around shapes, 3D, isometric projection, photographic textures pasted on shapes, and stock vector packs. We tried isometric cluster diagrams in January. They looked like every infrastructure startup's site, and they required a depth that flat paper cannot give.

## What to draw

The brand idea is a wick: the place where a fire is allowed to exist. Use that vocabulary and its everyday relatives.

| Idea | Shapes that work |
|---|---|
| Containment | A ring around a small flame, a tray, a snuffer held above a wick, a firebreak cut through paper grass |
| Isolation of a workload | One tile lifted out of a grid, a pod shape with a paper band around it |
| Posture and drift (Evenburn) | A row of even flames with one leaning, a level, a line of tiles slightly out of true |

| On-call | A lamp and a mug, a single lit window in a dark paper building |
| Fix order | Steps cut from paper, three stones across a stream |

Keep the flame small. A small flame contained is the entire idea, and a large one means disaster, so the flame should stay well under a tenth of the frame. If the concept seems to need a wall of fire, the concept is wrong.

Wickhold photography looks like it was taken by someone who was already in the room.

Noor Eskelund, Head of Brand. Written for the February 2026 rebrand, rewritten in April after the Containment Report went out, last edited in June. Comments go to #brand-review in Slack.

## Start at 3am

Anyone who writes for Wickhold should read an incident channel before writing a line of copy. Kofi Anselm's team keeps a few scrubbed transcripts for new hires. Skip the panic at the top of the thread and find the messages from whoever is running the incident. They tend to look like this:

> 03:14 UTC. A pod in `checkout` started a shell it has no reason to start.
> 03:14 UTC. Wickhold Quenchline froze the process and isolated the pod's network.
> 03:22 UTC. Rest of the namespace is quiet. Still unknown how the shell got there.
> Reading the image history now. Next update 03:45.

That is the voice. It says what happened, what is contained and what is next, in that order, and it stops. It has timestamps where other writers have adjectives. It admits the thing it does not know in the same flat tone as the thing it does. The person writing it is tired and is not going to make their tiredness your problem. Forty people are reading, half of them frightened, and the frightened ones calm down because of how the message is written.

Maren Tolliver and Dov Achterberg were on-call infrastructure leads before they founded this company in Denver in 2019. The voice is theirs by inheritance. The 2026 brand made it official: a wick is the one place a fire is allowed to exist. Production will catch fire in small ways, on ordinary nights, for dull reasons. The mission is to keep small failures from becoming big ones, and the copy should sound like it was written by people who consider that a normal day's work.

## The character

Wickhold is someone who has been paged more often than you have and is not going to bring it up.

**Unhurried.** Nothing in our copy is urgent. A page that hurries the reader is using the same trick as the alert fatigue they came to us to get away from.

**Exact.** "Isolated the pod's network" beats "took action". "220 nodes" beats "at scale". If two engineers would argue over what a sentence means, it isn't finished.

**Unimpressed by itself.** The product is useful. Copy that gasps at it reads as though the writer has not seen it fail. We have seen it fail, and the release notes say so.

**On your side of the pager.** The reader is a peer on the same rota, and we write to them as someone who could take the next shift. ## Banned terms

There are thirteen. They stay out of headlines, body copy, decks, alt text and speaker notes that leave the building. When one shows up in a draft it usually marks the spot where the writer ran out of facts, so deleting it rarely fixes the sentence. Find the fact.

| Term | Why it is out | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| seamless | Putting an eBPF agent on every node has seams: a kernel check, a Helm upgrade, a stretch in observe mode. Platform engineers know this and stop reading when told otherwise. | Say what the rollout takes. |
| robust | Strong against what? The word claims a result and skips the test. | Name the failure the thing survived. |
| leverage | A finance word doing a job that "use" does for free. | Use "use". |
| best-in-class | No class, no judge, no source. It cannot pass "say the number, then stop". | Give the figure and where it came from. |
| next-gen | Every product in this market has been next-gen at some point. The word ages the day it ships. | Say what it does on a node today. |
| single pane of glass | Our readers have been sold this pane many times and own several. It also describes watching, and the job here is containing. | Name the screen and what it shows. |
| holistic | Usually covering for a gap. If something spans cloud and cluster, those two words are shorter and checkable. | List what is covered. |
| unlock | Implies the customer's own work was locked up and we hold the key. Drags padlocks into the room as well. | Say what the reader can now do. |
| empower | The readers already have root. Nobody here hands out power. | Say what changed for them, in a verb they would use. |
| cutting-edge | A claim about us, and an undated one. eBPF is well past being new, and that is one reason it is safe to run in production. | Name the technique. |
| game-changing | An incident is nobody's game, and the claim has no number attached. | Give the before and after. |
| prevent all | A promise no security product can keep. Includes "prevents all", which is the same promise with better grammar. | See the verbs below. |
| stop all | Same promise, same problem. A CISO who reads this line once will discount the rest of the page. | See the verbs below. |

The prose test: if a sentence still reads as true after you swap the product for a toaster, it needed a fact and got an adjective.

> Wickhold is the runtime security company for teams that run Kubernetes.
> [See how it works]

Bad, from a 2025 agency concept:

> **Next-level cloud security for the modern enterprise**
> One powerful platform. Total confidence. Peace of mind at every layer of your stack.

Nothing in that hero says what the software does. It would fit a mattress company if you swapped "stack" for "bed".

"}, {"chunk_id": "c954e1a8-3bea-4b8c-9f2e-9284e8e1cfd0", "document_id": "ab4b093b-d68f-4576-9f75-861d2e99a564", "relative_path": "brand/channels/landing-page-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["Landing pages", "Proof"], "start_line": 79, "end_line": 88, "content": "## Proof

Each number sits with its source in the same block, so nobody has to scroll to a footnote to check it. These are approved as written:

- Lowmoor Credit Union, 220 nodes: time to contain fell from 4 hours to 11 minutes.
- Ostler Grocers, 1,900 nodes: 63% fewer open critical misconfigurations in 90 days.
- Under 2% CPU overhead on a typical node in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026.

Don't round them, combine them or place two customers' numbers in one sentence. One page gets one customer story. Stacking every number we have makes the page feel like a pitch deck, and readers trust a single detailed result more.

"}, {"chunk_id": "d7e32a81-295b-4582-b2b6-886d3e810933", "document_id": "ab4b093b-d68f-4576-9f75-861d2e99a564", "relative_path": "brand/channels/landing-page-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["Landing pages", "How-it-works blocks"], "start_line": 89, "end_line": 104, "content": "## How-it-works blocks

This is where the two audiences differ most. For engineers, show the thing itself. A short command block costs few words and earns more trust than a paragraph:

> **Install in observe mode**
> `helm install quenchline wickhold/quenchline --set agent.mode=observe`
> The agent attaches to each node. Nothing is contained until you change the mode.

For security leaders, give steps in terms of time and ownership:

> **Week one:** Quenchline runs in observe mode on one cluster.
> **Weeks two to four:** Your team reviews what it would have done.
> **After week four:** You decide which namespaces move to contain mode.

Both describe the same rollout. Neither should use a diagram that needs a paragraph to explain it.

"}, {"chunk_id": "99b64151-dd64-4f1d-afb3-b4f3e8dbee05", "document_id": "ab4b093b-d68f-4576-9f75-861d2e99a564", "relative_path": "brand/channels/landing-page-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["Landing pages", "FAQ"], "start_line": 105, "end_line": 114, "content": "## FAQ

Pull questions from sales calls, not from what we wish people asked. Answer in two sentences or fewer. A good FAQ answers the objection that would otherwise stop the form.

> **Will this take down production?**
> In observe mode, Wickhold Quenchline takes no action. You choose when and where contain mode starts.

> **How much overhead does the agent add?**
> Under 2% CPU overhead on a typical node in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026.

"}, {"chunk_id": "290018fd-fad0-4cf5-b375-94a2808fb554", "document_id": "ab4b093b-d68f-4576-9f75-861d2e99a564", "relative_path": "brand/channels/landing-page-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["Landing pages", "Matching the ad"], "start_line": 115, "end_line": 118, "content": "## Matching the ad

Paid pages must repeat the promise of the ad that sent the visitor there, in nearly the same words. If the ad says "fix order for misconfigurations", the headline says it too. Demand gen writes the ad and the hero together, in the same doc, so they don't drift. We clone a page per ad group only when the message differs. One page per keyword produced 60 near-identical pages in 2025, and the web team spent a month consolidating them.

"}, {"chunk_id": "1d93fc0d-d2cf-4ced-9b45-8e7998ccb7ff", "document_id": "ab4b093b-d68f-4576-9f75-861d2e99a564", "relative_path": "brand/channels/landing-page-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["Landing pages", "Forms"], "start_line": 119, "end_line": 125, "content": "## Forms

- Report pages are ungated as of April 2026. We ran the 2025 report behind a form and sales complained about lead quality for months.
- Demo forms: work email, company, cluster count. Three fields. We tested five, and completions dropped enough that nobody wanted a second test.
- Don't ask for job title. Enrichment handles it.
- The thank-you page tells people exactly what happens next and when. "A solutions engineer will reply within one business day" is what we can actually keep.

"}, {"chunk_id": "d9f2e784-f2b4-4f9e-b5e6-d57329727181", "document_id": "ab4b093b-d68f-4576-9f75-861d2e99a564", "relative_path": "brand/channels/landing-page-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["Landing pages", "Pricing on pages"], "start_line": 126, "end_line": 129, "content": "## Pricing on pages

Product pages link to the pricing page and don't repeat its contents. Tiers change, and the pages that repeat them never get updated. Paid-search pages for pricing queries can show a short tier summary pulled from the pricing page, reviewed by Priit before launch.

"}, {"chunk_id": "d97e9a51-4ed8-4abd-8345-0e8776039628", "document_id": "ab4b093b-d68f-4576-9f75-861d2e99a564", "relative_path": "brand/channels/landing-page-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["Landing pages", "Build and review"], "start_line": 130, "end_line": 140, "content": "## Build and review

1. Brief, with Noor's OK on audience and goal.
2. Copy in a shared doc with a word count at the top. Over 500 goes back.
3. Claims check by Priit, with sources pasted next to each claim.
4. Design and build. Web team needs five business days for a new layout and two for an existing one.
5. Staging review on a phone first. Most paid traffic arrives there.
6. Launch, then a check at two weeks: is anyone completing the form, and where do they drop off?

Use the existing layouts when you can. We have three (product, campaign and report) and each has been tested for load speed and for the mobile form. A page built from scratch needs a reason, and "it's a special campaign" isn't one.

"}, {"chunk_id": "a55aa74f-5cd7-4ad5-b930-7c95b442740a", "document_id": "ab4b093b-d68f-4576-9f75-861d2e99a564", "relative_path": "brand/channels/landing-page-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["Landing pages", "Old pages"], "start_line": 141, "end_line": 143, "content": "## Old pages

Any page without traffic for six months gets redirected. Campaign pages get an end date at launch. In the 2026 rebrand cleanup, the web team found pages from 2023 still live and indexed, which is how you end up with a stale claim ranking above the current one. Put the end date in the brief.
"}]}

{"channel": "email", "passages": [{"chunk_id": "5f590c06-fa98-48f5-82ff-5c20b8a3ac8f", "document_id": "ff395e4b-44dd-4972-9124-e1dfbb83733f", "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["Email playbook"], "start_line": 1, "end_line": 4, "content": "# Email playbook

Owner: Ilse Varga-Holm's team (lifecycle). Rewritten for the March 2026 platform migration, revised September 2026.

"}, {"chunk_id": "60fd8029-020c-42ea-8ffa-c11621d95fe2", "document_id": "ff395e4b-44dd-4972-9124-e1dfbb83733f", "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "The short version"], "start_line": 5, "end_line": 15, "content": "## The short version

| Thing | Limit |
|---|---|
| Email length | 220 words at most, body text, including the sign-off |
| Subject line | 48 characters at most, counted with spaces |
| Links | One main action. More links are fine in a newsletter, and a second link is fine in a customer notice |
| Sends per contact | Two marketing sends a week at most, customer notices excluded |

The 48-character limit comes from the phone inbox preview, where the back half of a longer subject gets cut. We pulled a sample of opens in early 2026 and most were on phones, so the preview is the version people actually read.

"}, {"chunk_id": "f83751e4-c684-4b91-ae78-8575ba2d6497", "document_id": "ff395e4b-44dd-4972-9124-e1dfbb83733f", "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "What we send"], "start_line": 16, "end_line": 29, "content": "## What we send

**Monthly newsletter.** Goes to everyone opted in, second Tuesday of the month. One lead item, three short items, nothing about us that we wouldn't want to read ourselves. Engineers are the bulk of this list, so it can carry a command or a config snippet.

**Nurture tracks.** Separate tracks for CISOs and platform leads, triggered by report downloads and demo requests. Four to six emails over about six weeks. Sales gets an alert on replies. If a contact opens a sales conversation, the track stops.

**Product announcements.** Goes to customers first, prospects a day later. New capabilities, deprecations, and anything that changes how a customer's agents behave. Deprecations go out at least 60 days ahead.

**Customer notices.** Security advisories, CVE guidance, scheduled maintenance. These bypass frequency caps and unsubscribe groups. Dov or a named engineer signs. Marketing can edit for clarity but never holds one back for scheduling reasons.

**Event email.** Slow Burn Summit and Field Day invites and reminders. The events team writes, lifecycle sends.

**Founder notes.** Maren writes to customers about twice a year, usually around pricing or product direction. It comes from her address. A reply goes to her, and she reads them.

"}, {"chunk_id": "553e84fa-ba99-4e6f-9d4b-fb35f8dc8671", "document_id": "ff395e4b-44dd-4972-9124-e1dfbb83733f", "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "Subject lines"], "start_line": 30, "end_line": 55, "content": "## Subject lines

Say the content. People decide in about a second, on a phone, in a queue of other things.

Good:

- `Containment Report 2026: where the hours go` (43)
- `Containment Report 2026 is out` (30)
- `Wickhold Quenchline October release notes` (41)
- `Field Day is coming to your city` (32)
- `Wickhold Evenburn: reading an exposure path` (43)
- `CVE note: what to check in your clusters` (40)

Bad, cut off in the preview:

- `Everything your platform team needs to know about runtime containment this quarter`
- `Join us for an exclusive conversation on the future of Kubernetes security`

Bad, vague:

- `A quick update`
- `Thought you'd want to see this`
- `Big news from Wickhold`

Don't use the recipient's company name in a subject. It looked clever for one quarter and then started to look like a phishing test, which is a poor impression for a security vendor. For the same reason avoid `Re:` and `Fwd:` tricks, urgency words and all caps. Security teams train people to distrust that kind of thing, and a share of our list has mail filters tuned to catch it.

"}, {"chunk_id": "9444a373-5e1b-44c8-b229-396932ea45d4", "document_id": "ff395e4b-44dd-4972-9124-e1dfbb83733f", "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "Body"], "start_line": 56, "end_line": 85, "content": "## Body

Most of our email has three parts.

1. **What happened or what's new.** One or two sentences.
2. **Why it matters to this reader.** Two to four sentences. Different for a CISO list and a platform list, which is why the tracks are separate.
3. **What to do.** One button or link. Then the sign-off.

The working drafts are in the email templates, and the merge fields there match the sending platform. Start from a template. A blank page tends to produce an email that's 400 words long.

Good body copy, platform track:

> You downloaded the Containment Report, so here's the practical follow-up. Our rollout guide starts with Wickhold Quenchline in observe mode on one namespace, then moves to contain mode once you've read two to four weeks of would-have-acted events.
>
> It takes about an hour, and the failure modes are listed at the end.

Good body copy, CISO track:

> Decide whether your team tracks time to contain today. Your board will ask how long a runtime incident takes to contain. In our survey of 412 platform and security leaders, the median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].
>
> The report sets out how teams measure that number and what they report upward. If your team doesn't track it, section two is a place to start.

Bad body copy:

> Hope you're having a great week! As a valued member of our community, we wanted to reach out and share some exciting content we think you'll love. In today's rapidly evolving threat landscape, security has never been more important.

Four sentences in and the reader has learned nothing. Cut until the first sentence is the news.

Personalization: first name in the greeting when we have it, and role-based copy through segments. Anything else, like company size, industry or recent page views, stays out of the visible copy. Being told what you browsed by a security company is unsettling.

"}, {"chunk_id": "1975eb41-cb8b-4500-bf9f-f4e741d528a9", "document_id": "ff395e4b-44dd-4972-9124-e1dfbb83733f", "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "Plain text"], "start_line": 86, "end_line": 91, "content": "## Plain text

Every send has a plain-text version, and we check it. Many of our engineers read mail in clients that don't render HTML, or that block images by default. An email must make sense with every image off. Button text must appear as a readable link in the plain-text part, not as `https://wickhold.example/t/8fa3c...` alone.

For the rules on header images, see the visual guidelines.

"}, {"chunk_id": "459b9ef8-bddf-4cff-908d-53322e51e731", "document_id": "ff395e4b-44dd-4972-9124-e1dfbb83733f", "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "Sender and footer"], "start_line": 92, "end_line": 99, "content": "## Sender and footer

- Default from name: `Wickhold`, from `hello@wickhold.example`. Replies go to a monitored queue.
- Newsletter from name: `Kofi at Wickhold`.
- Founder notes: `Maren Tolliver`, from `maren@wickhold.example`.
- Customer notices: `Wickhold Customer Notices`, from `notices@wickhold.example`.
- Footer carries the legal entity, Wickhold, Inc., a Denver postal address and the unsubscribe link.

"}, {"chunk_id": "d3e16b9a-7001-4119-b693-e318a563bf94", "document_id": "ff395e4b-44dd-4972-9124-e1dfbb83733f", "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "Lists and segments"], "start_line": 100, "end_line": 111, "content": "## Lists and segments

| Segment | Who | Tone in one line | Usual sends |
|---|---|---|---|
| Platform | Platform engineers, SREs, DevSecOps | Practical, can carry code | Newsletter, platform nurture, product announcements |
| Security leadership | CISOs, security directors | Short and plain | CISO nurture, report, Summit invite |
| Customers, technical | Named admins and on-call contacts | Facts and steps | Product announcements, customer notices |
| Customers, executive | Sponsors on the account | Short, rarely | Founder notes, Summit invite |
| Event-local | Contacts within driving distance of a Field Day | Friendly, practical | Field Day invite and reminder |

Role tags come from enrichment and are wrong about one time in ten. If a reply says "I'm not a CISO", fix the contact on the day. Never merge the platform and security leadership lists to reach a volume target. We did that for the 2025 report and the CISO list's unsubscribe rate doubled in a single send.

"}, {"chunk_id": "ac2ef319-64a9-42c8-b403-4fe159097fc2", "document_id": "ff395e4b-44dd-4972-9124-e1dfbb83733f", "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "Timing"], "start_line": 112, "end_line": 117, "content": "## Timing

Tuesday to Thursday, 9 to 11am in the recipient's time zone where the platform knows it. Customer notices go when they're ready, at any hour. Avoid the last week of a quarter for prospect sends, because sales wants clean inboxes for their own outreach, and avoid the week of the big cloud-native conference in November unless the send is about the conference.

If a customer notice is going out, hold marketing sends to the affected accounts for 48 hours. Nobody wants a newsletter in the same hour as a CVE note. Lifecycle owns the pause, and the on-call engineer writing the notice tells them in the channel.

"}, {"chunk_id": "a46a0775-894e-42be-977d-0610b7c892ae", "document_id": "ff395e4b-44dd-4972-9124-e1dfbb83733f", "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "Deliverability"], "start_line": 118, "end_line": 121, "content": "## Deliverability

A security vendor's mail gets scanned hard, and a lot of it lands in quarantine. Keep the sending domain authenticated, and check with IT before anyone adds a new sending tool. Avoid link shorteners. Don't attach files. Link to the page instead, as PDFs from vendors are often stripped at the gateway. Contacts with no opens in a year go to the re-engagement note, and if they don't respond, off the list.

"}, {"chunk_id": "5145b09f-4795-4c18-8ba2-f71cc42dda0e", "document_id": "ff395e4b-44dd-4972-9124-e1dfbb83733f", "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "Testing and approvals"], "start_line": 122, "end_line": 135, "content": "## Testing and approvals

Test one thing per send, on lists over about 5,000 contacts. Subject lines first, send time second. We no longer test emoji, since they lost every round in 2025.

Before anything goes out:

1. Send a proof to the seed list, which covers phone, desktop and text-only clients.
2. Click every link. Check that the UTM tags are in place.
3. Check word count and subject length.
4. Lifecycle reviews. Noor reviews any new template or any new claim.
5. Priit reviews customer names, new numbers, and anything about certifications.

Suppressions: exclude open opportunities from nurture, exclude churned customers from product mail, and always exclude contacts on the do-not-contact list that sales keeps. Lists are pulled the morning of the send, not the night before.

"}, {"chunk_id": "b7195205-6479-423b-bbc7-d14ba956b98e", "document_id": "ff395e4b-44dd-4972-9124-e1dfbb83733f", "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "What didn't work"], "start_line": 136, "end_line": 140, "content": "## What didn't work

- Fortnightly newsletter. Unsubscribes rose and we had nothing to say on the off weeks.
- "Webinar replay" emails after every webinar. Replaced by one line in the newsletter.
- A six-email welcome series. Most people stopped opening at the third. Now three emails.
"}]}

{"channel": "linkedin", "passages": [{"chunk_id": "08ed6196-965b-4faa-9751-01ebf0e4f4a2", "document_id": "af2f7190-800c-4853-bae8-1c9d3d57bed5", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook"], "start_line": 1, "end_line": 6, "content": "# LinkedIn playbook

Noor Eskelund. Last edit 12 August 2026, after the Leashgate early access posts. Ask in the brand channel before you ask me by email.

LinkedIn is the one channel where CISOs, platform leads and our own hiring pipeline all look at the same feed. Most of what we post there is read on a phone, between meetings, by someone who has never heard of us. Write for that person.

"}, {"chunk_id": "f1e93386-bd9e-4240-9294-b61ce8701dec", "document_id": "af2f7190-800c-4853-bae8-1c9d3d57bed5", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Who posts"], "start_line": 7, "end_line": 16, "content": "## Who posts

**Company page.** Marketing runs it. Two or three posts a week, Tuesday to Thursday, usually mid-morning Mountain time. Fridays stayed on the calendar through most of 2025 and did nothing, so they came off.

**Maren and Dov.** They post from their own profiles when they have something to say. Marketing can draft, but they rewrite. Do not schedule on their behalf without a yes in writing, and do not reply to comments as them. If a draft of Maren's has been sitting for two weeks, drop it. She has decided.

**Kofi and the DevRel team.** Kofi posts from his own profile about conference talks, open-source eBPF work and whatever broke in the demo cluster. He does not need brand review for those unless a post carries a customer name, a product claim or a number.

**Everyone else.** People can share company posts however they like. We ran an employee amplification program in 2025 with a shared doc of suggested captions. Forty people posted the same sentence on the same morning and it looked exactly like that. We stopped.

"}, {"chunk_id": "e4d55076-3313-4cf2-a4af-45a0ab945f2f", "document_id": "af2f7190-800c-4853-bae8-1c9d3d57bed5", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Format"], "start_line": 17, "end_line": 26, "content": "## Format

- A LinkedIn post is 180 words at most. Count everything, including the link line.
- About the first 200 characters show before the "see more" cut on most phones. The news has to fit in that space.
- Short paragraphs, one to three lines each, with a blank line between them.
- One link per post, at the end, on its own line. We tested putting links in the first comment for six weeks in 2025 and could not see a difference, and it annoyed people, so links stay in the post.
- Tag a customer only after their marketing contact has seen the post. Tag people, not company pages, when a named person spoke or wrote the thing.
- Use bullets only for real lists: three containment actions, the tiers, the steps of a rollout. A post that is all bullets reads as a slide.
- Image guidance sits with the visual rules. Every company page post gets one image, except short hiring notes.

"}, {"chunk_id": "41f8d6b1-1744-475c-b7dd-9cafc7d5a3e6", "document_id": "af2f7190-800c-4853-bae8-1c9d3d57bed5", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Structure"], "start_line": 27, "end_line": 36, "content": "## Structure

Most company posts follow the same order.

1. **The fact.** What shipped, what was measured, what happened. Put the number here if there is one.
2. **The context.** Two or three sentences on why it matters to someone running clusters or answering for them.
3. **The way out.** One link, with a short instruction in front of it.

Then stop. If you have a second point, it is a second post next week.

"}, {"chunk_id": "1539b083-de00-4738-8643-5b57c2f52acf", "document_id": "af2f7190-800c-4853-bae8-1c9d3d57bed5", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Examples"], "start_line": 37, "end_line": 82, "content": "## Examples

Good, report post:

> 41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].
>
> That figure comes from the Wickhold Containment Report 2026, our survey of 412 platform and security leaders. The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].
>
> 7.4 hours is most of an on-call shift, spent on one problem while everything else waits.
>
> Read the report: https://wickhold.example/containment-report

Good, customer post. The numbers are approved and the post leaves them alone:

> Lowmoor Credit Union runs Wickhold Quenchline across 220 nodes. Time to contain fell from 4 hours to 11 minutes.
>
> Quenchline is our runtime detection and containment product for Kubernetes. It uses an eBPF agent to isolate a pod's network, freeze a process or drain a node.
>
> Read the Lowmoor story: https://wickhold.example/customers/lowmoor

Good, product post:

> Wickhold Quenchline contains a known-bad process in a median of 38 seconds in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026.
>
> Lab conditions are kinder than your cluster on a bad night, so start in observe mode and read what it would have done. Then pick the namespaces where contain mode earns its place.
>
> See the rollout guide: https://wickhold.example/docs/rollout

Good, posture post:

> Ostler Grocers cut open critical misconfigurations by 63% in 90 days, across 1,900 nodes.
>

>
> Read the Ostler story: https://wickhold.example/customers/ostler

Good openers for founder posts. Only the first lines are shown here because Maren and Dov write the rest themselves:

> The worst page I ever took was for a disk that had filled up with logs about a disk filling up.

"}, {"chunk_id": "3ad8462a-c1af-4958-9ab6-5ba77d64a220", "document_id": "af2f7190-800c-4853-bae8-1c9d3d57bed5", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Examples"], "start_line": 83, "end_line": 90, "content": "Nothing happened in that post. | Post contains | Who approves | Turnaround |
|---|---|---|
| No claims, no customers (hiring, event logistics) | Anyone on the brand team | Two business days |

| Customer name or result | Noor and Priit Salonen, plus the customer's contact if we tag them | Five business days |

Reply to real questions within one business day, from the company page, in the same plain voice. Sales inquiries go to the sales queue by DM link. Leave vendor pitches alone. If someone corrects a fact and they're right, say so and fix the post.

Paid boosting is decided per post by demand gen. A boosted post goes through the same review as paid copy, even when it started life as an organic one.

{"channel": "x", "passages": [{"chunk_id": "b463cb57-17ad-45be-a529-05c9e37501e7", "document_id": "60c4bd29-2218-48dc-94dd-f8886ac3f1b4", "relative_path": "brand/channels/x-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["X playbook"], "start_line": 1, "end_line": 37, "content": "X playbook
==========

Kofi Anselm / DevRel. Written June 2026 when marketing handed the account over to us. Short on purpose.

The audience on X is platform engineers, SREs and the people who maintain the projects we depend on. Nobody on there is shopping. They follow accounts that post useful things and are funny about once a week.

**Length.** An X post from any Wickhold account is 240 characters at most. The platform allows more. We stop at 240 so a post can be quoted with a comment and still read whole, and because anything longer is usually two thoughts. Count the raw text, including the link as typed.

**Who has the password.** DevRel owns the main account. Marketing queues launch posts and report posts; DevRel reviews them. Noor can pull anything at any time. Two-factor is on the shared vault, and nobody posts from a personal phone without it.

**What goes out**

- Release notes in one line, with a link
- Findings from the Containment Report, one figure per post
- Practical tips: an eBPF gotcha, a kubectl one-liner, something odd about containerd
- Clips from Slow Burn Summit talks and Field Day
- CVE notes when a CVE touches something we ship or something our customers run a lot of, with facts and the fix

About three to five posts a week. More during Summit, fewer in December. Nothing goes out just to fill a slot in the calendar.

**What a good post looks like**

One thought. A concrete noun in the first few words. If there is a link, it comes last.

Good:

> Wickhold Quenchline can drain a node for you if your policy says so. It will not write the postmortem.

> 41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].

> Tip: run contain mode on one namespace first. Observe mode tells you what would have happened. Contain mode tells you who in that namespace forgot to mention a sidecar.

> The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. That is one whole on-call shift, plus a sandwich.

> Wickhold Evenburn's fix order will not make the list shorter. It will tell you which line to start on.

"}, {"chunk_id": "3c5d7e1c-9809-4a19-bba8-13e9c96d32b0", "document_id": "60c4bd29-2218-48dc-94dd-f8886ac3f1b4", "relative_path": "brand/channels/x-playbook.md", "heading_path": ["X playbook"], "start_line": 38, "end_line": 56, "content": "> Wickhold Leashgate, in early access: tool-call policy for AI agents, with agent identity on every call. It limits what a compromised agent can do. Request access: https://wickhold.example/leashgate

Bad, too long and too many ideas:

> Runtime security is more important than ever as Kubernetes adoption accelerates, which is why we're excited to share that our platform gives teams everything they need across detection, posture and policy, all in one place, and we'd love to show you how it works.

Bad, reads like an ad that wandered onto the timeline:

> Is your cluster safe? Book a demo today and see the difference.

**Threads.** Four posts at most, each one under the same 240 limit, and each one has to stand alone because people will only ever see one. Threads are for walkthroughs: how a pod gets isolated, what shows up in the audit log, what happens when the agent restarts. If a thread wants to be longer, it's a blog post, and the thread links to it.

**Replies.** Answer technical questions fast and link to docs rather than pasting paragraphs. Keep support issues out of public replies: ask for a ticket number and take it to the support queue. Don't argue with anyone about eBPF versus sidecars. It has never once ended well.

**Humor.** Dry, about the work, at our own expense or at the expense of YAML. Never at the expense of a person or a team having a bad day.

**Dropped.** We ran a "Friday failure" series in spring 2026 where engineers sent in their worst outage stories. Good engagement, but it took hours of editing each week to remove anything identifying, so it ended after five rounds. If a Field Day produces a good story and the teller says yes, post it as a one-off.

**Scheduling.** Launch posts are scheduled. Everything else is posted live by whoever is on the DevRel rota, because scheduled tips have a way of going out in the middle of someone else's bad news. If something big is happening in the industry, pause the queue and ask Kofi.
"}]}
