The mark is a geometric W whose center stroke rises as a wick, tipped by one Ember dot. It says the same thing as the brand idea: a straight, deliberate structure with one small, controlled point of heat at the top. The dot is the only warm thing in the mark, and that is the reason to protect it. Used alongside the wordmark "Wickhold", it forms the lockup, which is the default in most layouts.

There are four approved variants: ink on transparent, reversed on transparent, on a Tallow panel, and on a Soot panel. Exact file specifications, clear space and minimum sizes are in the logo and color addendum. How to choose among the variants for a given layout belongs to the logo-in-context guidance.

The 2024 shield-and-flame logo is retired. It still appears in the archive and in a few old files, and it should not be used in anything new.

The logo appears once in a layout, and it usually doesn't need to be large. Confidence in a mark shows in how much room it's given, so a modest logo with space around it is better than a big one crowded by other elements. In the product, the mark appears in the console header and on the sign-in page. Screens that a customer works in all day don't need it anywhere else.

Two pieces of history are worth keeping in mind. In the first month after launch, the product team shipped a loading state with a flickering dot, and customers read it as an error. It was withdrawn. The dot does not move. And early on, several people tried turning the W into a pattern for backgrounds and swag. The mark loses its meaning when it repeats, because the whole point is that there is one of it. Use it once per layout.

Agents are moving from demos into production clusters, and the tools they call are real: a ticketing API, a database, a deploy pipeline, a shell. An agent that reads a poisoned document or a hostile web page can be talked into calling those tools with the permissions its owner gave it. Leashgate prevents prompt injection from becoming an incident. It sits between the agent and its tools, gives each agent a verifiable identity, and checks every tool call against policy before the call goes through.

Runtime policy for AI agents and their tool calls: that is the whole product. It comes from the same place Wickhold Quenchline did. Assume something will go wrong inside the workload, decide ahead of time how far it can go, and make that limit hold on the platform where the workload runs.

The company did not change what it builds. Quenchline has offered detection and containment since September 2020. What changed is which half of that sentence the brand leads with. In the 2024 identity, the watching came first and containment was a feature. In the 2026 identity, containment is the point and detection is what makes it possible. Detection still matters to buyers and should be described accurately. It just isn't the headline.

Evenburn fits the same logic from the other direction. Posture work reduces how much there is to catch fire, and it gives the team a fix order so that the worst exposure path gets closed first. The story to tell is about keeping the fuel down, and it shouldn't be told as a second, separate product category.

Leashgate extends the idea to AI agents, which now take actions inside customers' environments. An agent with broad tools is a new kind of workload that can make a mistake quickly. Leashgate sets out what that agent may do and keeps a record of what it did. It is in early access, and the position should be described with that in mind: a direction the company is working in, with real customers trying it.

", "end_line": 80, "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "What Wickhold believes", "Admit limits"], "ref": "source_162", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "start_line": 77}, {"content": "## Contrast: 4.5:1 for text

Text on any image or graphic meets at least 4.5:1 against what is directly behind it. We apply the same floor to all sizes, including large headlines. A designer will point out that the web standard relaxes for large type. We know. The single number is easier to check, and a stat card shrinks to thumbnail size in a feed, where large type stops being large. This floor governs images. Layouts follow the logo and color addendum.

Measured ratios for the palette:

| Pair | Ratio | Text allowed? |
|---|---|---|
| Soot on Tallow | 15.5:1 | Yes |
| Tallow on Soot | 15.5:1 | Yes |
| Whetstone on Tallow | 4.8:1 | Yes |
| Verdigris on Soot | 4.5:1 | Yes, just. Test your export |
| Ember on Tallow | 4.1:1 | No |
| Soot on Ember | 3.8:1 | No |
| Ember on Soot | 3.8:1 | No |
| Tallow on Ember | 4.1:1 | No |
| Verdigris on Tallow | 3.4:1 | No |
| Whetstone on Soot | 3.2:1 | No |

This surprises people: Ember does not carry text on our grounds, and no text sits on Ember in an image. Ember is for shapes, rules and the focal element. Headlines on Tallow are Soot. Headlines on Soot are Tallow.

Over a photo, measure against the lightest spot behind the letters for Tallow text and the darkest spot for Soot text. An even-looking dark photo often has one bright lamp right under the word. If the text fails anywhere, put it on a solid Soot or Tallow panel. Do not add a gradient scrim: our illustration and graphic language has no gradients, and scrims tend to fail at their edges anyway.

", "end_line": 36, "heading_path": ["X images", "Replies and threads"], "ref": "source_167", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/x-image.md", "start_line": 30}, {"content": "## When the news is ours

We will have our own bad days: a bad agent release, a late fix, a false containment that drained a node it should have left alone. The values cover this before anything else does. Say what happened. Contain first. Admit limits. Leave it better for the next on-call.

In practice:

- Lead with what happened to the customer's systems, in their terms.
- Use "we" and an active verb. "We shipped a policy update that drained nodes it should not have." "An issue occurred" is not a sentence we publish.
- Apologize once, plainly, in one short sentence. Then get on with the facts.
- Say what is still unknown.
- Say when the next update comes, and hit that time even if there's nothing new.

Dov signs off anything technical. Priit Salonen reads anything that touches a contract. Nobody in marketing edits the facts for tone.

", "end_line": 9, "heading_path": ["WICKHOLD SECURITY BRAND GUIDELINES"], "ref": "source_173", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_v3_FINAL.md", "start_line": 1}, {"content": "## Banned terms

There are thirteen. They stay out of headlines, body copy, decks, alt text and speaker notes that leave the building. When one shows up in a draft it usually marks the spot where the writer ran out of facts, so deleting it rarely fixes the sentence. Find the fact.

| Term | Why it is out | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| seamless | Putting an eBPF agent on every node has seams: a kernel check, a Helm upgrade, a stretch in observe mode. Platform engineers know this and stop reading when told otherwise. | Say what the rollout takes. |
| robust | Strong against what? The word claims a result and skips the test. | Name the failure the thing survived. |
| leverage | A finance word doing a job that "use" does for free. | Use "use". |
| best-in-class | No class, no judge, no source. It cannot pass "say the number, then stop". | Give the figure and where it came from. |
| next-gen | Every product in this market has been next-gen at some point. The word ages the day it ships. | Say what it does on a node today. |
| single pane of glass | Our readers have been sold this pane many times and own several. It also describes watching, and the job here is containing. | Name the screen and what it shows. |
| holistic | Usually covering for a gap. If something spans cloud and cluster, those two words are shorter and checkable. | List what is covered. |
| unlock | Implies the customer's own work was locked up and we hold the key. Drags padlocks into the room as well. | Say what the reader can now do. |
| empower | The readers already have root. Nobody here hands out power. | Say what changed for them, in a verb they would use. |
| cutting-edge | A claim about us, and an undated one. eBPF is well past being new, and that is one reason it is safe to run in production. | Name the technique. |
| game-changing | An incident is nobody's game, and the claim has no number attached. | Give the before and after. |
| prevent all | A promise no security product can keep. Includes "prevents all", which is the same promise with better grammar. | See the verbs below. |
| stop all | Same promise, same problem. A CISO who reads this line once will discount the rest of the page. | See the verbs below. |

The prose test: if a sentence still reads as true after you swap the product for a toaster, it needed a fact and got an adjective.

", "end_line": 26, "heading_path": ["Word list", "Banned terms"], "ref": "source_174", "relative_path": "brand/voice/word-list.md", "start_line": 5}, {"content": "## Early access: what partners get

- Named engineering contact and a shared Slack channel
- Monthly policy review with the product team
- Roadmap input on tool adapters and approval workflows
- Support during business hours, Denver time. There is no SLA during early access
- Limit of a small number of clusters per customer, agreed in the addendum

What we ask in return: a named platform owner, a real agent in at least a staging environment, and permission to learn from anonymized policy patterns.

", "end_line": 135, "heading_path": ["Wickhold Leashgate", "Early access: what partners get"], "ref": "source_175", "relative_path": "brand/products/leashgate-overview.md", "start_line": 126}, {"content": "## What it does not do

- It does not decide whether an allowed call was wise. A policy that allows `tickets.update` allows a bad ticket update.

", "end_line": 125, "heading_path": ["Wickhold Leashgate", "What it does not do"], "ref": "source_176", "relative_path": "brand/products/leashgate-overview.md", "start_line": 118}, {"content": "## 3. Values

There are four, and they are written the way an on-call lead would say them.

**Say what happened.**
Report the event in plain order: what occurred, what was affected, what was done, what is next. This applies to incident reports, release notes, customer emails and the company's own mistakes. When a release goes badly, the customer note says so in the first sentence.

Good: "The last Wickhold Quenchline release raised CPU use on nodes running older kernels. A fix shipped on Tuesday. Here is how to check whether you were affected."

Bad: "We're always working to improve performance, and our latest update includes important enhancements."

**Contain first.**
In an incident, limit the damage before explaining it. In marketing, the same ordering applies: the first thing a reader gets is the thing that helps them, and the story of how it came about can wait. The value also sets the company's posture. Wickhold talks about containing, limiting and slowing. A promise of a world with no incidents is a promise no honest vendor can keep.

Good: "At Lowmoor Credit Union, time to contain fell from 4 hours to 11 minutes across 220 nodes."

That example gives the result with no adjectives around it and leaves the reader to decide what it means.

**Admit limits.**
Every product has edges, and engineers find them within a week. Naming a limit in advance costs less than having a customer discover it during a bad night, and it makes everything else the company says easier to believe.

Good: "Wickhold Quenchline works at runtime. It does not review code before it ships."

**Leave it better for the next on-call.**
This one comes straight from the founders. When an on-call shift ends, the next person should find the runbook updated, the noisy alert tuned and the handoff note written. Inside marketing it means naming source files sensibly, recording why a decision was made, and putting a correction in the document that was wrong and not only in a thread. It is why the "tried and dropped" list in section 1 exists.

", "end_line": 108, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "3. Values"], "ref": "source_177", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 83}, {"content": "## One screen, worked through

The request: show that Quenchline can freeze a process during an incident.

First attempt: the whole incident page at 1600x1000, with the timeline, three tiles, a side panel of pod details and a chat widget from the demo tenant. As a column image it was unreadable, and the one thing that mattered was a small status chip.

Second attempt: a crop to the timeline row showing the containment action and the status chip, with the page title kept above it. One Ember ring on the chip. One callout: "Process frozen, evidence kept". It reads at column width and it says one thing. That is the standard to aim for.

", "end_line": 94, "heading_path": ["Product UI screenshots", "One screen, worked through"], "ref": "source_178", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/product-ui-screenshots.md", "start_line": 87}, {"content": "## Preferred terms

**Workload, not asset.** Customers run workloads, and that is the word they use in their own runbooks. "Asset" comes from inventory spreadsheets and suggests a thing that sits still. A workload moves, restarts and misbehaves, which is why it needs a runtime product. Inside the marketing team "asset" still means a blog post or an image file; that use never reaches a customer.

**Contain, limit and slow, rather than prevent.** This is the company's argument in three verbs. Something will go wrong on a Tuesday night regardless of what anyone buys. Wickhold Quenchline contains what is already running. Wickhold Evenburn limits exposure. Wickhold Leashgate limits what an agent can reach. "Slow" is the honest verb when the action buys time and does not end the problem. Also keep "eliminate" and "eradicate" out of it; they are "prevent" in a bigger coat.

Use "contain" only when a containment action actually happens. Detection on its own is detection.

One exception came out of a release-notes review. A line saying a patch prevents a crash in the agent is describing our own bug, so it can stay. The rule covers promises about what happens to customers, and a changelog entry makes none.

**Customers, not clients.** Clients have an account manager and a lunch. Customers run our agent in production and page us. A "client" in the software sense stays: `kubectl` is a client, an email client is a client. "Users" is fine when you mean the people logged in to the console, because a customer is the whole company.

When two sources conflict, the higher one on this list wins:

1. **Legal-approved claims.** The approved claims, certification status, regional rules and customer quote policy owned by Priit Salonen, General Counsel.
2. **These 2026 guidelines**, together with the logo and color addendum, which has the same standing.
3. **Channel playbooks.** The working guides for each channel.
4. **Everything else.** This includes the voice and style documents, messaging, personas, product overviews, templates, sales material, meeting notes and Slack.

So the order is: legal-approved claims, then the 2026 guidelines, then channel playbooks, then everything else.

A lower source is not void. It applies wherever nothing above it speaks to the question. A template's rule, or a decision recorded in meeting notes or Slack by the person who owns the topic, is followed like any other rule until a higher source contradicts it. ", "end_line": 467, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "11. Governance", "Order of authority"], "ref": "source_181", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 455}, {"content": "## Founder voice and brand voice

There are two voices at Wickhold, and they have one hard line between them.

**Founder voice is first person singular, and it is signed.** Maren writes as "I". Her posts carry her name. She gets to have feelings and doubts, tell a story from a bad night in 2017, and be wrong in public. Dov's technical posts work the same way and are signed "Dov".

**Brand voice never says "I" or "we think".** Website, product pages, company LinkedIn, the company X account, email, decks, reports: no first person singular, ever. "We believe", "we feel" and "in our view" are "we think" in different shoes, and they go too.

**Brand voice uses "Wickhold" or "we" for facts only.** Things that happened, things that are true of the company, things a lawyer could check.

| Fine in brand voice | Not in brand voice |
|---|---|
| We renewed SOC 2 Type II in January 2026. | We think SOC 2 matters. |
| Wickhold serves more than 140 customers. | I've talked to a lot of platform teams. |
| Containment is where incidents are won or lost. | We believe containment is where incidents are won or lost. |

The third row is the useful one. Brand voice still holds opinions. It states them as flat sentences, the way the on-call lead does, and lets the reader disagree. "We think" adds nothing except a hedge.

Practicalities. Nobody else writes as "I" in Wickhold content. Kofi's developer posts and anything from the wider team run in brand voice under a byline, because a byline is credit and a founder post is a person speaking for themselves. Customer quotes are quotes and say whatever was approved. If the content team drafts for Maren, she reads it and changes it before her name goes on, and a post that she has not read does not go out. In the spring a joint Maren-and-Dov byline was tried on one post; "I" became unreadable after two paragraphs, so that was dropped. One author per post.

The library's metadata does not catch everything. Some old or off-brand photos are sitting in the library with an empty `restrictions` field, because nobody ever marked them. Some of them have sensible titles and tags. A clean record tells you nobody objected. You still have to look at the picture.

Open it at full size and ask:

1. **What color are the shadows?** Ours fall warm, toward brown or neutral. If the shadows go blue, it belongs to the 2024 era or to a stock site. The look of that era was bright, cold and very blue, and it clashes hard with Ember on the same page.
2. **Is the light real?** Even, shadowless light across a whole room means a set or a heavy edit.
3. **Is anybody posing?** Direct eye contact with the lens, crossed arms, a group laughing at a laptop: reject.
4. **Could this photo appear on any company's site?** If yes, reject it. We want to see a detail that belongs to this work.

If a photo fails one of these and has no restriction on it, do not use it, and tell Brand so the record can be updated. That second part helps the next person.

Examples from recent draft reviews:

| Draft used | Verdict | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Rack aisle, cold blue light, faint haze, no people | Rejected | Clean metadata, wrong look |
| Woman with headset smiling at the camera in a bright open office | Rejected | Posed and generic |
| Engineer's hands, laptop glow, dim closet behind | Approved | Warm, specific, one focal point |
| Three people at a whiteboard, one mid-gesture, late sun on the wall | Approved | Available light, real moment |

A title that says what the reader will get. Then the intro. Then three to five sections with descriptive headings. Then an ending that tells the reader what to do on Monday.

Titles we liked:

- Contain mode, one namespace at a time
- What drift looks like after a Helm upgrade
- The six hours after detection
- Writing your first tool-call policy for Wickhold Leashgate, in early access

Titles we rewrote:

- "5 Kubernetes Security Mistakes You're Making Right Now" became "Five findings we see in most new clusters"
- "Everything You Need To Know About eBPF" became "What our eBPF agent can and can't see"

Section headings should still make sense if they're all someone reads. "Background" and "The solution" tell the reader nothing.

Pinned for the web team after three separate spellings turned up on one page.

Full form on first mention, short form after. First mention means the first place the name appears in a piece, and a headline counts.

| First mention | After that |
|---|---|
| Wickhold Quenchline | Quenchline |
| Wickhold Evenburn | Evenburn |
| Wickhold Leashgate | Leashgate |

One capital each. Never QuenchLine, EvenBurn or LeashGate. No internal caps, no hyphens, no all-caps in slides or nav.

Each piece starts over. A blog post that says Wickhold Quenchline does not earn the short form in the email promoting it.

Evenburn took its name on March 2, 2026. Don't write the former name in current copy, including "formerly" lines. Support handles customers who still ask for it.

Right: "Wickhold Evenburn ranks drift by exposure path. Evenburn does not contain anything at runtime."

Wrong: "Evenburn ranks drift" as the opening line, with the full name saved for the footer.

Nav labels and pricing table rows can use the short form. The page's first heading or sentence still uses the full one.

Never combine products into one name ("Quenchline-Evenburn suite"). There is no suite. If you mean more than one, name them.

**Company:** Wickhold. "Wickhold Security" retired with the rebrand on February 10, 2026. Wickhold, Inc. appears in contracts and legal footers and nowhere else.

**Lowercase, always:** contain mode, observe mode, containment action, default containment policy, drift, exposure path, fix order, tool-call policy, agent identity. These are concepts, not features with a logo.

**Capitalized:** tiers (Core, Team, Enterprise), Slow Burn Summit, Field Day, Wickhold Containment Report. "The report" on second reference, lowercase. Series A and Series B take capitals; SOC 2 Type II is set as shown.

Possessives are fine (Quenchline's agent). Skip the article: "Quenchline contains", never "the Quenchline".

The report had a different name before 2025: Wickhold Field Report. Keep that name when citing an edition that carried it. Don't rename old editions.

Feature names don't get "Wickhold" in front of them, and they don't get a trademark symbol. Neither do the products in running copy.

Lowercase product names only in code, where the tool demands it.

Never say "GDPR compliant". Not about Wickhold, its products, its customers' deployments or any feature. The ban began with EU and UK copy and it now applies everywhere, including US pages that a European buyer can obviously read.

The approved wording is:

> Wickhold supports customers' GDPR obligations.

Use it as written. GDPR obligations belong to the controller and the processor and depend on what they do with the data. No vendor product can make a customer compliant, and a regulator or a procurement lawyer will read the phrase as a promise.

Variants that have turned up in drafts, all refused:

- "GDPR-ready"
- "fully GDPR aligned"
- "compliant with EU privacy law"
- "UK GDPR certified"

If a UK reader needs the point spelled out, the approved sentence covers UK GDPR. Do not add a second claim.

Examples:

| Bad | Good |
|---|---|
| Our GDPR compliant platform keeps EU workloads safe. | Wickhold supports customers' GDPR obligations. |
| Quenchline makes your clusters GDPR compliant. | Wickhold Quenchline records each containment action with a timestamp. Wickhold supports customers' GDPR obligations. |

A word on tone. European security buyers we've met through Field Day meetups tend to ask for the document and not the promise, so a short, flat statement does better than a paragraph about how seriously we take privacy. If a page has one line on GDPR, the approved sentence is that line. Don't surround it with "privacy-first" or "by design", which raise the same problem in softer words.

", "end_line": 34, "heading_path": ["Regional rules: EU and UK copy", "GDPR wording"], "ref": "source_237", "relative_path": "brand/legal/regional-rules-eu-uk.md", "start_line": 7}, {"content": "## Terminals and CLI output

Engineers often trust a terminal capture over a dashboard. Use a plain terminal at a normal size with IBM Plex Mono, on a Soot background, with the prompt trimmed to `$`. The command has to be real and its output has to be pasted from a real run in the demo environment. Do not edit output to shorten it. Use `...` on its own line if you must cut something, and do so only where the cut changes nothing. Remove usernames, internal hostnames and tokens by fixing the environment and running it again.

", "end_line": 86, "heading_path": ["Product UI screenshots", "Terminals and CLI output"], "ref": "source_238", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/product-ui-screenshots.md", "start_line": 83}, {"content": "### Tool-call policy

A tool-call policy is a declarative rule set, stored as a Kubernetes custom resource. It says which agent may call which tool, with what arguments, how often, and whether a person must approve first.

```yaml
apiVersion: leashgate.wickhold.example/v1alpha1
kind: ToolCallPolicy
metadata:
  name: support-triage-agent
  namespace: support
spec:
  agentSelector:
    matchLabels:
      agent: support-triage
  defaultAction: deny
  rules:
    - tool: tickets.search
      action: allow
    - tool: tickets.update
      action: allow
      arguments:
        status:
          oneOf: [open, pending, resolved]
      rate: 60/minute
    - tool: crm.export
      action: requireApproval
      approvers: [group:support-leads]
      timeout: 10m
    - tool: shell.*
      action: deny
```

`defaultAction: deny` is the default and we recommend leaving it there. Note the `v1alpha1` in the API version: field names may change during early access, and design partners should expect at least one schema migration.

Three layers, read in this order.

1. **This page.** Applies to everything.
2. **The category.** What kind of image is it? Photo, illustration, icon, logo, product screenshot, chart, social graphic, event graphic, legal and trust imagery, anything showing a person.
3. **The content type.** Where is it going? Blog hero, LinkedIn, X, email header, landing page.

Most images touch one rule from each layer, and some touch two categories. A photo of a staff member at a customer site is photography and consent at once, and it has to pass both.

A lower layer can narrow a higher one. The illustration category accepts several formats, for example, and the blog hero page accepts fewer of them. In that case follow the narrower rule for that placement, and the broader rule stays true everywhere else. A lower layer cannot loosen this page. If a content-type page seems to let you do something this page forbids, bring it to Brand, because one of the two pages is wrong and we want to fix it.

Per-campaign exceptions go through Noor's exception log. Without an entry there, if a campaign needs something new, the rule changes for everybody or the campaign changes.

", "end_line": 20, "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "How the visual rules are layered"], "ref": "source_263", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "start_line": 7}, {"content": "## The style

**Flat cut-paper shapes.** Crisp edges with a slight hand-cut irregularity. Layers can overlap. Depth comes from stacking, and the only shadow allowed is a hard offset shape in one flat, darker tone.

**One Ember focal element.** Exactly one thing in the picture is Ember. That is where the eye goes. Everything else is Soot, Tallow, or a small amount of Whetstone or Verdigris.

**On Tallow or Soot.** Those are the only two grounds for finished illustration. An Ember ground removes the focal element, because nothing can stand out from it. Whetstone and Verdigris grounds look muddy.

**No gradients.** None, anywhere: no soft shadows, glows, blurs, mesh fills or textured airbrush. If a shape needs to look lit, cut a second shape. In review, this is the rule most often broken by accident, usually by a shadow effect left on by default in the design tool or by an export that adds banding.

Also out: outlines around shapes, 3D, isometric projection, photographic textures pasted on shapes, and stock vector packs. We tried isometric cluster diagrams in January. They looked like every infrastructure startup's site, and they required a depth that flat paper cannot give.

", "end_line": 22, "heading_path": ["Illustration", "The style"], "ref": "source_264", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/illustration.md", "start_line": 11}, {"content": "## Body

Most of our email has three parts.

1. **What happened or what's new.** One or two sentences.
2. **Why it matters to this reader.** Two to four sentences. Different for a CISO list and a platform list, which is why the tracks are separate.
3. **What to do.** One button or link. Then the sign-off.

The working drafts are in the email templates, and the merge fields there match the sending platform. Start from a template. A blank page tends to produce an email that's 400 words long.

Good body copy, platform track:

> You downloaded the Containment Report, so here's the practical follow-up. Our rollout guide starts with Wickhold Quenchline in observe mode on one namespace, then moves to contain mode once you've read two to four weeks of would-have-acted events.
>
> It takes about an hour, and the failure modes are listed at the end.

Good body copy, CISO track:

> Decide whether your team tracks time to contain today. Your board will ask how long a runtime incident takes to contain. In our survey of 412 platform and security leaders, the median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].
>
> The report sets out how teams measure that number and what they report upward. If your team doesn't track it, section two is a place to start.

Bad body copy:

> Hope you're having a great week! As a valued member of our community, we wanted to reach out and share some exciting content we think you'll love. In today's rapidly evolving threat landscape, security has never been more important.

Four sentences in and the reader has learned nothing. Cut until the first sentence is the news.

Personalization: first name in the greeting when we have it, and role-based copy through segments. Anything else, like company size, industry or recent page views, stays out of the visible copy. Being told what you browsed by a security company is unsettling.

**Do not stretch, tint or recolor library files.** Crop freely within the category's limits. Stretching breaks the proportions of the art and recoloring breaks the palette. ", "end_line": 269, "heading_path": ["WICKHOLD SECURITY BRAND GUIDELINES", "6. Our Colors", "How much of each"], "ref": "source_277", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_v3_FINAL.md", "start_line": 263}, {"content": "## What Leashgate does

Leashgate sits between an agent and the tools it calls. It works with three concepts.

**Agent identity.** Each agent gets its own identity, separate from the human who launched it and from the service account of the pod it runs in. Logs and policies refer to that identity, so "which agent did this" has an answer.

**Tool-call policy.** A team writes down which tools an agent may call, with which arguments, on which targets. A support agent may read a customer record but may not export a table. A deployment agent may restart a service in staging but may not touch production. Calls outside the policy are blocked and logged.

**Containment.** A call that breaks policy can trigger the same kind of response platform teams already use with Quenchline. If an agent starts behaving badly, it can be cut off from its tools while a human takes a look, and the rest of the application keeps running.

Put simply, Leashgate limits what a compromised agent can do.

A short example of a tool-call policy, in the shape early access customers are using:

```yaml
agent: support-triage
tools:
  - name: crm.read_record
    allow: true
  - name: crm.export
    allow: false
  - name: tickets.update
    allow: true
    when:
      field: status
on_violation: suspend_agent
```

The format may change during early access. We will tell participants before it does.

", "end_line": 51, "heading_path": ["Wickhold Leashgate enters early access", "What Leashgate does"], "ref": "source_278", "relative_path": "brand/archive/blog/leashgate_early_access_notes.md", "start_line": 22}, {"content": "### With Quenchline

Leashgate can ask Quenchline to act. If a policy marks a repeated-denial pattern as suspicious, it can request a containment action, normally isolating the agent pod's network, through the same pipeline Quenchline uses for its own detections. This requires Quenchline on the node. The feature is off by default.

Every decision record goes to the same export path as Quenchline's, so a SIEM rule can correlate a denied tool call with the runtime events around it.

", "end_line": 17, "heading_path": ["Q2 brand review: meeting notes", "Rebrand cleanup status"], "ref": "source_282", "relative_path": "brand/internal/mtg-notes-q2-brand-review.md", "start_line": 9}, {"content": "## The look

Wickhold photography looks like it was taken by someone who was already in the room.

**Available light.** Windows, overhead tubes, the glow of a laptop, a desk lamp. No strobes, ring lights or colored gels. If a room is too dark for the shot, use a longer exposure or find a better room.

**Warm and slightly underexposed.** Think of the last hour of a working day. Skin tones stay warm and natural. Shadows may go deep, though they should not go black across half the frame. If the image histogram crowds the right side, it is too bright for us.

**Working rooms and real infrastructure.** Equipment rooms, cable trays, network closets, a shared office with coffee rings on the table, a laptop open at a kitchen counter during an on-call shift. Places where the work of running Kubernetes actually happens. The subject of a security company's photo library is the people on call and the things they keep running.

**Honest mess.** Leave the cables. Leave the sticky notes (after reading them). A tidied room reads as staged, and staged reads as an advertisement.

Wickhold Security was founded in Denver in March 2019 by Maren Tolliver and Dov Achterberg. Both had spent years as on-call infrastructure leads, and both had the same complaint: by the time anybody knew something was wrong in a cluster, it was already somebody's very long night. Existing tools were built for servers that stayed put, and Kubernetes workloads do anything but.

So they built the tool they wished they'd had. Wickhold Quenchline reached general availability in September 2020, bringing runtime detection and containment to Kubernetes through a lightweight eBPF agent. Our Series A followed in March 2022 at $18M, and with it came Wickhold Tallowatch, extending the same always-on approach to cloud and cluster posture. In June 2024 we closed our $46M Series B, led by Marlbank Partners, to take the platform further and faster.

Today over 80+ teams rely on Wickhold Security to know what is running, what has changed, and what needs attention right now.

When you tell this story, keep these three beats in order:

1. **Founders who carried the pager.** We are operators first.
2. **A product that never blinks.** Continuous beats periodic, every time.
3. **Momentum.** More teams, more funding, more coverage.

---

", "end_line": 108, "heading_path": ["Product UI screenshots", "Metadata for new captures"], "ref": "source_308", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/product-ui-screenshots.md", "start_line": 105}, {"content": "## March 2, 2026: Wickhold Tallowatch is now Wickhold Evenburn

", "end_line": 161, "heading_path": ["Release notes 2026", "March 2, 2026: Wickhold Tallowatch is now Wickhold Evenburn"], "ref": "source_309", "relative_path": "brand/products/release-notes-2026.md", "start_line": 145}, {"content": "## How it relates to what teams already run

Leashgate does not replace network policy, RBAC or Wickhold Quenchline, and it should be added to them. Network policy decides which hosts a pod can reach. RBAC decides what a service account can do in the cluster. Quenchline watches processes and connections on the node. None of them can tell that a permitted HTTPS call to the ticketing system was an agent closing every open ticket. That is the layer Leashgate works at: the named tool, its arguments and the identity making the call.

Because the agent's tool calls pass through Leashgate, every call is also logged with the agent identity attached. Several teams in our design conversations cared more about this record than about blocking. When a security reviewer asks what an agent did last Thursday, the team can answer without searching application logs.

", "end_line": 61, "heading_path": ["Wickhold Leashgate enters early access", "How it relates to what teams already run"], "ref": "source_310", "relative_path": "brand/archive/blog/leashgate_early_access_notes.md", "start_line": 56}, {"content": "## 10. Tried and dropped

", "end_line": 434, "heading_path": ["WICKHOLD SECURITY BRAND GUIDELINES", "9. Putting It All Together", "Data Sheets and Solution Briefs"], "ref": "source_314", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_v3_FINAL.md", "start_line": 422}, {"content": "## 12. Social and email formatting

- No emoji in brand posts or email. Founders can do as they like on their own accounts within reason.
- One link per post. Put it where it reads naturally; shortened links are for tracking and shouldn't appear as bare text where the full domain would fit.
- Line breaks on LinkedIn mark real paragraph breaks. No one-sentence-per-line posts.
- Greeting in email: "Hi Sam," with the first name and a comma, or no greeting for a broadcast. No "Dear". No "Hey there".

", "end_line": 210, "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "12. Social and email formatting"], "ref": "source_315", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "start_line": 202}, {"content": "X playbook
==========

Kofi Anselm / DevRel. Written June 2026 when marketing handed the account over to us. Short on purpose.

The audience on X is platform engineers, SREs and the people who maintain the projects we depend on. Nobody on there is shopping. They follow accounts that post useful things and are funny about once a week.

**Length.** An X post from any Wickhold account is 240 characters at most. The platform allows more. We stop at 240 so a post can be quoted with a comment and still read whole, and because anything longer is usually two thoughts. Count the raw text, including the link as typed.

**Who has the password.** DevRel owns the main account. Marketing queues launch posts and report posts; DevRel reviews them. Noor can pull anything at any time. Two-factor is on the shared vault, and nobody posts from a personal phone without it.

**What goes out**

- Release notes in one line, with a link
- Findings from the Containment Report, one figure per post
- Practical tips: an eBPF gotcha, a kubectl one-liner, something odd about containerd
- Clips from Slow Burn Summit talks and Field Day
- CVE notes when a CVE touches something we ship or something our customers run a lot of, with facts and the fix

About three to five posts a week. More during Summit, fewer in December. Nothing goes out just to fill a slot in the calendar.

**What a good post looks like**

One thought. A concrete noun in the first few words. If there is a link, it comes last.

Good:

> Wickhold Quenchline can drain a node for you if your policy says so. It will not write the postmortem.

> 41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].

> Tip: run contain mode on one namespace first. Observe mode tells you what would have happened. Contain mode tells you who in that namespace forgot to mention a sidecar.

> The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. That is one whole on-call shift, plus a sandwich.

> Wickhold Evenburn's fix order will not make the list shorter. It will tell you which line to start on.

", "end_line": 37, "heading_path": ["X playbook"], "ref": "source_316", "relative_path": "brand/channels/x-playbook.md", "start_line": 1}, {"content": "## Demo data

The demo environment is seeded with fictional clusters, namespaces and workloads. Keep it believable:

- **American spelling** in all copy, including copy going to UK and EU readers. Containerize, not containerise.
- **Oxford comma**, always. It has settled more than one argument in Kubernetes prose, where lists of nouns can double as lists of objects.
- **Active voice** with a named actor, wherever the actor is known. "Wickhold Quenchline drained the node." If the passive is hiding who did it and that person is us, it goes.
- **Tense.** Past for what happened, present for what the product does, and nothing in the future except where a date is public.
- **Contractions** are fine in the blog, on social and in email. Skip them on legal pages and in anything aimed at a board.
- **Colons** are our favorite punctuation mark and they're doing fine. Use them to introduce the fact.
- **Semicolons** at most once a page. If there are two, one wants to be a full stop.
- **Em dashes** rarely in body copy. Most are a full stop that lost its nerve. Spaced en dashes are not a substitute.
- **Parentheses** for the short aside only. If the aside matters, promote it to a sentence.
- **Quotation marks:** double, with commas and full stops inside, American style, except for literal strings in technical writing where the punctuation would change the meaning. Single quotes only inside double.
- **Italics:** titles of reports and the occasional stress only. They disappear on Soot grounds and in email.
- **Bold:** for scanning in long documents, once or twice per section. Bold on a landing page means the design isn't working.
- **Ampersands:** only in proper names. Plain "and" in headlines too.
- **"And/or"** is a legal term. Pick one.
- **Slashes** as a shortcut ("platform/security teams") get rewritten: "platform and security teams".

", "end_line": 48, "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "The two rules that come up every week", "One focal point"], "ref": "source_343", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "start_line": 37}, {"content": "## How it works

Leashgate has two parts, the gateway and the policy controller.

**The gateway** runs as a sidecar next to the agent or as a shared Deployment in the namespace. Agents point their tool endpoints at the gateway, either over HTTP or as an MCP server that proxies upstream MCP servers. For each call, the gateway verifies agent identity, evaluates the tool-call policy, writes a decision record and forwards or refuses the call. A refused call returns a structured error the agent can read, so a well-built agent can recover or ask for help rather than retry in a loop.

**The policy controller** watches `ToolCallPolicy` objects, validates them and distributes them to gateways. Gateways cache the last valid policy. If the gateway cannot evaluate a call for any reason, it refuses it. Leashgate fails closed, which means an outage of the gateway stops the agent's tools. That is the right behavior for a security control, and teams need to plan for it.

Install is one Helm chart, early access users only:

```bash
helm install leashgate wickhold/leashgate \
  --namespace wickhold-system \
  --set earlyAccess.token="$EA_TOKEN" \
  --set gateway.mode=sidecar
kubectl label namespace support leashgate.wickhold.example/inject=enabled
```

Requirements during early access: Kubernetes, any recent release, containerd, and agents that make tool calls over HTTP or MCP. Frameworks that call tools in-process, as plain function calls inside the agent's own memory, are out of scope unless the tool itself is reached over the network.

Every image has alt text. This covers blog images, email images, landing pages, social uploads where the platform offers the field, and images in PDFs. The author of the piece writes it, because the designer usually does not know why the image is there.

Write what the reader would lose if the image failed to load. One or two plain sentences, under about 125 characters when you can manage it. Skip "image of" and "picture of". Do not stuff keywords. Do not paste the `description` field from the library: that describes the file, and alt text describes what the image is doing in this piece.

|---|---|---|
| Photo | "Engineer, Kubernetes, security, on-call, data center" | "An engineer reads a terminal in a dim equipment room." |
| Product screenshot | "Screenshot of dashboard" | "Quenchline shows one pod isolated, with network access removed and the process frozen." |

Charts and screenshots carry the finding in the alt text, and the reader should not need the picture to get the number. If the chart has more than about four values, put the values in a table or the body copy under it and let the alt text state the point.

Wickhold is someone who has been paged more often than you have and is not going to bring it up.

**Unhurried.** Nothing in our copy is urgent. A page that hurries the reader is using the same trick as the alert fatigue they came to us to get away from.

**Exact.** "Isolated the pod's network" beats "took action". "220 nodes" beats "at scale". If two engineers would argue over what a sentence means, it isn't finished.

**Unimpressed by itself.** The product is useful. Copy that gasps at it reads as though the writer has not seen it fail. We have seen it fail, and the release notes say so.

**On your side of the pager.** The reader is a peer on the same rota, and we write to them as someone who could take the next shift. No lecturing, no "did you know", no explaining Kubernetes to people who run it.

What changed in 2026", "Why the company rebranded"], "ref": "source_373", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 11}, {"content": "# Wickhold opens early access to Wickhold Leashgate, runtime policy for AI agents

DENVER, May 2026 — Wickhold today opened early access to Wickhold Leashgate, a new product that applies runtime policy to AI agents and their tool calls. Early access is included in the Enterprise tier, and teams can apply through their account contact. Wickhold has not set a date for general availability.

Teams that run Kubernetes are starting to give AI agents real work: reading logs, opening pull requests, changing configuration, calling internal services. Those agents act with real credentials, and the tools they call are often the same ones an engineer would use. If an agent is manipulated or simply wrong, the damage depends on what it was allowed to reach.

Leashgate treats an agent as a workload with an identity and a boundary. In early access it provides:

- **Agent identity.** Each agent is identified at runtime, separately from the service or person who launched it.
- **Tool-call policy.** Teams define which tools an agent may call and with what limits. Leashgate applies that policy at the moment of the call and records the decision.
- **Blast radius of an agent.** Teams can see what an agent could reach under its current policy, and narrow it before the agent runs.

Leashgate limits what a compromised agent can do. It does not judge what a prompt says, and it does not make an agent's decisions correct. Those limits are deliberate: the product acts on tool calls, where an agent's actions become real.

"I keep hearing the same thing from platform teams: the agents arrived before the policy did," said Maren Tolliver, CEO and co-founder of Wickhold. "We started this company to keep small failures from becoming big ones. An agent with too many permissions is a small failure waiting for a reason. I'd like teams to have a boundary in place before they need one."

"The design is deliberately plain: deny by default, check every tool call, write down the decision," said Dov Achterberg, CTO and co-founder. "I'd rather give early access teams something narrow that behaves predictably and hear from them about what's missing. There's plenty missing. It runs on Kubernetes only for now, for one thing. That's why it's early access."

", "end_line": 18, "heading_path": ["Wickhold opens early access to Wickhold Leashgate, runtime policy for AI agents"], "ref": "source_374", "relative_path": "brand/press/pr-2026-leashgate-early-access.md", "start_line": 1}, {"content": "## Transparency and dark mode

This is where the two audiences differ most. For engineers, show the thing itself. A short command block costs few words and earns more trust than a paragraph:

> **Install in observe mode**
> `helm install quenchline wickhold/quenchline --set agent.mode=observe`
> The agent attaches to each node. Nothing is contained until you change the mode.

For security leaders, give steps in terms of time and ownership:

> **Week one:** Quenchline runs in observe mode on one cluster.
> **Weeks two to four:** Your team reviews what it would have done.

No image contains text produced by an image model or baked into artwork by a tool that does not treat it as live type. Models misspell product names, invent letterforms and produce near-English that survives one quick look and then gets screenshotted by a customer. Text in a Wickhold image is set by a person, in the design tool, in the brand typefaces, as a separate layer over finished art. That covers overlays, labels, chart annotations and callouts.

Three things do not count as generated text:

- Words that are really in the scene: a printed rack label, a whiteboard someone wrote on, a door sign. Check that they say nothing embarrassing and name nobody outside the company.

- The wordmark, which is a vector file, placed by a person.

- A LinkedIn post is 180 words at most. Count everything, including the link line.
- About the first 200 characters show before the "see more" cut on most phones. The news has to fit in that space.
- Short paragraphs, one to three lines each, with a blank line between them.
- One link per post, at the end, on its own line. We tested putting links in the first comment for six weeks in 2025 and could not see a difference, and it annoyed people, so links stay in the post.
- Tag a customer only after their marketing contact has seen the post. Tag people, not company pages, when a named person spoke or wrote the thing.
- Use bullets only for real lists: three containment actions, the tiers, the steps of a rollout. A post that is all bullets reads as a slide.
- Image guidance sits with the visual rules. Every company page post gets one image, except short hiring notes.

", "end_line": 26, "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Format"], "ref": "source_417", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md", "start_line": 17}, {"content": "## Color

Bars and lines use the palette.

- **Ember for the one series or bar that makes the point.** All others are Whetstone.
- On Soot, use Tallow for context series, with Ember as the highlight. Whetstone is too dim to read there.
- Verdigris is the second highlight, used only when two series truly need names, such as before and after.
- No Ember tints. If you need a ramp for ordered data, use Soot to Whetstone to pale Tallow steps.

Ember, Whetstone and Verdigris sit very close together in lightness. Printed in grayscale, or viewed by a reader with color blindness, they merge. So hue never works alone: label each series directly on the line or bar, and separate adjacent bars with a gap. Legends are a last resort, since they send the reader back and forth.

Red and green are not used for bad and good. A chart about containment should not look like a stock ticker or an alert console.

Read `restrictions` before you use an image, every time, including images you have used before. Restrictions are added after an image enters the library, so last quarter's check does not count.

The field is free text, written by whoever had the reason. There is no fixed vocabulary, so read the sentence instead of searching for a keyword. Three kinds of note turn up in practice:

- **Retirement.** The image is deprecated and must not be used. Some retired files look entirely normal in the grid and carry no other sign. Their tags and titles may even look current.
- **A limited context.** The image may be used in the named context and nowhere else. A note limiting an image to internal use keeps it out of anything a customer, a prospect or the press will see, and that includes sales decks.
- **A person or place.** Something about who or what is shown has changed.

A restriction binds even when the image would be perfect, when a senior person asks for it, and when you found it already published somewhere. If you think one is out of date, ask Brand to change the record. Do not use the image and sort it out later.

An empty `restrictions` field means nobody has recorded a limit. It does not mean the image is on brand. The field is one check among several, and the current-identity rule above still has to pass on your own judgment.

", "end_line": 476, "heading_path": ["WICKHOLD SECURITY BRAND GUIDELINES", "11. Asset Library and Requests"], "ref": "source_426", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_v3_FINAL.md", "start_line": 462}, {"content": "### Worked examples

**Two limits for the same channel.** A general voice document gives one length for a channel and that channel's playbook gives another. The playbook wins, because it sits higher in the list. Use its number, and tell Noor so the other one gets fixed.

**A claim in a deck.** A slide says something about the company that the approved claims do not support. The approved claims win, however recent or confident the slide looks, and however often the line has been used in the field. Sales material is not a source for a claim.

**Copy in this document versus Legal.** If a sentence in these guidelines turns out to conflict with the approved claims, Legal wins, and the guidelines get corrected.

**An old-looking rule with no rival.** A meeting note from the Q2 brand review covers something that the relevant playbook doesn't mention. Nothing conflicts, so the note stands.

**A file that says it's the latest.** File names, version numbers and words like FINAL or CURRENT decide nothing. Neither does the date on a file, on its own. Use this list.

**No source answers the question.** Ask the owner listed below. Do not fill the gap from the 2024 material or from what a competitor does. If the question is likely to come up again, the answer gets written down in the right document.

**Sources at the same level disagree.** Two channel playbooks can conflict on a shared element, such as a campaign running on both email and a landing page. Each playbook governs its own channel. If that doesn't settle it, Noor decides and the decision gets recorded.

", "end_line": 483, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "11. Governance", "Worked examples"], "ref": "source_427", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 468}, {"content": "## 11. Tables, charts and captions

- A table needs a header row and at least two rows of content. One row is a sentence.
- Right-align numbers in tables. Keep units in the header, not in each cell.
- A chart title states the finding in sentence case: "41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident". The axis says what was measured.
- Every chart carries its citation in the same bracket form, set small under the chart, so it survives being cropped into a slide.
- Captions are sentences. They end with a full stop and they don't begin "Figure 1 shows".
- No 3D, no donuts, and no chart for a single number. Write the number.

", "end_line": 201, "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "11. Tables, charts and captions"], "ref": "source_428", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "start_line": 193}, {"content": "### Fallback fonts

The strongest evidence for this position comes from Wickhold's own research. The Wickhold Containment Report 2026, published April 14, 2026, surveyed 412 platform and security leaders. It found that "41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident" and that "the median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours" [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].

The gap those numbers describe is between finding something and doing something about it. Detection has become cheap and common. Containment still depends on a person with enough access waking up, reading the alert, deciding, and acting. Wickhold's position lives in those hours.

", "end_line": 149, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning", "The market problem"], "ref": "source_430", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 144}, {"content": "### Blast radius of an agent

Leashgate reads an agent's policy, its service account's RBAC and its Secret mounts, then reports what the agent could reach: every tool it may call, each resource those tools touch, and any route around the gateway, such as a direct network path to a database the agent should only reach through a tool. The report is meant to be read in a security review.

```text
AGENT  support/support-triage      identity: spiffe://wickhold.example/ns/support/sa/triage
  tools allowed            2
  tools requiring approval 1
  tools denied             14
  bypass routes            1
    pod can reach postgres.support.svc:5432 directly (no NetworkPolicy)
```

Bypass routes matter more than anything else in that output. A gateway that an agent can walk around enforces nothing.

", "end_line": 160, "heading_path": ["Email templates", "T6. Nurture, platform track, first email"], "ref": "source_432", "relative_path": "brand/templates/email-templates.md", "start_line": 142}, {"content": "## Not banned, but expect a comment

Reviewers will ask about these. Sometimes the word survives.

- **solution.** Name the product, or say what it does. The word exists to avoid doing either.
- **visibility.** Seeing isn't the job. If the sentence ends at seeing, ask what happens next.
- **real-time.** Fine with a number next to it. Without one it means nothing.
- **AI-powered.** Tells the reader how something was built and nothing about what it does.
- **comprehensive.** Usually untrue, and a reader will go looking for the gap.
- **threat landscape.** A landscape has no one in it. Say which failure you mean.
- **peace of mind.** Nobody on a rota has ever had this.
- **modern.** Compared with what? Say which setup you mean.
- **mission-critical.** To the person on call, everything is.

", "end_line": 84, "heading_path": ["Landing page imagery", "Review"], "ref": "source_435", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/landing-page-imagery.md", "start_line": 80}, {"content": "## Keeping screenshots current

Screens age quickly, and old ones do damage in specific ways:

- **Before March 2026, Evenburn screens carry the product's previous name** in the navigation and page titles. Check `added_date` and look at the header. A screen with the old name is unusable, even when the part you want is elsewhere in the frame. Crop-around is not a fix, since the layout and colors are dated too.
- **Before the February 2026 rebrand, the product UI used the old blue theme and the old logo** in the corner. Same answer.
- **Removed features.** Product marketing reviews the library's screenshots against the release notes at each major release, and adds a `restrictions` note to anything that no longer matches.

If a screenshot's record is clean and the picture still looks out of date against the live product, trust your eyes and take a fresh one. The demo environment is reset each Monday, so captures are straightforward. Anything that shows a feature's name, a label or a flow that has changed needs replacing before the next use.

", "end_line": 104, "heading_path": ["Product UI screenshots", "Keeping screenshots current"], "ref": "source_436", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/product-ui-screenshots.md", "start_line": 95}, {"content": "## 5. Dates and times

- **Dates:** month, day, year, spelled out: April 14, 2026. No ordinals, no "14th of April".
- **Month and year:** March 2022, no comma. **Year only:** 2026.
- **Ranges:** an en dash with no spaces within a month: September 15–16. Use "to" across months: "March 30 to April 2".
- **Tables, logs, front matter:** ISO, 2026-04-14. Never slashes. 04/10 has already caused one wrong webinar invite, and that's enough.
- **Quarters:** fine internally. In public copy, name the month.
- **Avoid relative dates** in anything that stays online. "Recently", "last year", "this spring" and "soon" all rot. Write the date. Press releases and dated posts can say "today".
- **Roadmap language:** no dates, no "coming soon". Product marketing has a separate process for that.

**Times.** Incident timelines use 24-hour UTC with the zone on every line or at the top of the block: 03:14 UTC. It's how our readers' tools show it. Event and webinar times use 12-hour with the zone: 2:00 p.m. MT. In prose, "3am" with no space is fine as a phrase, and the voice document uses it constantly. It's a figure of speech and shouldn't be used for an actual appointment.

", "end_line": 72, "heading_path": ["Illustration", "Color limits"], "ref": "source_441", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/illustration.md", "start_line": 67}, {"content": "## 7. Rulings from this year

Requests I have already answered. They are listed so that I do not answer them again.

| Request | Ruling |
|---|---|
| "Trusted by more than 140 customers" | Allowed. The count stays exact |
| "Trusted by credit unions" | Refused. One customer is not a plural |
| "Agentless" or "agent-free" for Quenchline | Refused. It uses an eBPF agent. Say so |
| "Lightweight" | Allowed only next to the CPU overhead figure and its qualifier |
| "Real-time" for Quenchline | Allowed for detection. For containment, use the lab figure or leave it out |
| "Stops the attack" | Refused. Name the containment action: isolate a pod's network, freeze a process, drain a node |
| "Automatic remediation" for Evenburn | Refused. Evenburn gives a fix order and people do the fixing |
| "AI-powered" for any product | Refused unless product confirms in writing what the model does. Writing about AI agents does not make the product AI-powered |
| "Secures your AI" or "safe AI" for Leashgate | Refused. Describe tool-call policy and agent identity |
| "SOC 2 certified" | Refused. Say "holds SOC 2 Type II" |
| "Used by your peers" in a sector email | Refused unless a named, approved customer in that sector is shown |

**Monthly newsletter.** Goes to everyone opted in, second Tuesday of the month. One lead item, three short items, nothing about us that we wouldn't want to read ourselves. Engineers are the bulk of this list, so it can carry a command or a config snippet.

", "end_line": 29, "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "What we send"], "ref": "source_449", "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md", "start_line": 16}, {"content": "### The promise at each level

| Level | What is promised |
|---|---|
| Company | Small fires stay small. |
| Quenchline | When something goes wrong at runtime, a defined containment action happens quickly and the team sees exactly what it did |
| Evenburn | The team sees where the drift and exposure paths are, and gets a fix order |
| Leashgate | AI agents work inside a tool-call policy, so the blast radius of an agent is known in advance |

", "end_line": 218, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning", "The promise at each level"], "ref": "source_450", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 210}, {"content": "## 3. Banned claims

| Do not say | Say instead, or do this | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| "prevents prompt injection" | "limits what a compromised agent can do" | Leashgate acts on tool calls. It does not read intent and it cannot promise that an agent will not be manipulated. The claim is false as a matter of product design |
| "FedRAMP Authorized", "FedRAMP certified" | See section 4 | Neither is true |
| "GDPR compliant" | Use the regional rules | Regional wording sits there, and the ban is not limited to that region |
| "breach-proof", "unhackable", "impossible to escape" | Describe the containment action | No security product can support an absolute |
| "zero false positives", "100% detection", "catches everything" | Give a sourced figure or say nothing | We hold no such evidence |
| "guarantee", "guaranteed", "warranty" outside a contract | Remove | These words have legal effect. Service credits live in the order form |
| "the leading", "the fastest", "No. 1", "the only" | Remove, or bring me the comparison data | Superlatives need current comparative substantiation, and we do not hold any |
| "certified by", "endorsed by", "partner of" for any standards body or open-source project | Remove | Using eBPF or Helm is not an endorsement from anyone |
| "saves $X", any return-on-investment figure | Remove | We have no approved financial outcome for any customer |

Two refinements, because they keep coming back:

"Helps prevent" is a banned claim dressed up. A qualifier in front of a promise does not make it a limited promise.

"Compliance-ready" and "audit-ready" were requested in June for a trust page and refused. Wickhold can describe what the product records. Whether a customer passes an audit depends on the customer and the auditor.

", "end_line": 98, "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "3. Banned claims"], "ref": "source_451", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md", "start_line": 79}, {"content": "## 8. Technical writing in marketing copy

Kofi Anselm's team reviews anything containing code, and their rules are short.

- **Code formatting** for commands, flags, file names, field names, namespaces, node names and anything a person might type: `kubectl get pods`, `--namespace`, `values.yaml`.
- **Every snippet is run before it's published.** Say which version it was run against. A snippet nobody ran does not go out, even in a slide.
- **Placeholder values** look like placeholders or like real workloads: `payments`, `checkout`, `worker-7`. Don't use `foo`, and don't use the name of a real company, a real customer or a celebrity.
- **Domains and email addresses in examples** use `wickhold.example`.
- **Long output** gets trimmed, with a line saying so. Don't silently edit output.
- **Failure modes** are part of the example. If a command fails in a common way, say how it looks.

", "end_line": 153, "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "8. Technical writing in marketing copy"], "ref": "source_452", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "start_line": 143}, {"content": "## 4. Numbers

", "end_line": 72, "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "4. Numbers"], "ref": "source_453", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "start_line": 71}, {"content": "### Color in common pieces

", "end_line": 222, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "5. Brand architecture"], "ref": "source_456", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 219}, {"content": "## Who should apply

Early access suits platform and security teams that already have at least one agent in production, or are about to, and have someone who can own policy. Teams still deciding whether to run agents at all should wait. There will be plenty to read as we learn more.

Your account team can tell you more, or you can apply directly.

[Request early access](https://wickhold.example/leashgate)

*Wickhold is the runtime security company for teams that run Kubernetes. Its products contain failures early, so small fires stay small. Founded in 2019 and based in Denver, Wickhold serves more than 140 customers.*
", "end_line": 81, "heading_path": ["Wickhold Leashgate enters early access", "Who should apply"], "ref": "source_457", "relative_path": "brand/archive/blog/leashgate_early_access_notes.md", "start_line": 73}, {"content": "## What Leashgate does not do

Leashgate does not read prompts and it does not judge whether a model has been manipulated. It has no opinion on the quality of an agent's output, and it will not catch an agent that gives a customer bad advice through a tool it is allowed to use. What it controls is the set of actions available to the agent. A permitted action that happens to be a poor decision will still go through, so policy needs the same care you would give any access review.

", "end_line": 55, "heading_path": ["Wickhold Leashgate enters early access", "What Leashgate does not do"], "ref": "source_458", "relative_path": "brand/archive/blog/leashgate_early_access_notes.md", "start_line": 52}, {"content": "### Fear is not a sales tool

No threat-actor drama. No ticking clocks.

The rule is simple to state and gets broken constantly, because fear copy is the easiest copy in security to write. It covers attackers portrayed as characters with motives and nicknames, anything of the "while you read this" kind, countdowns, "it's only a matter of time", "every second counts", and any sentence that asks the reader to imagine the phone call to the board. Our readers carry a pager. They do not need help imagining it.

Give the same fact without the dread.

Bad: "Attackers are already inside your cluster, and the clock is ticking."

Good: "41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]."

The second sentence is more uncomfortable than the first, and it did not raise its voice. Trust the number to do that work.

1. A photo of real work, with no overlay at all
2. A stat card from the social templates. Quote cards rarely fit the cap
3. A short product crop showing one action, large enough to read in the feed
4. A hero illustration, cropped

Wickhold Leashgate reaches general availability on Tuesday, January 26, 2027. Product and Legal have confirmed the status change, and this brief is Product Marketing's announcement of it for everyone working on the campaign.
Two things follow from that.
The early access label comes off for this campaign. The numbers here are internal and do not go in copy.
Customers hear it from us first, on launch day, with enough detail for a platform team to judge whether it applies to them.
60 demo requests by March 31, 2027 from teams with an agent running against real tools, in staging or production.
Get the blast radius report into security reviews. We want platform leads to bring it to their next one, as the answer to "what is the worst this agent could do on a bad day?" Sales will track how often it comes up on calls.

Secondary: security leaders and security architects writing internal rules for agent use. They need something more enforceable than a policy document. Lead with the decision they have to make. No humor for this group.
Existing customers get the news first, through the technical customer list. Several asked about agents at Slow Burn Summit, and most were not running any in production yet, so do not write as if they all are.

Treat an agent as a workload with credentials, and give it a boundary. This is pillar 3 of the messaging house and the argument under everything else. Talk about tool calls in a cluster. Leave the future of work to other people.
What it does. Leashgate gives each agent an identity, checks every tool call against a tool-call policy, writes a decision record, and reports the blast radius of an agent, including any route around the gateway.

For platform leads. defaultAction: deny. Your agent framework stays the same. Leashgate fails closed, so an outage of the gateway stops the agent's tools, and teams need to plan for that. Say so plainly.
For security leaders. Before an agent goes live, know its blast radius. Every decision leaves a record your team can read in a security review.
What it does not do. Leashgate sees tool calls, and it does not read or judge prompts. It runs on Kubernetes only, and frameworks that call tools in-process, with no network hop, are out of scope. Being plain about this is part of the pitch.
Channels and assets
Eleven assets, on owned channels only. This is my starting list, so if the mix is wrong, say so when you bring the plan on November 6. The release note, press and sales enablement run separately and are not part of this brief.
