Leashgate at launch is what the product overview and the 2026 release notes describe: agent identity, tool-call policy, and the blast radius report, with a gateway running as a sidecar or as a shared Deployment, for agents that make tool calls over HTTP or MCP. Approvals can be answered from Slack. The tie-in that lets Leashgate ask Wickhold Quenchline for a containment action is optional, off by default, and needs Quenchline on the node.", "heading": "Product scope and behavior"}, {"content": "The numbers here are internal and do not go in copy. Customers hear it from us first, on launch day, with enough detail for a platform team to judge whether it applies to them. 60 demo requests by March 31, 2027 from teams with an agent running against real tools, in staging or production. Get the blast radius report into security reviews. We want platform leads to bring it to their next one, as the answer to "what is the worst this agent could do on a bad day?" Sales will track how often it comes up on calls.", "heading": "Goals and internal metrics"}, {"content": "Primary: platform leads who have been asked to get an agent into production and have a security review standing in their way. They already have the concern, and the budget conversation has started. They read docs first, want the failure behavior early, and trust a config snippet over a paragraph. Secondary: security leaders and security architects writing internal rules for agent use. They need something more enforceable than a policy document. Lead with the decision they have to make. No humor for this group. Existing customers get the news first, through the technical customer list. Several asked about agents at Slow Burn Summit, and most were not running any in production yet, so do not write as if they all are. Keep these audiences apart. Platform and security leadership are separate email lists, and they stay separate here. The landing page is written for platform leads. Security leaders get their own email and the launch post.", "heading": "Audiences"}, {"content": "Treat an agent as a workload with credentials, and give it a boundary. This is pillar 3 of the messaging house and the argument under everything else. Talk about tool calls in a cluster. Leave the future of work to other people. What it does. Leashgate gives each agent an identity, checks every tool call against a tool-call policy, writes a decision record, and reports the blast radius of an agent, including any route around the gateway. The outcome statement. Leashgate "limits what a compromised agent can do". Use those words exactly. For platform leads. defaultAction: deny. Your agent framework stays the same. Leashgate fails closed, so an outage of the gateway stops the agent's tools, and teams need to plan for that. Say so plainly. For security leaders. Before an agent goes live, know its blast radius. Every decision leaves a record your team can read in a security review. What it does not do. Leashgate sees tool calls, and it does not read or judge prompts. It runs on Kubernetes only, and frameworks that call tools in-process, with no network hop, are out of scope. Being plain about this is part of the pitch.", "heading": "Messages and required wording"}, {"content": "Eleven assets, on owned channels only. This is my starting list, so if the mix is wrong, say so when you bring the plan on November 6. The release note, press and sales enablement run separately and are not part of this brief.", "heading": "Campaign scope and channel context"}, {"content": "The landing page is the product page, so it has no end date. Use the existing product layout. Its main action is "Book a demo", with a secondary link to the docs for readers who are not ready for a form. A visitor arrives from one of the emails, a social post or the docs, and needs to see what the product does and how it fails.", "heading": "Landing page requirements"}, {"content": "2026-11-06: Asset plan agreed with me, and Noor's OK on audience and goal. 2026-12-11: Outlines for both blog posts to Kofi. 2027-01-08: All drafts in. 2027-01-15: Claims check back from Priit. Page copy to the web team. Maren's draft to Maren. 2027-01-21: X posts to Kofi for review and scheduling. 2027-01-26: Launch. Release note, landing page, customer email, LinkedIn, X. 2027-01-27: Launch post and prospect emails, one day after customers and after the release note. 2027-01-28: Second company LinkedIn post. 2027-02-02: How-to post and its X post. Kofi moves both to February 3 if a release note lands on the 2nd. 2027-02-09: Two-week check on the landing page form. 2027-03-31: Read the goals.", "heading": "Timeline and dependencies"}, {"content": "Claims. The approved claims and the certification sheet apply as usual. Only the status of Leashgate changes. Proof. There is no customer proof for Leashgate and there is no lab figure for it. Do not name early access partners, quote them or count them. Do not quote a latency figure, since we have none. The Lowmoor Credit Union and Ostler Grocers results belong to other products and do not go on Leashgate assets as if they were Leashgate results. A thin page beats a borrowed number. Market framing. Use figures from the Wickhold Containment Report 2026, or a fresh third-party statistic with its source. Web research is welcome where it helps, under the usual rules for third-party figures.", "heading": "Claims, proof and market framing"}, {"content": "Pricing. Pricing after early access is not settled, and I am handling the pricing page separately before launch. Do not state a price or a tier for Leashgate in any asset. Link to the pricing page where a reader needs it, and send buying questions to sales. Support terms. Say nothing about SLAs or support levels. Those live in the order form. Roadmap. Describe what the product does on launch day. No future features, no adapter lists, no dates beyond the launch itself. Competitors. Leashgate stays out of competitive positioning. No comparisons and no comparison blog in this campaign.", "heading": "Pricing, support, roadmap and competitors"}, {"content": "Code in copy. Excerpts of ToolCallPolicy rules are welcome. Leave out the apiVersion line, build numbers and the install command. The early access versions do not carry over, and Kofi adds the final block at the paste test. Images. Use the library. Design's console screens for launch will not be ready in time, and the Leashgate console screens in the library carry the early access pill, which is not to be cropped off. Keep them off every asset in this campaign. The landing page hero is a working room.", "heading": "Code and image requirements"}, {"content": "Maren's post. It is a draft for her to rewrite. Do not schedule it, and do not assume a yes. Questions come to me. Anything that touches the claims goes to Priit first.", "heading": "Draft handling and routing"}], "unknowns": []}}

{"passages": [{"content": "### Our three pillars

**Pillar 1: Every Workload.**
Complete coverage. Every pod, every node, every cluster, every cloud account. There are no blind spots on the Wickhold Security platform.

Supporting language: *full coverage*, *no blind spots*, *one single pane of glass for runtime and posture*.

**Pillar 2: Always Watched.**
Security that never sleeps! Our eBPF agent and continuous scanning mean you find out in seconds, not in next quarter's audit.

Supporting language: *always on*, *continuous*, *real time*, *24/7 visibility*.

**Pillar 3: Built by Operators.**
Maren and Dov carried the pager. Our product respects the people who run production, with lightweight deployment, sensible defaults and robust integrations that fit how platform teams already work.

Supporting language: *by operators, for operators*, *lightweight*, *fast to deploy*.

", "end_line": 129, "heading_path": ["WICKHOLD SECURITY BRAND GUIDELINES", "4. Our Messaging", "Our three pillars"], "ref": "source_0", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_v3_FINAL.md", "start_line": 113}, {"content": "## Size

16:9, 1600x900. Keep the focal point in the middle, as the timeline crops and phone previews trim the edges. Long screenshots of text get a "show more" crop, so do not post them. Write a thread.

", "end_line": 19, "heading_path": ["X images", "Size"], "ref": "source_1", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/x-image.md", "start_line": 16}, {"content": "---
title: Content style guide
version: 4
owner: Noor Eskelund
updated: 2026-07-09
---

", "end_line": 7, "heading_path": [], "ref": "source_2", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "start_line": 1}, {"content": "### A worked hierarchy

A typical landing section might read:

- Page headline, Bricolage Grotesque Bold: "Small fires stay small."
- Subhead, Plex Sans SemiBold: "Wickhold Quenchline contains runtime failures on your Kubernetes nodes, within limits your team sets."
- Body, Plex Sans Regular: one short paragraph.
- Inline literal, Plex Mono: `kubectl get containmentpolicy`.

Four levels is plenty. If a layout seems to need a fifth, the content usually needs editing.

", "end_line": 380, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "8. Typography", "A worked hierarchy"], "ref": "source_3", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 370}, {"content": "# LinkedIn images

Social lead's notes, updated August 2026.

", "end_line": 4, "heading_path": ["LinkedIn images"], "ref": "source_4", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/linkedin-image.md", "start_line": 1}, {"content": "## Who signs off

Product marketing checks accuracy. Brand checks the crop and annotations. If a screenshot shows a feature that engineering has not shipped to all customers, the product manager for that area also signs off. Allow two working days.
", "end_line": 115, "heading_path": ["Product UI screenshots", "Who signs off"], "ref": "source_5", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/product-ui-screenshots.md", "start_line": 113}, {"content": "### File Names

Name working files clearly so that everyone can find them: project, piece, version. For example, `summit_booth_backwall_v2`. When a file is done, add `FINAL` to the name and move it to the shared drive so that nobody has to guess which one is approved.

---

", "end_line": 448, "heading_path": ["WICKHOLD SECURITY BRAND GUIDELINES", "9. Putting It All Together", "File Names"], "ref": "source_6", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_v3_FINAL.md", "start_line": 443}, {"content": "### The primary logo

Our logo combines two elements: the **shield**, which stands for protection, and the **flame** rising from inside it, which stands for the constant, watchful light of runtime visibility. Beside the shield sits the **Wickhold Security wordmark**, set in Inter Bold with a custom tight fit.

The shield and the wordmark are a single unit. In nearly all cases, use them together.

", "end_line": 203, "heading_path": ["WICKHOLD SECURITY BRAND GUIDELINES", "5. Our Logo", "The primary logo"], "ref": "source_7", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_v3_FINAL.md", "start_line": 198}, {"content": "## Copy on cards

Cards follow the voice rules with no special allowance for being short. Good:

- Small fires stay small.
- 11 minutes to contain, down from 4 hours.
- Contain mode, explained.

Bad:

- Hackers never sleep. Neither do we.
- The future of cloud security is HERE!
- Is your cluster on fire right now?

The 11-minute line needs Lowmoor named in the post or on the card, so that the number has a source.

A card should not repeat the post word for word. Use the post to expand on the card.

", "end_line": 52, "heading_path": ["Social graphics", "Copy on cards"], "ref": "source_8", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/social-graphics.md", "start_line": 35}, {"content": "### Claims made in a hurry

Launches and field events are when unapproved language tends to appear, usually from someone trying to help. If you see a claim in circulation that isn't on the approved list, tell Priit the same day, including where you saw it. There is no blame in reporting one. The aim is to get it corrected before it's copied into something else.

", "end_line": 532, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "11. Governance", "Claims made in a hurry"], "ref": "source_9", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 529}, {"content": "## 9. People and companies

- Full name and title on first mention, in this order: Hana Brandvold, CISO, Lowmoor Credit Union.
- After that, surname for external people, in the press-release style: Brandvold said. First name for our founders only where they signed the piece.
- Job titles are capitalized in a byline or attribution line and lowercase in a sentence: "the company's head of developer relations".
- Companies are singular. "Wickhold is", "Ostler Grocers has".
- Use "they" for an unnamed person. "On-call lead", not "on-call guy". "Staffed", not "manned".
- Teams are lowercase: the platform team, the brand team.

", "end_line": 186, "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "9. People and companies"], "ref": "source_10", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "start_line": 178}, {"content": "### Product behavior

Wickhold Quenchline takes a containment action only in contain mode. In observe mode it records what it would have done. Copy describing automatic containment must therefore be true of contain mode and should say so where a reader could assume otherwise. Containment actions are isolating a pod's network, freezing a process and draining a node. Do not add to the list without product confirmation.

Wickhold Evenburn reports drift, exposure paths and a fix order. It does not change a customer's environment by itself, and copy should not imply that it does.

", "end_line": 72, "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "2. Claims that need a qualifier", "Product behavior"], "ref": "source_11", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md", "start_line": 67}, {"content": "## Things we tried

Polls brought a lot of votes from people outside our audience and no replies worth reading. Dropped in late 2025.

Document posts and carousels are off the plan. Swipes fell away after the third page.

Paid boosting is decided per post by demand gen. A boosted post goes through the same review as paid copy, even when it started life as an organic one.
", "end_line": 110, "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Things we tried"], "ref": "source_12", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md", "start_line": 104}, {"content": "## What works

- A code or YAML card on Soot, from the engineering post format
- A tight product crop of one containment action
- One chart with its title
- A spot illustration, flattened on Tallow or Soot, for a light post

This is narrower than the social graphics rules in two ways. No overlay text on photos here, since the feed crop is unpredictable. And no quote cards: on X, type the quote into the post with the customer's name.

", "end_line": 15, "heading_path": ["X images", "What works"], "ref": "source_13", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/x-image.md", "start_line": 7}, {"content": "# Wickhold Leashgate

*Product marketing overview for the May 2026 early access. First draft for field and web teams, May 4, updated September 2026.*

", "end_line": 4, "heading_path": ["Wickhold Leashgate"], "ref": "source_14", "relative_path": "brand/products/leashgate-overview.md", "start_line": 1}, {"content": "## June 23, 2026: Leashgate early access build 0.4

First schema migration. Argument constraints moved under `rules[].arguments`. Policies need rewriting by hand in this one case, and partners have a migration note from their engineering contact.

- MCP proxy mode now supports multiple upstream servers per gateway
- Human-user identity can be passed through to policy evaluation
- Agent credential lifetime is configurable, default 15 minutes

", "end_line": 100, "heading_path": ["Release notes 2026", "June 23, 2026: Leashgate early access build 0.4"], "ref": "source_15", "relative_path": "brand/products/release-notes-2026.md", "start_line": 93}, {"content": "# LinkedIn playbook

Noor Eskelund. Last edit 12 August 2026, after the Leashgate early access posts. Ask in the brand channel before you ask me by email.

LinkedIn is the one channel where CISOs, platform leads and our own hiring pipeline all look at the same feed. Most of what we post there is read on a phone, between meetings, by someone who has never heard of us. Write for that person.

", "end_line": 6, "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook"], "ref": "source_16", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md", "start_line": 1}, {"content": "### Data location and processing

Do not state where customer data is stored, or use "EU-hosted", "data residency" or "sovereign", unless the sentence has been cleared for that specific asset. Questions on data location go to the account team and then to me. The answers depend on the deployment, and marketing copy should not try to summarize them.

Sub-processor lists and the data processing agreement are shared on request. They are not marketing assets. Do not screenshot them into a deck.

", "end_line": 40, "heading_path": ["Regional rules: EU and UK copy", "Data location and processing"], "ref": "source_17", "relative_path": "brand/legal/regional-rules-eu-uk.md", "start_line": 35}, {"content": "### Swag

Quality over quantity. Pick items people keep, such as good bottles, thick socks and well-cut T-shirts. Navy or Cobalt base with the reversed shield. Any vendor needs the vector logo files from Marketing, and we check a sample before we approve a run.

", "end_line": 378, "heading_path": ["WICKHOLD SECURITY BRAND GUIDELINES", "9. Putting It All Together", "Swag"], "ref": "source_18", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_v3_FINAL.md", "start_line": 375}, {"content": "## March 2026: pricing

New Core and Team prices took effect this month. No product entitlement changed for existing contracts until renewal.

", "end_line": 165, "heading_path": ["Release notes 2026", "March 2026: pricing"], "ref": "source_19", "relative_path": "brand/products/release-notes-2026.md", "start_line": 162}, {"content": "# Data visualization

Charts are built from data by a person, in code or the design tool. They are never drawn by an image model and never traced from somebody else's report. Written for the 2026 Containment Report and kept for everything since.

", "end_line": 4, "heading_path": ["Data visualization"], "ref": "source_20", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/data-viz.md", "start_line": 1}, {"content": "# Wickhold brand guidelines 2026

Noor Eskelund, Head of Brand. Issued February 10, 2026, with the rebrand. Revised September 2026.

These guidelines replace the 2024 guidelines in full. They cover what the brand is, what it stands for and how it looks at the level a writer, designer or marketer needs to make decisions. The detailed working rules for words, claims, channels and images sit in their own documents, and this one does not repeat them.

", "end_line": 6, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026"], "ref": "source_21", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 1}, {"content": "### Co-marketing

Partners write their own claims about their own products. When a joint asset says anything about Wickhold and data protection, the approved sentence is used, and the partner's version is not. If a partner insists on the banned phrase about itself, the phrase stays in the part of the asset that is clearly theirs, and it comes to me first.

", "end_line": 55, "heading_path": ["Regional rules: EU and UK copy", "Co-marketing"], "ref": "source_22", "relative_path": "brand/legal/regional-rules-eu-uk.md", "start_line": 52}, {"content": "## Narrower than the category pages

Not everything in the illustration category qualifies here:

- **Hero illustrations only.** A spot illustration is transparent and square, and it sits inside body copy. Set as a hero, it leaves a small object floating in a wide band, so it is out.
- **No abstract backgrounds.** They have no focal point on their own, and a hero has no type set over it.
- **Tallow or Soot, matched to the post.** Illustration category rules allow either. For blog heroes, default to Tallow. Use Soot for incident retrospectives and long technical posts, so that the list page has some rhythm.

And from photography:

- **Landscape only.** Portrait photos in the library cannot become 16:9 without losing most of the frame.
- **A person is allowed as the subject, but the post has to be about the work** and not a staff profile.

No text on the hero at all, including the post title. The blog template sets the title in live type below the image. Older posts had titles burned into the image, and they looked wrong in every preview card that also printed the title.

", "end_line": 23, "heading_path": ["Blog hero images", "Narrower than the category pages"], "ref": "source_23", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/blog-hero.md", "start_line": 9}, {"content": "## May 2026: Leashgate early access build 0.3

Fix release for the first partners. Corrects sidecar injection on namespaces with restrictive pod security settings and adds a readiness gate so an agent pod does not start before its gateway.

", "end_line": 116, "heading_path": ["Release notes 2026", "May 2026: Leashgate early access build 0.3"], "ref": "source_24", "relative_path": "brand/products/release-notes-2026.md", "start_line": 113}, {"content": "## Templates first

The library holds a small set of social templates, built in HTML and rendered with Playwright so the type is live and the layout stays exact. Start from one. Copy it, change the content, render it. A file marked as a template is a master and should not be posted unfilled.

Do not rebuild a template in a slide app. That is where off-size margins and the wrong weight of Bricolage Grotesque come from.

If you need a layout the templates do not cover, ask a designer. Do not stretch the stat card to hold a quote.

", "end_line": 14, "heading_path": ["Social graphics", "Templates first"], "ref": "source_25", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/social-graphics.md", "start_line": 7}, {"content": "## The problem with agents in production

An agent in a production cluster is a workload that makes its own decisions about what to call next. Platform teams are being asked to run these agents, often with credentials that were copied from a developer's laptop during a pilot. The agent can reach a database, a ticketing system and a deployment pipeline, because during the pilot that was convenient.

Most of the time this works fine. When it does not, the failure is hard to reason about. A model may be manipulated by content it read, or it may simply make a poor decision. Either way, the question for the on-call engineer is the same as for any other incident: how far can this get?

Some topics drag writers back toward the register the rebrand left behind. These are the ones reviewers see most.

**AI agents.** Wickhold Leashgate, in early access, attracts the worst habits in the building, because the whole market is shouting about agents. Treat an agent as a workload with credentials and questionable judgment. Talk about tool calls, agent identity and the blast radius of an agent. Leave the future of work to other people. Anyone who has run production will recognize the problem from there, and that recognition is worth more than any amount of excitement.

**Compliance.** Dull on purpose. Certification status is a fact with one correct wording, and legal owns that wording. Copy the approved sentence and do not improve it. A nicer phrasing here is how a company ends up saying something untrue.

**Money.** Prices are stated flatly, with no "just", "only" or "starting from". Core is $18 per node per month. The reader can decide how they feel about that.

**Company news.** Funding, awards, headcount. Nobody is thrilled, excited or proud. The Series B was $46M in June 2024; that is a date and a number, and the sentence after it should say what changed for customers. If nothing changed for customers, ask whether the post needs to exist.

**Customers.** They did the work. Lowmoor Credit Union's on-call team runs its own incidents, and the product took one job off their list. Avoid "partnered with", "journey" and anything that casts us as the guide who showed them the way.

**Other approaches.** The voice doesn't sneer. Other kinds of product make real trade-offs, and a colleague would describe them as trade-offs: a heavier agent can see more and costs more on the node. Readers respect the writer who can state the other side accurately. Reviewers will cut anything that sounds like a playground.

**Open source.** Kubernetes, eBPF and Helm were here before us. We are users and we say so. Credit the projects, don't imply we invented the kernel feature, and don't describe a community as an "ecosystem we're proud to be part of".

This is the demo story, and it is the one we use with design partners.

A support triage agent reads incoming tickets and updates them. A customer email contains hidden text telling the agent to export the customer list to an outside address. The agent, doing what agents do, tries it.

1. The agent calls `crm.export` through the gateway. The policy says `requireApproval`, so the call waits.
2. A support lead sees the request in Slack, with the agent identity, the arguments and the ticket that triggered it. They decline.
3. The agent tries `shell.exec` to get at the data another way. Policy denies it, and the gateway returns a structured refusal.
4. After a third denial in a minute, a rule marks the pattern as suspicious. Leashgate requests network isolation from Quenchline, and the pod is contained.
5. The on-call engineer gets a timeline with four decision records and the ticket ID.

The agent was fooled, and the demo does not pretend otherwise. What matters is how little it managed to do afterward.

Three values.

- `transparent`: no ground at all. The image takes on whatever is behind it, which is why `safe_on` matters so much for these files.
- `solid`: a flat ground is part of the file, such as a logo on its panel or a hero illustration on Tallow.
- `scene`: the image has its own environment, as every photograph does. You never cut a scene out of its background, and we do not mask people or equipment out of photos.

The voice stays the same. How much of it you get changes with the room.

**Landing pages.** The flattest we get. Mechanical, confident, short. The reader is deciding whether to spend ten more minutes, so tell them what the thing does on a cluster and let them go. "Wickhold Quenchline isolates the pod, freezes the process or drains the node, then writes down what it did."

**Blog.** The most room to think. Brand-voice posts walk through how something fails. Dov's posts can argue, and they should. A good post leaves the reader able to do one thing they could not do before, even if they never buy. Avoid the summary paragraph at the end. If the post worked, the reader was there.

**LinkedIn.** The company page is brand voice. Founder posts are where the personality lives. A post runs about 200 words, which suits one story and one point. Write as a person with a job, not a thought leader: no line breaks after every sentence, no "here's what I learned", no lists of lessons from an outage.

**X.** One fact, or one observation, in a dry tone. The account does not chase the news and does not reply to arguments about vendors. It's fine for a post to be plain. "The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. That is most of a night shift."

**Email.** One person writing to one person who is busy. Say why you are writing in the first sentence. Assume it is being read on a phone in a hallway. No "I hope this finds you well", and since these are brand emails, no "I" at all unless Maren signed it. Customer notices are the exception to everything else in this list and sound like the incident channel at the top of this document.

**Product UI and error text.** The closest thing we have to pure voice. What happened, what state things are in, what to do. "Containment action failed on node `ip-10-2-14-7`: agent unreachable. ", "end_line": 62, "heading_path": ["Release notes 2026", "September 15, 2026: Slow Burn Summit release"], "ref": "source_51", "relative_path": "brand/products/release-notes-2026.md", "start_line": 53}, {"content": "## Start at 3am

Anyone who writes for Wickhold should read an incident channel before writing a line of copy. Kofi Anselm's team keeps a few scrubbed transcripts for new hires. Skip the panic at the top of the thread and find the messages from whoever is running the incident. They tend to look like this:

> 03:14 UTC. A pod in `checkout` started a shell it has no reason to start.
> 03:14 UTC. Wickhold Quenchline froze the process and isolated the pod's network.
> 03:22 UTC. Rest of the namespace is quiet. Still unknown how the shell got there.
> Reading the image history now. Next update 03:45.

That is the voice. It says what happened, what is contained and what is next, in that order, and it stops. It has timestamps where other writers have adjectives. It admits the thing it does not know in the same flat tone as the thing it does. The person writing it is tired and is not going to make their tiredness your problem. Forty people are reading, half of them frightened, and the frightened ones calm down because of how the message is written.

Maren Tolliver and Dov Achterberg were on-call infrastructure leads before they founded this company in Denver in 2019. The voice is theirs by inheritance. The 2026 brand made it official: a wick is the one place a fire is allowed to exist. Production will catch fire in small ways, on ordinary nights, for dull reasons. The mission is to keep small failures from becoming big ones, and the copy should sound like it was written by people who consider that a normal day's work.

Owner: lifecycle, with product. Sent only to accounts product has approved.

**Subject:** Wickhold Leashgate, in early access
**Preheader:** Tool-call policy for AI agents, in early access for a limited group of teams.

Hi {{first_name}},

Your team is running AI agents with access to real tools, so you may want to look at Wickhold Leashgate, in early access.

Leashgate (early access) sets tool-call policy at runtime and gives each agent an identity. If an agent is compromised, the policy limits what a compromised agent can do. It keeps the blast radius of an agent to what you've allowed.

Early access means you work directly with our engineers and the product will change while you use it.

Three values, each describing the ground the image is designed to sit on.

- `light`: Tallow and other pale grounds only.
- `dark`: Soot and other deep grounds only.

Treat `safe_on` as a limit, the same way you treat `restrictions`. A `light` image on a dark layout is a defect even if you can still more or less see it. | Write | Not |
|---|---|

**Citations give the source name, the year and the link, in brackets, right after the claim.**

```text

- Source name in full, as the source spells it.
- Comma, year. Comma, link. The full stop for the sentence goes outside the bracket.
- Link goes to the report or page itself, not a press release about it and not a search result. In a PDF or on a slide print the link out, because hyperlinks do not survive a screenshot.
- Use the same form everywhere, including LinkedIn and X. Yes, it's long on X. Plan the post around it.

- In long pieces (report summaries, the blog), mention the survey base once near the first figure: "a survey of 412 platform and security leaders".

Customer results don't take a bracket when the customer is named in the sentence and the case study is linked from the page. Naming them is the source.

", "end_line": 6, "heading_path": ["Email templates"], "ref": "source_94", "relative_path": "brand/templates/email-templates.md", "start_line": 1}, {"content": "### Using them well

Bricolage Grotesque is a display face. Below about 20 px its quirks turn into noise, so it should not be used for body text, buttons or table cells. Limit a page to the two headline weights in the table.

Plex Sans carries nearly everything else. Keep line lengths between 60 and 80 characters. On long pages a wider column is the first thing to go wrong.

Plex Mono has a job beyond code. Commands, flags, file names, YAML keys and other literal strings are set in mono inside body text, so a reader can see what to type. Node counts and timings in a table can also use it, because the digits line up. Do not use it for decoration or to make something feel technical. Engineers notice.

Email is the known exception. Mail clients ignore most web fonts, so the email stack falls back to a system sans-serif, and headlines in an email rely on weight and spacing to do the work.

Italic is for titles of reports and for the occasional stress. All caps are limited to small labels in a layout, and never to whole sentences.

**CISOs.** Level and measured. Assume the reader will forward your paragraph to an audit committee without editing it, and write something they can forward. **Platform engineers.** A good pull-request comment from a colleague you respect. Exact, brief, assumes competence, and shows its working. If there is a YAML snippet that makes the point, the prose can get out of its way. Marketing English reads as noise here and the page will be closed.

This section sets how Wickhold may talk about breaches and other public incidents, in any channel.

1. Never name a victim. That covers company names, product names, and descriptions that identify one ("a large regional retailer in the week it made the news").
2. No humor. Not in the copy, not in the image, not in a speaker's aside.
3. Nothing within 30 days of a public incident. Count from the first public disclosure. For the 30 days, Wickhold does not publish, post, send or sponsor anything that refers to the incident or that is plainly timed to it. An incident is not a marketing hook.

After 30 days, a breach may be discussed in general terms only, as a pattern and without identifying anyone. A technical analysis of a technique is fine if it does not rely on the incident for attention.

The rules cover paid media, social, email, blog posts, sales sequences, talks and replies to journalists. They apply to personal LinkedIn accounts when the post mentions Wickhold or its products. Press inquiries about a live incident go to Ilse Varga-Holm, and nobody comments before she has spoken to me.

If a campaign in market could be read as a reaction to a new public incident, whoever notices it pauses it and tells Ilse. Nobody will be criticized for pausing. Sales may answer a direct customer question about an incident with facts about the customer's own deployment. It may not use the question as an opening.

Incidents at Wickhold customers are never discussed without the customer's written approval, whatever their age. The approved Lowmoor material is the model. It has a figure and no drama.

Not approved:

> After last week's breach at a regional bank, can your team afford another six hours?

Approved, more than 30 days after any related event:

> When a pod misbehaves, Wickhold Quenchline in contain mode can isolate its network while the on-call engineer works out what happened.

", "end_line": 150, "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "6. Breach and incident references"], "ref": "source_110", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md", "start_line": 127}, {"content": "## 2. Mission

**Keep small failures from becoming big ones.**

The mission is written for the people who run production. A failed deployment, a process that should not be running, a credential in the wrong place: these happen every week in any serious cluster, and they stay dull when somebody contains them early. The company exists to keep them dull.

Three things follow from that wording, and they are the reasons it was chosen.

It accepts that failures happen. A company that claims failures will not happen has stopped talking to engineers. Founders Maren and Dov spent years as on-call infrastructure leads before starting Wickhold in Denver in March 2019, and neither of them has ever met a system that did not fail.

It measures success by size. A contained incident still gets logged, reviewed and fixed. The win is that it stayed at one pod and did not reach the node, or stayed at one node and did not reach the cluster.

It says "keep", which is ongoing work. Containment is something a team does with good tools, every week. The mission gives the product a role in that work and leaves the credit for the outcome with the customer's on-call team.

Use the mission on recruiting pages, in all-hands decks and in the opening of long-form pieces about the company. It is an internal compass first. It should not be pasted on product pages as a slogan, because the tagline already does that job.

A few sentences show the difference between using the mission and hanging it on the wall.

Good, from a recruiting page: "We build software that keeps small failures from becoming big ones. If you have been paged at 3am, you already know why that matters."

Weak: "Our mission is to revolutionize the way the world thinks about failure." It's bigger than the company, and it says nothing an on-call engineer would recognize.

", "end_line": 139, "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "Three picks, worked through"], "ref": "source_115", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "start_line": 132}, {"content": "## 10. Accessibility summary

Accessible work is part of the brand standard, and it is checked at review alongside everything else. The reasoning is simple enough: engineers read documentation on bad monitors, on phones and at 3am, and some of them have low vision or are color-blind. Work that only functions in perfect conditions fails the people it is meant for.

In summary, four commitments apply across all marketing work:

- Text is readable against its background. The palette has been measured, and not every pairing is suitable for small text. Ember in particular needs care.
- Images carry a text description, so nobody loses the point of a piece because an image did not load or cannot be seen.
- Meaning is never carried by color alone. A chart or status needs a label, a shape or a pattern too.
- Pages work with a keyboard and at high zoom, and video has captions.

The misses that come up most at review are predictable. A chart legend that relies on Ember versus Verdigris alone is hard to read for some color-blind readers, since those two are close in lightness. An Ember link in a paragraph looks fine on a designer's monitor and is hard to read on a laptop in daylight. Text set into an image can't be read by a screen reader and can't be translated. Video exported from a webinar tool often ships with captions switched off.

Accessibility review belongs to whoever does the brand check on a piece, and it isn't a separate stage. If a template fails, Noor's team fixes the template, so the same miss doesn't come back in every piece made from it.

The specific requirements are in the visual accessibility guidance, and the measured color pairs are in the logo and color addendum. Bricolage Grotesque's limit on small sizes, in section 8, is as much an accessibility point as a matter of taste.

Most company posts follow the same order.

1. **The fact.** What shipped, what was measured, what happened. Put the number here if there is one.
2. **The context.** Two or three sentences on why it matters to someone running clusters or answering for them.
3. **The way out.** One link, with a short instruction in front of it.

Then stop. If you have a second point, it is a second post next week.

The brand idea is a wick: the place where a fire is allowed to exist. Use that vocabulary and its everyday relatives.

| Idea | Shapes that work |
|---|---|
| Containment | A ring around a small flame, a tray, a snuffer held above a wick, a firebreak cut through paper grass |
| Isolation of a workload | One tile lifted out of a grid, a pod shape with a paper band around it |
| Posture and drift (Evenburn) | A row of even flames with one leaning, a level, a line of tiles slightly out of true |
| Tool-call policy (Leashgate) | A short tether, a gate latch, a loop of cord around a post |
| On-call | A lamp and a mug, a single lit window in a dark paper building |
| Fix order | Steps cut from paper, three stones across a stream |

Keep the flame small. A small flame contained is the entire idea, and a large one means disaster, so the flame should stay well under a tenth of the frame. If the concept seems to need a wall of fire, the concept is wrong.

Kubernetes has its own visual habit of hexagons and ship wheels. Do not draw the Kubernetes logo, which is someone else's mark. Pods are tiles. Nodes are trays or shelves. Clusters are groups of those on a shared ground.

The mark is a geometric W whose center stroke rises as a wick, tipped by one Ember dot. It says the same thing as the brand idea: a straight, deliberate structure with one small, controlled point of heat at the top. The dot is the only warm thing in the mark, and that is the reason to protect it. Used alongside the wordmark "Wickhold", it forms the lockup, which is the default in most layouts.

There are four approved variants: ink on transparent, reversed on transparent, on a Tallow panel, and on a Soot panel. Exact file specifications, clear space and minimum sizes are in the logo and color addendum. How to choose among the variants for a given layout belongs to the logo-in-context guidance.

The 2024 shield-and-flame logo is retired. It still appears in the archive and in a few old files, and it should not be used in anything new.

The logo appears once in a layout, and it usually doesn't need to be large. Confidence in a mark shows in how much room it's given, so a modest logo with space around it is better than a big one crowded by other elements. In the product, the mark appears in the console header and on the sign-in page. Screens that a customer works in all day don't need it anywhere else.

Two pieces of history are worth keeping in mind. In the first month after launch, the product team shipped a loading state with a flickering dot, and customers read it as an error. It was withdrawn. The dot does not move. And early on, several people tried turning the W into a pattern for backgrounds and swag. The mark loses its meaning when it repeats, because the whole point is that there is one of it. Use it once per layout.

Agents are moving from demos into production clusters, and the tools they call are real: a ticketing API, a database, a deploy pipeline, a shell. An agent that reads a poisoned document or a hostile web page can be talked into calling those tools with the permissions its owner gave it. Leashgate prevents prompt injection from becoming an incident. It sits between the agent and its tools, gives each agent a verifiable identity, and checks every tool call against policy before the call goes through.

Runtime policy for AI agents and their tool calls: that is the whole product. It comes from the same place Wickhold Quenchline did. Assume something will go wrong inside the workload, decide ahead of time how far it can go, and make that limit hold on the platform where the workload runs.

The company did not change what it builds. Quenchline has offered detection and containment since September 2020. What changed is which half of that sentence the brand leads with. In the 2024 identity, the watching came first and containment was a feature. In the 2026 identity, containment is the point and detection is what makes it possible. Detection still matters to buyers and should be described accurately. It just isn't the headline.

Evenburn fits the same logic from the other direction. Posture work reduces how much there is to catch fire, and it gives the team a fix order so that the worst exposure path gets closed first. The story to tell is about keeping the fuel down, and it shouldn't be told as a second, separate product category.

Leashgate extends the idea to AI agents, which now take actions inside customers' environments. An agent with broad tools is a new kind of workload that can make a mistake quickly. Leashgate sets out what that agent may do and keeps a record of what it did. It is in early access, and the position should be described with that in mind: a direction the company is working in, with real customers trying it.

", "end_line": 9, "heading_path": ["WICKHOLD SECURITY BRAND GUIDELINES"], "ref": "source_173", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_v3_FINAL.md", "start_line": 1}, {"content": "## Banned terms

There are thirteen. They stay out of headlines, body copy, decks, alt text and speaker notes that leave the building. When one shows up in a draft it usually marks the spot where the writer ran out of facts, so deleting it rarely fixes the sentence. Find the fact.

| Term | Why it is out | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| seamless | Putting an eBPF agent on every node has seams: a kernel check, a Helm upgrade, a stretch in observe mode. Platform engineers know this and stop reading when told otherwise. | Say what the rollout takes. |
| robust | Strong against what? The word claims a result and skips the test. | Name the failure the thing survived. |
| leverage | A finance word doing a job that "use" does for free. | Use "use". |
| best-in-class | No class, no judge, no source. It cannot pass "say the number, then stop". | Give the figure and where it came from. |
| next-gen | Every product in this market has been next-gen at some point. The word ages the day it ships. | Say what it does on a node today. |
| single pane of glass | Our readers have been sold this pane many times and own several. It also describes watching, and the job here is containing. | Name the screen and what it shows. |
| holistic | Usually covering for a gap. If something spans cloud and cluster, those two words are shorter and checkable. | List what is covered. |
| unlock | Implies the customer's own work was locked up and we hold the key. Drags padlocks into the room as well. | Say what the reader can now do. |
| empower | The readers already have root. Nobody here hands out power. | Say what changed for them, in a verb they would use. |
| cutting-edge | A claim about us, and an undated one. eBPF is well past being new, and that is one reason it is safe to run in production. | Name the technique. |
| game-changing | An incident is nobody's game, and the claim has no number attached. | Give the before and after. |
| prevent all | A promise no security product can keep. Includes "prevents all", which is the same promise with better grammar. | See the verbs below. |
| stop all | Same promise, same problem. A CISO who reads this line once will discount the rest of the page. | See the verbs below. |

The prose test: if a sentence still reads as true after you swap the product for a toaster, it needed a fact and got an adjective.

", "end_line": 26, "heading_path": ["Word list", "Banned terms"], "ref": "source_174", "relative_path": "brand/voice/word-list.md", "start_line": 5}, {"content": "## Early access: what partners get

", "end_line": 135, "heading_path": ["Wickhold Leashgate", "Early access: what partners get"], "ref": "source_175", "relative_path": "brand/products/leashgate-overview.md", "start_line": 126}, {"content": "## What it does not do

- It does not decide whether an allowed call was wise. A policy that allows `tickets.update` allows a bad ticket update.

", "end_line": 125, "heading_path": ["Wickhold Leashgate", "What it does not do"], "ref": "source_176", "relative_path": "brand/products/leashgate-overview.md", "start_line": 118}, {"content": "## 3. Values

There are four, and they are written the way an on-call lead would say them.

**Say what happened.**
Report the event in plain order: what occurred, what was affected, what was done, what is next. This applies to incident reports, release notes, customer emails and the company's own mistakes. When a release goes badly, the customer note says so in the first sentence.

Good: "The last Wickhold Quenchline release raised CPU use on nodes running older kernels. A fix shipped on Tuesday. Here is how to check whether you were affected."

Bad: "We're always working to improve performance, and our latest update includes important enhancements."

**Contain first.**
In an incident, limit the damage before explaining it. In marketing, the same ordering applies: the first thing a reader gets is the thing that helps them, and the story of how it came about can wait. The value also sets the company's posture. Wickhold talks about containing, limiting and slowing. A promise of a world with no incidents is a promise no honest vendor can keep.

Good: "At Lowmoor Credit Union, time to contain fell from 4 hours to 11 minutes across 220 nodes."

That example gives the result with no adjectives around it and leaves the reader to decide what it means.

**Admit limits.**
Every product has edges, and engineers find them within a week. Naming a limit in advance costs less than having a customer discover it during a bad night, and it makes everything else the company says easier to believe.

Good: "Wickhold Quenchline works at runtime. It does not review code before it ships."

**Leave it better for the next on-call.**
This one comes straight from the founders. When an on-call shift ends, the next person should find the runbook updated, the noisy alert tuned and the handoff note written. Inside marketing it means naming source files sensibly, recording why a decision was made, and putting a correction in the document that was wrong and not only in a thread. It is why the "tried and dropped" list in section 1 exists.

", "end_line": 108, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "3. Values"], "ref": "source_177", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 83}, {"content": "## One screen, worked through

The request: show that Quenchline can freeze a process during an incident.

First attempt: the whole incident page at 1600x1000, with the timeline, three tiles, a side panel of pod details and a chat widget from the demo tenant. As a column image it was unreadable, and the one thing that mattered was a small status chip.

Second attempt: a crop to the timeline row showing the containment action and the status chip, with the page title kept above it. One Ember ring on the chip. One callout: "Process frozen, evidence kept". It reads at column width and it says one thing. That is the standard to aim for.

", "end_line": 94, "heading_path": ["Product UI screenshots", "One screen, worked through"], "ref": "source_178", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/product-ui-screenshots.md", "start_line": 87}, {"content": "## Preferred terms

**Workload, not asset.** Customers run workloads, and that is the word they use in their own runbooks. "Asset" comes from inventory spreadsheets and suggests a thing that sits still. A workload moves, restarts and misbehaves, which is why it needs a runtime product. Inside the marketing team "asset" still means a blog post or an image file; that use never reaches a customer.

**Contain, limit and slow, rather than prevent.** This is the company's argument in three verbs. Something will go wrong on a Tuesday night regardless of what anyone buys. Wickhold Quenchline contains what is already running. Wickhold Evenburn limits exposure. Wickhold Leashgate limits what an agent can reach. "Slow" is the honest verb when the action buys time and does not end the problem. Also keep "eliminate" and "eradicate" out of it; they are "prevent" in a bigger coat.

Use "contain" only when a containment action actually happens. Detection on its own is detection.

One exception came out of a release-notes review. A line saying a patch prevents a crash in the agent is describing our own bug, so it can stay. The rule covers promises about what happens to customers, and a changelog entry makes none.

**Customers, not clients.** Clients have an account manager and a lunch. Customers run our agent in production and page us. A "client" in the software sense stays: `kubectl` is a client, an email client is a client. "Users" is fine when you mean the people logged in to the console, because a customer is the whole company.

", "end_line": 108, "heading_path": ["WICKHOLD SECURITY BRAND GUIDELINES", "4. Our Messaging"], "ref": "source_180", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_v3_FINAL.md", "start_line": 107}, {"content": "### Order of authority

When two sources conflict, the higher one on this list wins:

1. **Legal-approved claims.** The approved claims, certification status, regional rules and customer quote policy owned by Priit Salonen, General Counsel.
2. **These 2026 guidelines**, together with the logo and color addendum, which has the same standing.
3. **Channel playbooks.** The working guides for each channel.
4. **Everything else.** This includes the voice and style documents, messaging, personas, product overviews, templates, sales material, meeting notes and Slack.

So the order is: legal-approved claims, then the 2026 guidelines, then channel playbooks, then everything else.

A lower source is not void. It applies wherever nothing above it speaks to the question. A template's rule, or a decision recorded in meeting notes or Slack by the person who owns the topic, is followed like any other rule until a higher source contradicts it. The order settles conflicts and does not rank importance. If a document at the bottom of the list has the only rule on a subject, that is the rule.

", "end_line": 467, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "11. Governance", "Order of authority"], "ref": "source_181", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 455}, {"content": "## Founder voice and brand voice

There are two voices at Wickhold, and they have one hard line between them.

**Founder voice is first person singular, and it is signed.** Maren writes as "I". Her posts carry her name. She gets to have feelings and doubts, tell a story from a bad night in 2017, and be wrong in public. Dov's technical posts work the same way and are signed "Dov".

**Brand voice never says "I" or "we think".** Website, product pages, company LinkedIn, the company X account, email, decks, reports: no first person singular, ever. "We believe", "we feel" and "in our view" are "we think" in different shoes, and they go too.

**Brand voice uses "Wickhold" or "we" for facts only.** Things that happened, things that are true of the company, things a lawyer could check.

| Fine in brand voice | Not in brand voice |
|---|---|
| We renewed SOC 2 Type II in January 2026. | We think SOC 2 matters. |
| Wickhold serves more than 140 customers. | I've talked to a lot of platform teams. |
| Containment is where incidents are won or lost. | We believe containment is where incidents are won or lost. |

The third row is the useful one. Brand voice still holds opinions. It states them as flat sentences, the way the on-call lead does, and lets the reader disagree. "We think" adds nothing except a hedge.

Practicalities. Nobody else writes as "I" in Wickhold content. Kofi's developer posts and anything from the wider team run in brand voice under a byline, because a byline is credit and a founder post is a person speaking for themselves. Customer quotes are quotes and say whatever was approved. If the content team drafts for Maren, she reads it and changes it before her name goes on, and a post that she has not read does not go out. In the spring a joint Maren-and-Dov byline was tried on one post; "I" became unreadable after two paragraphs, so that was dropped. One author per post.

", "end_line": 179, "heading_path": ["Release notes 2026", "February 3, 2026: Quenchline 4.6.1"], "ref": "source_191", "relative_path": "brand/products/release-notes-2026.md", "start_line": 176}, {"content": "## Judging library photos by eye

The library's metadata does not catch everything. Some old or off-brand photos are sitting in the library with an empty `restrictions` field, because nobody ever marked them. Some of them have sensible titles and tags. A clean record tells you nobody objected. You still have to look at the picture.

Open it at full size and ask:

1. **What color are the shadows?** Ours fall warm, toward brown or neutral. If the shadows go blue, it belongs to the 2024 era or to a stock site. The look of that era was bright, cold and very blue, and it clashes hard with Ember on the same page.
2. **Is the light real?** Even, shadowless light across a whole room means a set or a heavy edit.
3. **Is anybody posing?** Direct eye contact with the lens, crossed arms, a group laughing at a laptop: reject.
4. **Could this photo appear on any company's site?** If yes, reject it. We want to see a detail that belongs to this work.

If a photo fails one of these and has no restriction on it, do not use it, and tell Brand so the record can be updated. That second part helps the next person.

Examples from recent draft reviews:

| Draft used | Verdict | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Rack aisle, cold blue light, faint haze, no people | Rejected | Clean metadata, wrong look |
| Woman with headset smiling at the camera in a bright open office | Rejected | Posed and generic |
| Engineer's hands, laptop glow, dim closet behind | Approved | Warm, specific, one focal point |
| Three people at a whiteboard, one mid-gesture, late sun on the wall | Approved | Available light, real moment |

", "end_line": 62, "heading_path": ["Photography", "Judging library photos by eye"], "ref": "source_192", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/photography.md", "start_line": 41}, {"content": "## 4. Shape of a post

A title that says what the reader will get. Then the intro. Then three to five sections with descriptive headings. Then an ending that tells the reader what to do on Monday.

Titles we liked:

- Contain mode, one namespace at a time
- What drift looks like after a Helm upgrade
- The six hours after detection
- Writing your first tool-call policy for Wickhold Leashgate, in early access

Titles we rewrote:

- "5 Kubernetes Security Mistakes You're Making Right Now" became "Five findings we see in most new clusters"
- "Everything You Need To Know About eBPF" became "What our eBPF agent can and can't see"

Section headings should still make sense if they're all someone reads. "Background" and "The solution" tell the reader nothing.

End on the practical next step, then one call to action to the most relevant page. Don't summarize what you just said. If the post was good, they remember. Don't add a paragraph about Wickhold at the bottom either, as the footer handles that.

", "end_line": 4, "heading_path": ["Email header images"], "ref": "source_223", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/email-header.md", "start_line": 1}, {"content": "## 3. Banned claims

| Do not say | Say instead, or do this | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| "prevents prompt injection" | "limits what a compromised agent can do" | Leashgate acts on tool calls. It does not read intent and it cannot promise that an agent will not be manipulated. The claim is false as a matter of product design |
| "FedRAMP Authorized", "FedRAMP certified" | See section 4 | Neither is true |
| "GDPR compliant" | Use the regional rules | Regional wording sits there, and the ban is not limited to that region |
| "breach-proof", "unhackable", "impossible to escape" | Describe the containment action | No security product can support an absolute |
| "zero false positives", "100% detection", "catches everything" | Give a sourced figure or say nothing | We hold no such evidence |
| "guarantee", "guaranteed", "warranty" outside a contract | Remove | These words have legal effect. Service credits live in the order form |
| "the leading", "the fastest", "No. 1", "the only" | Remove, or bring me the comparison data | Superlatives need current comparative substantiation, and we do not hold any |
| "certified by", "endorsed by", "partner of" for any standards body or open-source project | Remove | Using eBPF or Helm is not an endorsement from anyone |
| "saves $X", any return-on-investment figure | Remove | We have no approved financial outcome for any customer |

Two refinements, because they keep coming back:

"Helps prevent" is a banned claim dressed up. A qualifier in front of a promise does not make it a limited promise.

"Compliance-ready" and "audit-ready" were requested in June for a trust page and refused. Wickhold can describe what the product records. Whether a customer passes an audit depends on the customer and the auditor.

", "end_line": 98, "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "3. Banned claims"], "ref": "source_451", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md", "start_line": 79}, {"content": "## 8. Technical writing in marketing copy

Kofi Anselm's team reviews anything containing code, and their rules are short.

- **Code formatting** for commands, flags, file names, field names, namespaces, node names and anything a person might type: `kubectl get pods`, `--namespace`, `values.yaml`.
- **Every snippet is run before it's published.** Say which version it was run against. A snippet nobody ran does not go out, even in a slide.
- **Placeholder values** look like placeholders or like real workloads: `payments`, `checkout`, `worker-7`. Don't use `foo`, and don't use the name of a real company, a real customer or a celebrity.
- **Domains and email addresses in examples** use `wickhold.example`.
- **Long output** gets trimmed, with a line saying so. Don't silently edit output.
- **Failure modes** are part of the example. If a command fails in a common way, say how it looks.

", "end_line": 153, "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "8. Technical writing in marketing copy"], "ref": "source_452", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "start_line": 143}, {"content": "## 4. Numbers

", "end_line": 222, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "5. Brand architecture"], "ref": "source_456", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 219}, {"content": "## Who should apply

Early access suits platform and security teams that already have at least one agent in production, or are about to, and have someone who can own policy. Teams still deciding whether to run agents at all should wait. There will be plenty to read as we learn more.

Your account team can tell you more, or you can apply directly.

*Wickhold is the runtime security company for teams that run Kubernetes. Its products contain failures early, so small fires stay small. Founded in 2019 and based in Denver, Wickhold serves more than 140 customers.*
", "end_line": 81, "heading_path": ["Wickhold Leashgate enters early access", "Who should apply"], "ref": "source_457", "relative_path": "brand/archive/blog/leashgate_early_access_notes.md", "start_line": 73}, {"content": "## What Leashgate does not do

Leashgate does not read prompts and it does not judge whether a model has been manipulated. It has no opinion on the quality of an agent's output, and it will not catch an agent that gives a customer bad advice through a tool it is allowed to use. What it controls is the set of actions available to the agent. A permitted action that happens to be a poor decision will still go through, so policy needs the same care you would give any access review.

No threat-actor drama. No ticking clocks.

The rule is simple to state and gets broken constantly, because fear copy is the easiest copy in security to write. {"passages": [{"content": "## Photos by setting

**Team and office.** Real desks, real clutter. Aim for moments between people, with one person clearly the focus of the frame. Conference-room shots work when something is happening on the table. The office kitchen works better than the boardroom.

**Infrastructure.** Shoot close. A patch panel with handwritten labels says more than a long aisle. Cables, breakers, fans, a rack door left open. Whatever the room's own lighting does, keep it warm in the edit, and if the room is lit cold and cannot be corrected, get closer to a warm lamp or drop the shot.

**Customer scenes.** The grocery distribution office, the credit union's back room, a store's network closet. These are the most valuable photos we have, since they show Kubernetes and its operators somewhere other than a startup. They also have the most paperwork behind them. A customer scene looks ordinary and that is the point: no hero angles.

**Remote on-call.** Kitchen tables and spare rooms, a laptop at dusk, a phone face-up beside it. On-call happens at home and most stock libraries do not show it. Keep faces turned away unless the person is a signed volunteer.

", "end_line": 123, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning"], "ref": "source_231", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 122}, {"content": "# Capitalization + product names (quick sheet)

Pinned for the web team after three separate spellings turned up on one page.

Full form on first mention, short form after. First mention means the first place the name appears in a piece, and a headline counts.

| First mention | After that |
|---|---|
| Wickhold Quenchline | Quenchline |
| Wickhold Evenburn | Evenburn |
| Wickhold Leashgate | Leashgate |

One capital each. Never QuenchLine, EvenBurn or LeashGate. No internal caps, no hyphens, no all-caps in slides or nav.

Each piece starts over. A blog post that says Wickhold Quenchline does not earn the short form in the email promoting it.

Evenburn took its name on March 2, 2026. Don't write the former name in current copy, including "formerly" lines. Support handles customers who still ask for it.

Right: "Wickhold Evenburn ranks drift by exposure path. Evenburn does not contain anything at runtime."

Wrong: "Evenburn ranks drift" as the opening line, with the full name saved for the footer.

Nav labels and pricing table rows can use the short form. The page's first heading or sentence still uses the full one.

Never combine products into one name ("Quenchline-Evenburn suite"). There is no suite. If you mean more than one, name them.

**Company:** Wickhold. "Wickhold Security" retired with the rebrand on February 10, 2026. Wickhold, Inc. appears in contracts and legal footers and nowhere else.

**Lowercase, always:** contain mode, observe mode, containment action, default containment policy, drift, exposure path, fix order, tool-call policy, agent identity. These are concepts, not features with a logo.

**Capitalized:** tiers (Core, Team, Enterprise), Slow Burn Summit, Field Day, Wickhold Containment Report. "The report" on second reference, lowercase. Series A and Series B take capitals; SOC 2 Type II is set as shown.

Possessives are fine (Quenchline's agent). Skip the article: "Quenchline contains", never "the Quenchline".

The report had a different name before 2025: Wickhold Field Report. Keep that name when citing an edition that carried it. Don't rename old editions.

Feature names don't get "Wickhold" in front of them, and they don't get a trademark symbol. Neither do the products in running copy.

Lowercase product names only in code, where the tool demands it.
", "end_line": 39, "heading_path": ["Capitalization + product names (quick sheet)"], "ref": "source_232", "relative_path": "brand/style/capitalization-product-names.md", "start_line": 1}, {"content": "## One rewrite, start to finish

> We're excited to announce that we think our powerful new drift capabilities will transform how modern teams approach cloud risk, giving you the confidence you need in an increasingly dangerous world.

The edit went like this.

"We're excited to announce" went first. The reader's interest in our excitement is zero.

"We think" is out, because this is brand voice.

"Powerful", "new" and "modern" were doing nothing. Remove them and the sentence gets more honest and no less informative.

"Increasingly dangerous world" is the fear habit, and it also isn't something we can source.

Never say "GDPR compliant". Not about Wickhold, its products, its customers' deployments or any feature. The ban began with EU and UK copy and it now applies everywhere, including US pages that a European buyer can obviously read.

The approved wording is:

> Wickhold supports customers' GDPR obligations.

Use it as written. GDPR obligations belong to the controller and the processor and depend on what they do with the data. No vendor product can make a customer compliant, and a regulator or a procurement lawyer will read the phrase as a promise.

Variants that have turned up in drafts, all refused:

- "GDPR-ready"
- "fully GDPR aligned"
- "compliant with EU privacy law"
- "UK GDPR certified"

If a UK reader needs the point spelled out, the approved sentence covers UK GDPR. Do not add a second claim.

Examples:

| Bad | Good |
|---|---|
| Our GDPR compliant platform keeps EU workloads safe. | Wickhold supports customers' GDPR obligations. |
| Quenchline makes your clusters GDPR compliant. | Wickhold Quenchline records each containment action with a timestamp. Wickhold supports customers' GDPR obligations. |

A word on tone. European security buyers we've met through Field Day meetups tend to ask for the document and not the promise, so a short, flat statement does better than a paragraph about how seriously we take privacy. If a page has one line on GDPR, the approved sentence is that line. Don't surround it with "privacy-first" or "by design", which raise the same problem in softer words.

", "end_line": 34, "heading_path": ["Regional rules: EU and UK copy", "GDPR wording"], "ref": "source_237", "relative_path": "brand/legal/regional-rules-eu-uk.md", "start_line": 7}, {"content": "## Terminals and CLI output

Engineers often trust a terminal capture over a dashboard. Use a plain terminal at a normal size with IBM Plex Mono, on a Soot background, with the prompt trimmed to `$`. The command has to be real and its output has to be pasted from a real run in the demo environment. Do not edit output to shorten it. ", "end_line": 86, "heading_path": ["Product UI screenshots", "Terminals and CLI output"], "ref": "source_238", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/product-ui-screenshots.md", "start_line": 83}, {"content": "### Tool-call policy

A tool-call policy is a declarative rule set, stored as a Kubernetes custom resource. It says which agent may call which tool, with what arguments, how often, and whether a person must approve first.

```yaml
apiVersion: leashgate.wickhold.example/v1alpha1
kind: ToolCallPolicy
metadata:
  name: support-triage-agent
  namespace: support
spec:
  agentSelector:
    matchLabels:
      agent: support-triage
  defaultAction: deny
  rules:
    - tool: tickets.search
      action: allow
    - tool: tickets.update
      action: allow
      arguments:
        status:
          oneOf: [open, pending, resolved]
      rate: 60/minute
    - tool: crm.export
      action: requireApproval
      approvers: [group:support-leads]
      timeout: 10m
    - tool: shell.*
      action: deny
```

`defaultAction: deny` is the default and we recommend leaving it there. Note the `v1alpha1` in the API version: field names may change during early access, and design partners should expect at least one schema migration.

Every approved image lives in the image library, and every image in it has a metadata record. Do not pick from the thumbnail grid and stop there. The thumbnail does not show you the limits on the image.

| Field | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| `id`, `filename` | Identity. Filenames were set by different people across several years and tell you little. |
| `type`, `title` | Rough category and a human label. |
| `description` | What is in the picture. Often thin, sometimes empty. |
| `tags` | Search help. Inconsistent, so never treat a missing tag as meaning anything. |
| `usage_rights` | The grant we hold for the file. |
| `restrictions` | The limits on this particular image. See below. |
| `added_date` | When it entered the library, which is not when it was made. |
| `source`, `attribution` | Where it came from. In-house work reads `internal-production`, and `attribution` is usually empty or names the in-house team. Empty attribution means no credit line is needed. |
| `width`, `height` | Pixel size. Check before you plan a crop. |
| `background` | How the image relates to what sits behind it. See below. |
| `safe_on` | Which grounds it can sit on. See below. |
| `variant_of` | Points at the parent when the image is one version of another. |

Every agent gets an identity tied to the workload rather than a shared API key. Leashgate takes a projected, audience-bound service account token from the pod and exchanges it for a short-lived agent credential, by default valid for 15 minutes. Policies and logs refer to that identity, so "which agent did this" has a precise answer even when ten agents share a framework and a namespace.

Agents acting for a human user can pass that user's identity along. Policy can then require both, so an agent cannot use a tool its current user could not use directly. This is the case design partners ask about most.

", "end_line": 28, "heading_path": ["Wickhold Leashgate", "Core concepts", "Agent identity"], "ref": "source_262", "relative_path": "brand/products/leashgate-overview.md", "start_line": 23}, {"content": "## How the visual rules are layered

Three layers, read in this order.

1. **This page.** Applies to everything.
2. **The category.** What kind of image is it? Photo, illustration, icon, logo, product screenshot, chart, social graphic, event graphic, legal and trust imagery, anything showing a person.
3. **The content type.** Where is it going? Blog hero, LinkedIn, X, email header, landing page.

", "end_line": 20, "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "How the visual rules are layered"], "ref": "source_263", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "start_line": 7}, {"content": "## The style

**Flat cut-paper shapes.** Crisp edges with a slight hand-cut irregularity. Layers can overlap. Depth comes from stacking, and the only shadow allowed is a hard offset shape in one flat, darker tone.

**One Ember focal element.** Exactly one thing in the picture is Ember. That is where the eye goes. Everything else is Soot, Tallow, or a small amount of Whetstone or Verdigris.

**On Tallow or Soot.** Those are the only two grounds for finished illustration. An Ember ground removes the focal element, because nothing can stand out from it. Whetstone and Verdigris grounds look muddy.

**No gradients.** None, anywhere: no soft shadows, glows, blurs, mesh fills or textured airbrush. If a shape needs to look lit, cut a second shape. In review, this is the rule most often broken by accident, usually by a shadow effect left on by default in the design tool or by an export that adds banding.

Also out: outlines around shapes, 3D, isometric projection, photographic textures pasted on shapes, and stock vector packs. We tried isometric cluster diagrams in January. They looked like every infrastructure startup's site, and they required a depth that flat paper cannot give.

", "end_line": 269, "heading_path": ["WICKHOLD SECURITY BRAND GUIDELINES", "6. Our Colors", "How much of each"], "ref": "source_277", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_v3_FINAL.md", "start_line": 263}, {"content": "## What Leashgate does

Leashgate sits between an agent and the tools it calls. It works with three concepts.

**Agent identity.** Each agent gets its own identity, separate from the human who launched it and from the service account of the pod it runs in. Logs and policies refer to that identity, so "which agent did this" has an answer.

**Tool-call policy.** A team writes down which tools an agent may call, with which arguments, on which targets. A support agent may read a customer record but may not export a table. A deployment agent may restart a service in staging but may not touch production. Calls outside the policy are blocked and logged.

**Containment.** A call that breaks policy can trigger the same kind of response platform teams already use with Quenchline. If an agent starts behaving badly, it can be cut off from its tools while a human takes a look, and the rest of the application keeps running.

Put simply, Leashgate limits what a compromised agent can do.

A short example of a tool-call policy, in the shape early access customers are using:

```yaml
agent: support-triage
tools:
  - name: crm.read_record
    allow: true
  - name: crm.export
    allow: false
  - name: tickets.update
    allow: true
    when:
      field: status
on_violation: suspend_agent
```

The format may change during early access. We will tell participants before it does.

Leashgate can ask Quenchline to act. If a policy marks a repeated-denial pattern as suspicious, it can request a containment action, normally isolating the agent pod's network, through the same pipeline Quenchline uses for its own detections. This requires Quenchline on the node. The feature is off by default.

Every decision record goes to the same export path as Quenchline's, so a SIEM rule can correlate a denied tool call with the runtime events around it.

Wickhold Security was founded in Denver in March 2019 by Maren Tolliver and Dov Achterberg. Both had spent years as on-call infrastructure leads, and both had the same complaint: by the time anybody knew something was wrong in a cluster, it was already somebody's very long night. Existing tools were built for servers that stayed put, and Kubernetes workloads do anything but.

So they built the tool they wished they'd had. Wickhold Quenchline reached general availability in September 2020, bringing runtime detection and containment to Kubernetes through a lightweight eBPF agent. Our Series A followed in March 2022 at $18M, and with it came Wickhold Tallowatch, extending the same always-on approach to cloud and cluster posture. In June 2024 we closed our $46M Series B, led by Marlbank Partners, to take the platform further and faster.

Today over 80+ teams rely on Wickhold Security to know what is running, what has changed, and what needs attention right now.

When you tell this story, keep these three beats in order:

1. **Founders who carried the pager.** We are operators first.
2. **A product that never blinks.** Continuous beats periodic, every time.
3. **Momentum.** More teams, more funding, more coverage.

---

", "end_line": 108, "heading_path": ["Product UI screenshots", "Metadata for new captures"], "ref": "source_308", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/product-ui-screenshots.md", "start_line": 105}, {"content": "## March 2, 2026: Wickhold Tallowatch is now Wickhold Evenburn
