", "end_line": 161, "heading_path": ["Release notes 2026", "March 2, 2026: Wickhold Tallowatch is now Wickhold Evenburn"], "ref": "source_309", "relative_path": "brand/products/release-notes-2026.md", "start_line": 145}, {"content": "## How it relates to what teams already run

Leashgate does not replace network policy, RBAC or Wickhold Quenchline, and it should be added to them. Network policy decides which hosts a pod can reach. RBAC decides what a service account can do in the cluster. Quenchline watches processes and connections on the node. None of them can tell that a permitted HTTPS call to the ticketing system was an agent closing every open ticket. That is the layer Leashgate works at: the named tool, its arguments and the identity making the call.

Because the agent's tool calls pass through Leashgate, every call is also logged with the agent identity attached. Several teams in our design conversations cared more about this record than about blocking. When a security reviewer asks what an agent did last Thursday, the team can answer without searching application logs.

", "end_line": 61, "heading_path": ["Wickhold Leashgate enters early access", "How it relates to what teams already run"], "ref": "source_310", "relative_path": "brand/archive/blog/leashgate_early_access_notes.md", "start_line": 56}, {"content": "## 10. Tried and dropped

==========

Kofi Anselm / DevRel. Written June 2026 when marketing handed the account over to us. Short on purpose.

The audience on X is platform engineers, SREs and the people who maintain the projects we depend on. Nobody on there is shopping. They follow accounts that post useful things and are funny about once a week.

**Length.** An X post from any Wickhold account is 240 characters at most. The platform allows more. We stop at 240 so a post can be quoted with a comment and still read whole, and because anything longer is usually two thoughts. Count the raw text, including the link as typed.

**Who has the password.** DevRel owns the main account. Marketing queues launch posts and report posts; DevRel reviews them. Noor can pull anything at any time. Two-factor is on the shared vault, and nobody posts from a personal phone without it.

**What goes out**

- Release notes in one line, with a link
- Findings from the Containment Report, one figure per post
- Practical tips: an eBPF gotcha, a kubectl one-liner, something odd about containerd
- Clips from Slow Burn Summit talks and Field Day
- CVE notes when a CVE touches something we ship or something our customers run a lot of, with facts and the fix

About three to five posts a week. More during Summit, fewer in December. Nothing goes out just to fill a slot in the calendar.

**What a good post looks like**

One thought. A concrete noun in the first few words. If there is a link, it comes last.

Good:

> Wickhold Quenchline can drain a node for you if your policy says so. It will not write the postmortem.

> 41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].

> Tip: run contain mode on one namespace first. Observe mode tells you what would have happened. Contain mode tells you who in that namespace forgot to mention a sidecar.

> The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. That is one whole on-call shift, plus a sandwich.

> Wickhold Evenburn's fix order will not make the list shorter. It will tell you which line to start on.

", "end_line": 37, "heading_path": ["X playbook"], "ref": "source_316", "relative_path": "brand/channels/x-playbook.md", "start_line": 1}, {"content": "## Demo data

**Headlines are in sentence case.** Capitalize the first word and any proper noun. Everything else is lowercase.

This covers page titles, blog titles, section headings, email subject lines, slide titles, buttons, nav labels, form labels, table headers and any text set over an image. If it looks like a heading, it is one.

| Right | Wrong |
|---|---|
| What contain mode does to a running pod | What Contain Mode Does To A Running Pod |
| Wickhold Containment Report 2026 | WICKHOLD CONTAINMENT REPORT 2026 |
| How Ostler Grocers cut its open critical misconfigurations | How Ostler Grocers Cut Its Open Critical Misconfigurations |

Details:

- Product names, event names and the report title keep their capitals, as do Kubernetes, Helm, CVE and the rest of the proper vocabulary. `containerd` and `eBPF` keep their lowercase starts even as the first word, though it's nicer to rewrite so that neither opens a headline.
- The word after a colon is lowercase: "Drift: what it is and how to read it".
- No full stop on headlines. The tagline is the one exception, and it keeps its full stop everywhere.
- No code formatting in headlines. They break in email clients and in link previews.
- Keep a headline to one idea. If it needs a colon and a dash, it's two headlines.

The old sheet used Title Case for everything over 24px. That went in the rebrand, and pages still carrying it get fixed when someone next touches them.

", "end_line": 35, "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "1. Headlines"], "ref": "source_321", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "start_line": 14}, {"content": "### The Wickhold Field Report

The Field Report is our flagship piece of research and the source of our best numbers, so it gets the full treatment. Covers are full-bleed Cobalt with a large statistic set in Inter ExtraBold White, and inside pages use White with Sky chart accents. The lead finding from the 2023 edition, that 68% of runtime incidents began with a misconfigured workload, is the model to follow: one sharp number that a reporter can repeat. When you quote a Field Report figure, quote it exactly and name the edition.

", "end_line": 230, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "5. Brand architecture", "Writing the company name"], "ref": "source_323", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 227}, {"content": "### Email and event lists

A great customer story follows the arc of challenge, solution, results. Lead with the team's name and logo where we have permission, and pull one quote into a Cobalt callout box. Marketing tracks who has agreed to what, so please check with us before naming anybody.

", "end_line": 438, "heading_path": ["WICKHOLD SECURITY BRAND GUIDELINES", "9. Putting It All Together", "Customer Stories"], "ref": "source_325", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_v3_FINAL.md", "start_line": 435}, {"content": "### Say the number, then stop

Claims carry a figure and a source. No adjective stacks.

"Fast" is not a claim. "A fast, powerful, highly scalable runtime platform" is three non-claims in a row. Write the number, say where it came from, and end the sentence. The urge to add a second sentence explaining why the number is impressive is the urge to resist. A reader who needs that sentence is the wrong reader; a reader who doesn't will think less of us for it.

Bad: "Lowmoor Credit Union saw an incredible, game-changing reduction in response times."

Good: "Lowmoor Credit Union cut time to contain from 4 hours to 11 minutes across 220 nodes."

Bad: "Quenchline is extremely lightweight and blazingly quick."

Good: "Wickhold Quenchline contains a known-bad process in a median of 38 seconds in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026."

If there is no figure, there is usually no claim, and the honest move is to describe what the product does in plain mechanical terms. "Isolates a pod's network" needs no number and no source. It's a description. "Industry-leading isolation" needs both and has neither.

", "end_line": 46, "heading_path": ["Blog hero images", "Avoiding repeats"], "ref": "source_329", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/blog-hero.md", "start_line": 43}, {"content": "### Products

", "end_line": 242, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "5. Brand architecture", "Products"], "ref": "source_330", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 231}, {"content": "## What the metadata means for photos

All photographs carry `background: scene`. A photograph keeps its environment: we do not cut people or objects out of their rooms, and we do not swap the sky through an office window. If you need a subject on a plain ground, you need an illustration.

Most photos are 1536x1024 landscape, with a few 1024x1536 portrait. Check `width` and `height` before you plan a layout around one. Upscaling a photo by more than about 20% shows.

`safe_on` is mostly `any` for photos, since a scene brings its own ground. A photo edge can still fight the layout. A dark, underexposed photo set straight on Soot loses its edges entirely, so give it margin or move it to a Tallow section.

`source` will read `internal-production` for in-house work, and `attribution` is often empty. We do not run photographer credits.

- **American spelling** in all copy, including copy going to UK and EU readers. Containerize, not containerise.
- **Oxford comma**, always. It has settled more than one argument in Kubernetes prose, where lists of nouns can double as lists of objects.

- **Contractions** are fine in the blog, on social and in email. Skip them on legal pages and in anything aimed at a board.
- **Colons** are our favorite punctuation mark and they're doing fine. Use them to introduce the fact.
- **Semicolons** at most once a page. If there are two, one wants to be a full stop.
- **Em dashes** rarely in body copy. Most are a full stop that lost its nerve. Spaced en dashes are not a substitute.
- **Parentheses** for the short aside only. If the aside matters, promote it to a sentence.
- **Quotation marks:** double, with commas and full stops inside, American style, except for literal strings in technical writing where the punctuation would change the meaning. Single quotes only inside double.

Leashgate has two parts, the gateway and the policy controller.

**The gateway** runs as a sidecar next to the agent or as a shared Deployment in the namespace. Agents point their tool endpoints at the gateway, either over HTTP or as an MCP server that proxies upstream MCP servers. For each call, the gateway verifies agent identity, evaluates the tool-call policy, writes a decision record and forwards or refuses the call. A refused call returns a structured error the agent can read, so a well-built agent can recover or ask for help rather than retry in a loop.

**The policy controller** watches `ToolCallPolicy` objects, validates them and distributes them to gateways. Gateways cache the last valid policy. If the gateway cannot evaluate a call for any reason, it refuses it. Leashgate fails closed, which means an outage of the gateway stops the agent's tools. That is the right behavior for a security control, and teams need to plan for it.

Install is one Helm chart, early access users only:

```bash
helm install leashgate wickhold/leashgate \
  --namespace wickhold-system \
  --set earlyAccess.token="$EA_TOKEN" \
  --set gateway.mode=sidecar
kubectl label namespace support leashgate.wickhold.example/inject=enabled
```

Requirements during early access: Kubernetes, any recent release, containerd, and agents that make tool calls over HTTP or MCP. Frameworks that call tools in-process, as plain function calls inside the agent's own memory, are out of scope unless the tool itself is reached over the network.

", "end_line": 262, "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "Reading old copy"], "ref": "source_352", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "start_line": 257}, {"content": "## 5. Statistics: 12-month age limit

A market statistic may not be older than 12 months at publication. This is the limit on how old a statistic can be, and it is measured on the day the piece goes out, not the day it was drafted. A post queued in March for release in May is checked against May.

The limit applies to market and survey statistics only. It covers any figure that describes the industry, the market, or a population of teams. It does not apply to customer results such as the Lowmoor and Ostler outcomes, or to product metrics such as the lab figures, which have their own qualifier.

The age of a statistic runs from the publication date of its source. Fieldwork dates do not matter. A report re-quoted in a newer article keeps its original date, so a 2026 article quoting a 2024 survey is a 2024 statistic.

Applied to our own reports:

| Source | Published | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Wickhold Containment Report 2026 | April 14, 2026 | Usable for publication through April 14, 2027 |
| Wickhold Field Report 2024 | 2024 | Past the 12 months limit |
| Wickhold Field Report 2023 | 2023 | Past the 12 months limit |

The two Containment Report statistics in section 1 are the only market statistics of ours inside the limit today. The Field Report figures still appear in old decks and old posts. That is an archive problem and not a permission. Do not reuse them. Do not reword them to make them feel new, and do not refer to them as "historically" true.

Fresh third-party statistics are allowed without coming to me first, with the source link and the date of the source in the copy. The source must be a named publisher and the figure must appear on the page you link to. A figure found in a vendor's blog, quoting another vendor's blog, gets traced to the original or is dropped. Wickhold is someone who has been paged more often than you have and is not going to bring it up.

**Unhurried.** Nothing in our copy is urgent. A page that hurries the reader is using the same trick as the alert fatigue they came to us to get away from.

**Exact.** "Isolated the pod's network" beats "took action". "220 nodes" beats "at scale". If two engineers would argue over what a sentence means, it isn't finished.

**Unimpressed by itself.** The product is useful. Copy that gasps at it reads as though the writer has not seen it fail. We have seen it fail, and the release notes say so.

**On your side of the pager.** The reader is a peer on the same rota, and we write to them as someone who could take the next shift. No lecturing, no "did you know", no explaining Kubernetes to people who run it.

When the character slips, it usually slips into one of four people:

- **The hero.** Rushes in, saves the day, gets the credit. Early rebrand drafts leaned on firefighters and helmets until Maren pointed out that a firefighter arriving means it already went badly. The customer's on-call team is the competent party in every story we tell.
- **The prophet.** Sees doom everywhere and sells shelter from it. The whole security industry's default register, which makes it invisible to the people we want to reach.
- **The buddy.** "Hey there, Kubernetes friends." Nobody paged at 3am wants a pal.
- **The analyst.** "In today's rapidly evolving threat landscape." Sentences with no one in them. If nothing would change when the paragraph is deleted, delete it.

The 2024 brand made a promise about watching. It suited a company that sold visibility, and it stopped fitting as the product moved on. By 2025 the feature customers talked about in renewals was the moment Wickhold Quenchline isolated a pod's network at 3am and nobody had to get out of bed. Sales calls kept going the same way: the prospect would say every tool they owned could see a problem, and then ask what happens next.

Ilse Varga-Holm, who owns the rebrand, started the work in spring 2025 with a set of about 30 customer and on-call interviews. Maren Tolliver and Dov Achterberg sat in on most of them. The clearest finding was that nobody wanted another thing watching them. They wanted the blast of an incident to be smaller and the morning after to be shorter. That finding drove every decision below.

What changed in 2026", "Why the company rebranded"], "ref": "source_373", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 11}, {"content": "# Wickhold opens early access to Wickhold Leashgate, runtime policy for AI agents

DENVER, May 2026 — Wickhold today opened early access to Wickhold Leashgate, a new product that applies runtime policy to AI agents and their tool calls. Early access is included in the Enterprise tier, and teams can apply through their account contact. Wickhold has not set a date for general availability.

Teams that run Kubernetes are starting to give AI agents real work: reading logs, opening pull requests, changing configuration, calling internal services. Those agents act with real credentials, and the tools they call are often the same ones an engineer would use. If an agent is manipulated or simply wrong, the damage depends on what it was allowed to reach.

Leashgate treats an agent as a workload with an identity and a boundary. In early access it provides:

- **Agent identity.** Each agent is identified at runtime, separately from the service or person who launched it.
- **Tool-call policy.** Teams define which tools an agent may call and with what limits. Leashgate applies that policy at the moment of the call and records the decision.
- **Blast radius of an agent.** Teams can see what an agent could reach under its current policy, and narrow it before the agent runs.

Leashgate limits what a compromised agent can do. It does not judge what a prompt says, and it does not make an agent's decisions correct. Those limits are deliberate: the product acts on tool calls, where an agent's actions become real.

"I keep hearing the same thing from platform teams: the agents arrived before the policy did," said Maren Tolliver, CEO and co-founder of Wickhold. "We started this company to keep small failures from becoming big ones. An agent with too many permissions is a small failure waiting for a reason. I'd like teams to have a boundary in place before they need one."

"The design is deliberately plain: deny by default, check every tool call, write down the decision," said Dov Achterberg, CTO and co-founder. "I'd rather give early access teams something narrow that behaves predictably and hear from them about what's missing. There's plenty missing. It runs on Kubernetes only for now, for one thing. That's why it's early access."

", "end_line": 18, "heading_path": ["Wickhold opens early access to Wickhold Leashgate, runtime policy for AI agents"], "ref": "source_374", "relative_path": "brand/press/pr-2026-leashgate-early-access.md", "start_line": 1}, {"content": "## Transparency and dark mode

Two product figures come from Wickhold's own lab. Both must carry the phrase "in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026", in the same sentence as the figure.

| Figure | Required form |
|---|---|
| CPU overhead | "under 2% CPU overhead on a typical node in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026" |
| Containment speed | "contains a known-bad process in a median of 38 seconds in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026" |

A footnote does not meet this requirement. An asterisk does not meet it. A qualifier on the slide before does not meet it. In a chart, the phrase goes in the chart title or directly under it. In a talk, the speaker says it aloud.

The figures describe a lab, so they may not be presented as field results or customer averages. "Known-bad process" is part of the claim: it does not extend to unknown processes, novel techniques, or "threats" in general. Reports may repeat the figures only if the benchmark year stays attached. When the 2027 benchmarks run, the year changes and this table is reissued. Nobody edits the year by hand.

Approved:

> Wickhold Quenchline adds under 2% CPU overhead on a typical node in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026.

Not approved:

> Quenchline contains attacks in 38 seconds.

> Under 2% overhead. Guaranteed.

| Format | Size | `background` | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hero illustration | 1536x1024 | `solid` | Wide placements, full scene with ground included |
| Spot illustration | 1024x1024 | `transparent` | Inline in body copy, feature grids, beside text |
| Abstract background | 1536x1024 | `solid` | Behind type in designed layouts. No focal element |

Hero illustrations already contain their ground. Check whether the file is the Tallow or the Soot version and place it in a section where it does not produce a visible box edge against a slightly different ground. Sample the color: if the layout ground is exactly Tallow or Soot, the edge disappears, which is what you want.

Spot illustrations take on whatever sits behind them, so `safe_on` matters. Many spots use Soot shapes and are `safe_on: light`, and those shapes vanish on a dark layout, leaving a floating Ember fragment. Others are built for dark and carry Tallow shapes. Check the record, look at `variant_of` for a sibling, and preview on the real ground. If an image is `any`, still look for a pale fringe along cut edges on Soot.

Do not put a spot illustration on a photograph. Do not put a spot on an Ember band. Do not put a box behind a spot to make it safe on the wrong ground, because the box will look like a mistake. Use the correct version or ask for one.

Abstract backgrounds exist to carry type. On their own they have no focal point, so they are never published without the layout on top of them.

No image contains text produced by an image model or baked into artwork by a tool that does not treat it as live type. Models misspell product names, invent letterforms and produce near-English that survives one quick look and then gets screenshotted by a customer. We had a test hero in spring where a wall sign read almost like "Quenchline". Nobody caught it until it was in a review deck.

Text in a Wickhold image is set by a person, in the design tool, in the brand typefaces, as a separate layer over finished art. That covers overlays, labels, chart annotations and callouts.

Three things do not count as generated text:

- Words that are really in the scene: a printed rack label, a whiteboard someone wrote on, a door sign. Check that they say nothing embarrassing and name nobody outside the company.
- Real interface text in a true product screenshot.
- The wordmark, which is a vector file, placed by a person.

Some placements allow no overlay at all and others cap it. The content-type page has the number.

", "end_line": 26, "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Format"], "ref": "source_417", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md", "start_line": 17}, {"content": "## Color

Bars and lines use the palette.

- **Ember for the one series or bar that makes the point.** All others are Whetstone.
- On Soot, use Tallow for context series, with Ember as the highlight. Whetstone is too dim to read there.
- Verdigris is the second highlight, used only when two series truly need names, such as before and after.
- No Ember tints. If you need a ramp for ordered data, use Soot to Whetstone to pale Tallow steps.

Ember, Whetstone and Verdigris sit very close together in lightness. Printed in grayscale, or viewed by a reader with color blindness, they merge. So hue never works alone: label each series directly on the line or bar, and separate adjacent bars with a gap. Legends are a last resort, since they send the reader back and forth.

Red and green are not used for bad and good. A chart about containment should not look like a stock ticker or an alert console.

The field is free text, written by whoever had the reason. There is no fixed vocabulary, so read the sentence instead of searching for a keyword. Three kinds of note turn up in practice:

- **A limited context.** The image may be used in the named context and nowhere else. A note limiting an image to internal use keeps it out of anything a customer, a prospect or the press will see, and that includes sales decks.
- **A person or place.** Something about who or what is shown has changed.

A restriction binds even when the image would be perfect, when a senior person asks for it, and when you found it already published somewhere. If you think one is out of date, ask Brand to change the record. Do not use the image and sort it out later.

**Two limits for the same channel.** A general voice document gives one length for a channel and that channel's playbook gives another. The playbook wins, because it sits higher in the list. Use its number, and tell Noor so the other one gets fixed.

**A claim in a deck.** A slide says something about the company that the approved claims do not support. The approved claims win, however recent or confident the slide looks, and however often the line has been used in the field. Sales material is not a source for a claim.

**Copy in this document versus Legal.** If a sentence in these guidelines turns out to conflict with the approved claims, Legal wins, and the guidelines get corrected.

**An old-looking rule with no rival.** A meeting note from the Q2 brand review covers something that the relevant playbook doesn't mention. Nothing conflicts, so the note stands.

**A file that says it's the latest.** File names, version numbers and words like FINAL or CURRENT decide nothing. Neither does the date on a file, on its own. Use this list.

**No source answers the question.** Ask the owner listed below. Do not fill the gap from the 2024 material or from what a competitor does. If the question is likely to come up again, the answer gets written down in the right document.

**Sources at the same level disagree.** Two channel playbooks can conflict on a shared element, such as a campaign running on both email and a landing page. Each playbook governs its own channel. If that doesn't settle it, Noor decides and the decision gets recorded.

", "end_line": 483, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "11. Governance", "Worked examples"], "ref": "source_427", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 468}, {"content": "## 11. Tables, charts and captions

- A table needs a header row and at least two rows of content. One row is a sentence.
- Right-align numbers in tables. Keep units in the header, not in each cell.
- A chart title states the finding in sentence case: "41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident". The axis says what was measured.
- Every chart carries its citation in the same bracket form, set small under the chart, so it survives being cropped into a slide.
- Captions are sentences. They end with a full stop and they don't begin "Figure 1 shows".
- No 3D, no donuts, and no chart for a single number. Write the number.

", "end_line": 201, "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "11. Tables, charts and captions"], "ref": "source_428", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "start_line": 193}, {"content": "### Fallback fonts

The strongest evidence for this position comes from Wickhold's own research. The Wickhold Containment Report 2026, published April 14, 2026, surveyed 412 platform and security leaders. It found that "41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident" and that "the median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours" [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].

The gap those numbers describe is between finding something and doing something about it. Detection has become cheap and common. Containment still depends on a person with enough access waking up, reading the alert, deciding, and acting. Wickhold's position lives in those hours.

", "end_line": 149, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning", "The market problem"], "ref": "source_430", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 144}, {"content": "### Blast radius of an agent

Leashgate reads an agent's policy, its service account's RBAC and its Secret mounts, then reports what the agent could reach: every tool it may call, each resource those tools touch, and any route around the gateway, such as a direct network path to a database the agent should only reach through a tool. The report is meant to be read in a security review.

```text
AGENT  support/support-triage      identity: spiffe://wickhold.example/ns/support/sa/triage
  tools allowed            2
  tools requiring approval 1
  tools denied             14
  bypass routes            1
    pod can reach postgres.support.svc:5432 directly (no NetworkPolicy)
```

Bypass routes matter more than anything else in that output. A gateway that an agent can walk around enforces nothing.

", "end_line": 77, "heading_path": ["Wickhold Leashgate", "Core concepts", "Blast radius of an agent"], "ref": "source_431", "relative_path": "brand/products/leashgate-overview.md", "start_line": 63}, {"content": "## T6. Nurture, platform track, first email

", "end_line": 160, "heading_path": ["Email templates", "T6. Nurture, platform track, first email"], "ref": "source_432", "relative_path": "brand/templates/email-templates.md", "start_line": 142}, {"content": "## Not banned, but expect a comment

Reviewers will ask about these. Sometimes the word survives.

- **solution.** Name the product, or say what it does. The word exists to avoid doing either.
- **visibility.** Seeing isn't the job. If the sentence ends at seeing, ask what happens next.
- **real-time.** Fine with a number next to it. Without one it means nothing.
- **AI-powered.** Tells the reader how something was built and nothing about what it does.
- **comprehensive.** Usually untrue, and a reader will go looking for the gap.
- **threat landscape.** A landscape has no one in it. Say which failure you mean.
- **peace of mind.** Nobody on a rota has ever had this.
- **modern.** Compared with what? Say which setup you mean.
- **mission-critical.** To the person on call, everything is.

", "end_line": 52, "heading_path": ["Word list", "Not banned, but expect a comment"], "ref": "source_433", "relative_path": "brand/voice/word-list.md", "start_line": 39}, {"content": "### The shield on its own

Screens age quickly, and old ones do damage in specific ways:

- **Before March 2026, Evenburn screens carry the product's previous name** in the navigation and page titles. Check `added_date` and look at the header. A screen with the old name is unusable, even when the part you want is elsewhere in the frame. Crop-around is not a fix, since the layout and colors are dated too.
- **Before the February 2026 rebrand, the product UI used the old blue theme and the old logo** in the corner. Same answer.
- **Removed features.** Product marketing reviews the library's screenshots against the release notes at each major release, and adds a `restrictions` note to anything that no longer matches.

If a screenshot's record is clean and the picture still looks out of date against the live product, trust your eyes and take a fresh one. The demo environment is reset each Monday, so captures are straightforward. Anything that shows a feature's name, a label or a flow that has changed needs replacing before the next use.

", "end_line": 104, "heading_path": ["Product UI screenshots", "Keeping screenshots current"], "ref": "source_436", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/product-ui-screenshots.md", "start_line": 95}, {"content": "## 5. Dates and times

- **Dates:** month, day, year, spelled out: April 14, 2026. No ordinals, no "14th of April".
- **Month and year:** March 2022, no comma. **Year only:** 2026.
- **Ranges:** an en dash with no spaces within a month: September 15–16. Use "to" across months: "March 30 to April 2".
- **Tables, logs, front matter:** ISO, 2026-04-14. Never slashes. 04/10 has already caused one wrong webinar invite, and that's enough.
- **Quarters:** fine internally. In public copy, name the month.
- **Avoid relative dates** in anything that stays online. "Recently", "last year", "this spring" and "soon" all rot. Write the date. Press releases and dated posts can say "today".
- **Roadmap language:** no dates, no "coming soon". Product marketing has a separate process for that.

**Times.** Incident timelines use 24-hour UTC with the zone on every line or at the top of the block: 03:14 UTC. It's how our readers' tools show it. Event and webinar times use 12-hour with the zone: 2:00 p.m. MT. In prose, "3am" with no space is fine as a phrase, and the voice document uses it constantly. It's a figure of speech and shouldn't be used for an actual appointment.

", "end_line": 114, "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "5. Dates and times"], "ref": "source_437", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "start_line": 103}, {"content": "## Engineering posts

For posts aimed at platform engineers, a clean terminal or YAML snippet is often better than a designed card. Set it in IBM Plex Mono on a Soot ground, in a real, tested snippet of no more than twelve lines. Dry humor in a code comment is acceptable. Check the audience first.

```yaml
# drains the node. does not drain your weekend.
spec:
  action: drain-node
  mode: contain
```

Code cards still get checked by someone who can run them. This is a sample of the style, and its field names are not a reference.

", "end_line": 65, "heading_path": ["Social graphics", "Engineering posts"], "ref": "source_438", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/social-graphics.md", "start_line": 53}, {"content": "## Who posts

**Company page.** Marketing runs it. Two or three posts a week, Tuesday to Thursday, usually mid-morning Mountain time. Fridays stayed on the calendar through most of 2025 and did nothing, so they came off.

**Maren and Dov.** They post from their own profiles when they have something to say. Marketing can draft, but they rewrite. Do not schedule on their behalf without a yes in writing, and do not reply to comments as them. If a draft of Maren's has been sitting for two weeks, drop it. She has decided.

**Kofi and the DevRel team.** Kofi posts from his own profile about conference talks, open-source eBPF work and whatever broke in the demo cluster. He does not need brand review for those unless a post carries a customer name, a product claim or a number.

**Everyone else.** People can share company posts however they like. We ran an employee amplification program in 2025 with a shared doc of suggested captions. Forty people posted the same sentence on the same morning and it looked exactly like that. We stopped.

", "end_line": 16, "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Who posts"], "ref": "source_439", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md", "start_line": 7}, {"content": "### Partners

", "end_line": 262, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "5. Brand architecture", "Partners"], "ref": "source_440", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 259}, {"content": "## Color limits

All colors are exact palette values. Do not use tints of Ember. Tints turn it toward pink and off brand.

", "end_line": 72, "heading_path": ["Illustration", "Color limits"], "ref": "source_441", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/illustration.md", "start_line": 67}, {"content": "## 7. Rulings from this year

Requests I have already answered. They are listed so that I do not answer them again.

| Request | Ruling |
|---|---|
| "Trusted by more than 140 customers" | Allowed. The count stays exact |
| "Trusted by credit unions" | Refused. One customer is not a plural |
| "Agentless" or "agent-free" for Quenchline | Refused. It uses an eBPF agent. Say so |
| "Lightweight" | Allowed only next to the CPU overhead figure and its qualifier |
| "Real-time" for Quenchline | Allowed for detection. For containment, use the lab figure or leave it out |
| "Stops the attack" | Refused. Name the containment action: isolate a pod's network, freeze a process, drain a node |
| "Automatic remediation" for Evenburn | Refused. Evenburn gives a fix order and people do the fixing |
| "AI-powered" for any product | Refused unless product confirms in writing what the model does. Writing about AI agents does not make the product AI-powered |
| "Secures your AI" or "safe AI" for Leashgate | Refused. Describe tool-call policy and agent identity |
| "SOC 2 certified" | Refused. Say "holds SOC 2 Type II" |
| "Used by your peers" in a sector email | Refused unless a named, approved customer in that sector is shown |
| "Battle-tested" | Refused. It implies a history of incidents at customers that we have not disclosed and may not disclose |

", "end_line": 169, "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "7. Rulings from this year"], "ref": "source_442", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md", "start_line": 151}, {"content": "## Agency and contractors

Ilse confirmed the keyword agency contract ended in May. The two blog contractors stay through Q3. Noor asked that contractors get read access to the brand folder only once it has been tidied, otherwise they'll quote old files. Until then Noor sends them the specific documents they need. Kofi asked for one contractor to help with the throwaway test cluster docs. Not approved.

", "end_line": 69, "heading_path": ["Q2 brand review: meeting notes", "Agency and contractors"], "ref": "source_443", "relative_path": "brand/internal/mtg-notes-q2-brand-review.md", "start_line": 66}, {"content": "## Where screenshots come from

Screens are captured from the product running in the demo environment, or rendered from the demo environment's HTML with Playwright at 1600x1000. Library dashboards are that size and opaque.

Never capture from:

- A customer tenant, even with their permission and even if you blur things
- Our own production tenant, which contains real incidents and real people's names
- A design file. Mockups of features that do not exist are not screenshots. If we need to show something unreleased, it must be labeled as a concept and approved by product marketing and Legal
- A model. Interface images are never generated

Do not paint over or blur a screenshot to hide data. Blurred regions imply the original had something worth hiding. Fix the demo data and take it again.

", "end_line": 19, "heading_path": ["Product UI screenshots", "Where screenshots come from"], "ref": "source_444", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/product-ui-screenshots.md", "start_line": 7}, {"content": "### Illustration

Illustration is flat cut-paper shapes with one Ember focal element on Tallow or Soot, and no gradients. The cut-paper style was chosen because it looks made by hand and sits comfortably next to the warm photography. It also holds up small. Shapes should be simple enough to be cut with scissors, which is a good test when a design starts picking up detail.

Illustration tends to work best for ideas that have no honest photograph, such as a policy, a blast radius or an exposure path. Containment is the recurring theme: something small, held inside something that keeps it there.

The isometric style and the line graphic from the 2024 identity have been retired, along with the Cobalt gradient behind them.

", "end_line": 402, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "9. Photography and illustration direction", "Illustration"], "ref": "source_445", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 395}, {"content": "## T8c. Renewal notice

{{csm_first_name}}, Wickhold

", "end_line": 253, "heading_path": ["Email templates", "T8c. Renewal notice"], "ref": "source_446", "relative_path": "brand/templates/email-templates.md", "start_line": 235}, {"content": "### Analytics, cookies and tracking

Localized landing pages use the consent banner supplied by web ops. Don't add a new tag, pixel or form tool to an EU or UK page without asking first. Paid retargeting on EU and UK traffic stays off unless the banner has recorded consent. A partner's tracking link is a new tag.

", "end_line": 51, "heading_path": ["Regional rules: EU and UK copy", "Analytics, cookies and tracking"], "ref": "source_447", "relative_path": "brand/legal/regional-rules-eu-uk.md", "start_line": 48}, {"content": "### Agencies and freelancers

", "end_line": 512, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "11. Governance", "Agencies and freelancers"], "ref": "source_448", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 509}, {"content": "## What we send

**Monthly newsletter.** Goes to everyone opted in, second Tuesday of the month. One lead item, three short items, nothing about us that we wouldn't want to read ourselves. Engineers are the bulk of this list, so it can carry a command or a config snippet.

**Nurture tracks.** Separate tracks for CISOs and platform leads, triggered by report downloads and demo requests. Four to six emails over about six weeks. Sales gets an alert on replies. If a contact opens a sales conversation, the track stops.

**Product announcements.** Goes to customers first, prospects a day later. New capabilities, deprecations, and anything that changes how a customer's agents behave. Deprecations go out at least 60 days ahead.

**Customer notices.** Security advisories, CVE guidance, scheduled maintenance. These bypass frequency caps and unsubscribe groups. Dov or a named engineer signs. Marketing can edit for clarity but never holds one back for scheduling reasons.

**Event email.** Slow Burn Summit and Field Day invites and reminders. The events team writes, lifecycle sends.

**Founder notes.** Maren writes to customers about twice a year, usually around pricing or product direction. It comes from her address. A reply goes to her, and she reads them.

", "end_line": 29, "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "What we send"], "ref": "source_449", "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md", "start_line": 16}, {"content": "### The promise at each level

| Level | What is promised |
|---|---|
| Company | Small fires stay small. |
| Quenchline | When something goes wrong at runtime, a defined containment action happens quickly and the team sees exactly what it did |
| Evenburn | The team sees where the drift and exposure paths are, and gets a fix order |
| Leashgate | AI agents work inside a tool-call policy, so the blast radius of an agent is known in advance |

", "end_line": 218, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning", "The promise at each level"], "ref": "source_450", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 210}, {"content": "## 3. Banned claims

| Do not say | Say instead, or do this | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| "prevents prompt injection" | "limits what a compromised agent can do" | Leashgate acts on tool calls. It does not read intent and it cannot promise that an agent will not be manipulated. The claim is false as a matter of product design |
| "FedRAMP Authorized", "FedRAMP certified" | See section 4 | Neither is true |
| "GDPR compliant" | Use the regional rules | Regional wording sits there, and the ban is not limited to that region |
| "breach-proof", "unhackable", "impossible to escape" | Describe the containment action | No security product can support an absolute |
| "zero false positives", "100% detection", "catches everything" | Give a sourced figure or say nothing | We hold no such evidence |
| "guarantee", "guaranteed", "warranty" outside a contract | Remove | These words have legal effect. Service credits live in the order form |
| "the leading", "the fastest", "No. 1", "the only" | Remove, or bring me the comparison data | Superlatives need current comparative substantiation, and we do not hold any |
| "certified by", "endorsed by", "partner of" for any standards body or open-source project | Remove | Using eBPF or Helm is not an endorsement from anyone |
| "saves $X", any return-on-investment figure | Remove | We have no approved financial outcome for any customer |

Two refinements, because they keep coming back:

"Helps prevent" is a banned claim dressed up. A qualifier in front of a promise does not make it a limited promise.

"Compliance-ready" and "audit-ready" were requested in June for a trust page and refused. Wickhold can describe what the product records. Whether a customer passes an audit depends on the customer and the auditor.

", "end_line": 98, "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "3. Banned claims"], "ref": "source_451", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md", "start_line": 79}, {"content": "## 8. Technical writing in marketing copy

Kofi Anselm's team reviews anything containing code, and their rules are short.

- **Code formatting** for commands, flags, file names, field names, namespaces, node names and anything a person might type: `kubectl get pods`, `--namespace`, `values.yaml`.
- **Every snippet is run before it's published.** Say which version it was run against. A snippet nobody ran does not go out, even in a slide.
- **Placeholder values** look like placeholders or like real workloads: `payments`, `checkout`, `worker-7`. Don't use `foo`, and don't use the name of a real company, a real customer or a celebrity.
- **Domains and email addresses in examples** use `wickhold.example`.
- **Long output** gets trimmed, with a line saying so. Don't silently edit output.
- **Failure modes** are part of the example. If a command fails in a common way, say how it looks.

", "end_line": 153, "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "8. Technical writing in marketing copy"], "ref": "source_452", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "start_line": 143}, {"content": "## 4. Numbers

", "end_line": 72, "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "4. Numbers"], "ref": "source_453", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "start_line": 71}, {"content": "### Color in common pieces

| Report | Tallow pages, Soot cover | Chart highlights and one rule on the cover |
| Product documentation | Follows the docs theme | Links are not Ember on small text |
| Booth | Soot backwall, Tallow counter | The dot in the logo and one line of type |
| Swag | Soot or undyed fabric | The dot |

Dark layouts should use Soot, and pure black should not stand in for it. Soot has a slight cool cast that keeps Ember from buzzing against it. On Tallow pages, photographs and screenshots sit best with a thin Whetstone rule around them, since a light screenshot can otherwise dissolve into the page.

", "end_line": 322, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "7. Color", "Color in common pieces"], "ref": "source_454", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 310}, {"content": "### Booth and events

", "end_line": 374, "heading_path": ["WICKHOLD SECURITY BRAND GUIDELINES", "9. Putting It All Together", "Booth and events"], "ref": "source_455", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_v3_FINAL.md", "start_line": 371}, {"content": "## 5. Brand architecture

", "end_line": 222, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "5. Brand architecture"], "ref": "source_456", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 219}, {"content": "## Who should apply

Early access suits platform and security teams that already have at least one agent in production, or are about to, and have someone who can own policy. Teams still deciding whether to run agents at all should wait. There will be plenty to read as we learn more.

Your account team can tell you more, or you can apply directly.

[Request early access](https://wickhold.example/leashgate)

*Wickhold is the runtime security company for teams that run Kubernetes. Its products contain failures early, so small fires stay small. Founded in 2019 and based in Denver, Wickhold serves more than 140 customers.*
", "end_line": 81, "heading_path": ["Wickhold Leashgate enters early access", "Who should apply"], "ref": "source_457", "relative_path": "brand/archive/blog/leashgate_early_access_notes.md", "start_line": 73}, {"content": "## What Leashgate does not do

Leashgate does not read prompts and it does not judge whether a model has been manipulated. It has no opinion on the quality of an agent's output, and it will not catch an agent that gives a customer bad advice through a tool it is allowed to use. What it controls is the set of actions available to the agent. A permitted action that happens to be a poor decision will still go through, so policy needs the same care you would give any access review.

", "end_line": 55, "heading_path": ["Wickhold Leashgate enters early access", "What Leashgate does not do"], "ref": "source_458", "relative_path": "brand/archive/blog/leashgate_early_access_notes.md", "start_line": 52}, {"content": "### Fear is not a sales tool

No threat-actor drama. No ticking clocks.

The rule is simple to state and gets broken constantly, because fear copy is the easiest copy in security to write. It covers attackers portrayed as characters with motives and nicknames, anything of the "while you read this" kind, countdowns, "it's only a matter of time", "every second counts", and any sentence that asks the reader to imagine the phone call to the board. Our readers carry a pager. They do not need help imagining it.

Give the same fact without the dread.

Bad: "Attackers are already inside your cluster, and the clock is ticking."

Good: "41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]."

The second sentence is more uncomfortable than the first, and it did not raise its voice. Trust the number to do that work.

Breach references have their own rules in the claims document. Read them before you mention one.

", "end_line": 56, "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "What Wickhold believes", "Fear is not a sales tool"], "ref": "source_459", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "start_line": 41}, {"content": "# Landing pages

", "end_line": 6, "heading_path": ["Landing pages"], "ref": "source_460", "relative_path": "brand/channels/landing-page-playbook.md", "start_line": 1}, {"content": "## What goes in the frame

{"candidate": null, "conversation": [{"role": "user", "text": "Campaign brief: Wickhold Leashgate general availability
From: Ilse Varga-Holm, VP Marketing
Date: October 20, 2026
Status: Approved to plan. Internal until launch day
Reviewers: Noor Eskelund (audience, goal, voice), Priit Salonen (claims), Dov Achterberg (technical read), Kofi Anselm (developer content, X)
What is happening
Wickhold Leashgate reaches general availability on Tuesday, January 26, 2027. Product and Legal have confirmed the status change, and this brief is Product Marketing's announcement of it for everyone working on the campaign.
Two things follow from that.
The early access label comes off for this campaign. Every asset below publishes on or after January 26, so it says "Wickhold Leashgate" on first mention and "Leashgate" after that, with no early access label. On launch day it is correct to say Wickhold Leashgate is generally available. The label rule in the 2026 release notes, the early access wording in the messaging house and the Leashgate section of the approved claims all stay in force for everything else until January 26. Those documents get updated for launch. Where one of them conflicts with this brief on Leashgate's status alone, this brief wins for these assets. On anything else, they stand.
Nothing external mentions general availability or the date before January 26. No teasers, no "coming soon", no countdown. Early access copy already in market stays as it is until launch day.
General availability changes the status of the product and not its scope. Leashgate at launch is what the product overview and the 2026 release notes describe: agent identity, tool-call policy, and the blast radius report, with a gateway running as a sidecar or as a shared Deployment, for agents that make tool calls over HTTP or MCP. Approvals can be answered from Slack. The tie-in that lets Leashgate ask Wickhold Quenchline for a containment action is optional, off by default, and needs Quenchline on the node.
Goals
The numbers here are internal and do not go in copy.
Customers hear it from us first, on launch day, with enough detail for a platform team to judge whether it applies to them.
60 demo requests by March 31, 2027 from teams with an agent running against real tools, in staging or production.
Get the blast radius report into security reviews. We want platform leads to bring it to their next one, as the answer to "what is the worst this agent could do on a bad day?" Sales will track how often it comes up on calls.
Audience
Primary: platform leads who have been asked to get an agent into production and have a security review standing in their way. They already have the concern, and the budget conversation has started. They read docs first, want the failure behavior early, and trust a config snippet over a paragraph.
Secondary: security leaders and security architects writing internal rules for agent use. They need something more enforceable than a policy document. Lead with the decision they have to make. No humor for this group.
Existing customers get the news first, through the technical customer list. Several asked about agents at Slow Burn Summit, and most were not running any in production yet, so do not write as if they all are.
Keep these audiences apart. Platform and security leadership are separate email lists, and they stay separate here. The landing page is written for platform leads. Security leaders get their own email and the launch post.
Key messages
Treat an agent as a workload with credentials, and give it a boundary. This is pillar 3 of the messaging house and the argument under everything else. Talk about tool calls in a cluster. Leave the future of work to other people.
What it does. Leashgate gives each agent an identity, checks every tool call against a tool-call policy, writes a decision record, and reports the blast radius of an agent, including any route around the gateway.
The outcome statement. Leashgate "limits what a compromised agent can do". Use those words exactly.
For platform leads. defaultAction: deny. Your agent framework stays the same. Leashgate fails closed, so an outage of the gateway stops the agent's tools, and teams need to plan for that. Say so plainly.
For security leaders. Before an agent goes live, know its blast radius. Every decision leaves a record your team can read in a security review.
What it does not do. Leashgate sees tool calls, and it does not read or judge prompts. It runs on Kubernetes only, and frameworks that call tools in-process, with no network hop, are out of scope. Being plain about this is part of the pitch.
Channels and assets
Eleven assets, on owned channels only. This is my starting list, so if the mix is wrong, say so when you bring the plan on November 6. The release note, press and sales enablement run separately and are not part of this brief.

They already have the concern, and the budget conversation has started. They read docs first, want the failure behavior early, and trust a config snippet over a paragraph. Secondary: security leaders and security architects writing internal rules for agent use. They need something more enforceable than a policy document. Lead with the decision they have to make. No humor for this group. Existing customers get the news first, through the technical customer list. Several asked about agents at Slow Burn Summit, and most were not running any in production yet, so do not write as if they all are. Keep these audiences apart. Platform and security leadership are separate email lists, and they stay separate here. The landing page is written for platform leads. Security leaders get their own email and the launch post.", "heading": "Audiences"}, {"content": "Treat an agent as a workload with credentials, and give it a boundary. This is pillar 3 of the messaging house and the argument under everything else. Talk about tool calls in a cluster. Leave the future of work to other people. What it does. Leashgate gives each agent an identity, checks every tool call against a tool-call policy, writes a decision record, and reports the blast radius of an agent, including any route around the gateway. The outcome statement. Leashgate "limits what a compromised agent can do". Use those words exactly. For platform leads. defaultAction: deny. Your agent framework stays the same. Leashgate fails closed, so an outage of the gateway stops the agent's tools, and teams need to plan for that. Say so plainly. For security leaders. Before an agent goes live, know its blast radius. Every decision leaves a record your team can read in a security review. What it does not do. Leashgate sees tool calls, and it does not read or judge prompts. It runs on Kubernetes only, and frameworks that call tools in-process, with no network hop, are out of scope. Being plain about this is part of the pitch.", "heading": "Messages and required wording"}, {"content": "Eleven assets, on owned channels only. This is my starting list, so if the mix is wrong, say so when you bring the plan on November 6. The release note, press and sales enablement run separately and are not part of this brief.", "heading": "Campaign scope and channel context"}, {"content": "The landing page is the product page, so it has no end date. Use the existing product layout. Its main action is "Book a demo", with a secondary link to the docs for readers who are not ready for a form. A visitor arrives from one of the emails, a social post or the docs, and needs to see what the product does and how it fails.", "heading": "Landing page requirements"}, {"content": "2026-11-06: Asset plan agreed with me, and Noor's OK on audience and goal. 2026-12-11: Outlines for both blog posts to Kofi. 2027-01-08: All drafts in. 2027-01-15: Claims check back from Priit. Page copy to the web team. Maren's draft to Maren. 2027-01-21: X posts to Kofi for review and scheduling. 2027-01-26: Launch. Release note, landing page, customer email, LinkedIn, X. 2027-01-27: Launch post and prospect emails, one day after customers and after the release note. 2027-01-28: Second company LinkedIn post. 2027-02-02: How-to post and its X post. Kofi moves both to February 3 if a release note lands on the 2nd. 2027-02-09: Two-week check on the landing page form. 2027-03-31: Read the goals.", "heading": "Timeline and dependencies"}, {"content": "Claims. The approved claims and the certification sheet apply as usual. Only the status of Leashgate changes. Proof. There is no customer proof for Leashgate and there is no lab figure for it. Do not name early access partners, quote them or count them. Do not quote a latency figure, since we have none. The Lowmoor Credit Union and Ostler Grocers results belong to other products and do not go on Leashgate assets as if they were Leashgate results. A thin page beats a borrowed number. Market framing. Use figures from the Wickhold Containment Report 2026, or a fresh third-party statistic with its source. Web research is welcome where it helps, under the usual rules for third-party figures.", "heading": "Claims, proof and market framing"}, {"content": "Pricing. Pricing after early access is not settled, and I am handling the pricing page separately before launch. Do not state a price or a tier for Leashgate in any asset. Link to the pricing page where a reader needs it, and send buying questions to sales. Support terms. Say nothing about SLAs or support levels. Those live in the order form. Roadmap. Describe what the product does on launch day. No future features, no adapter lists, no dates beyond the launch itself. Competitors. Leashgate stays out of competitive positioning. No comparisons and no comparison blog in this campaign.", "heading": "Pricing, support, roadmap and competitors"}, {"content": "Code in copy. Excerpts of ToolCallPolicy rules are welcome. Leave out the apiVersion line, build numbers and the install command. The early access versions do not carry over, and Kofi adds the final block at the paste test. Images. Use the library. Design's console screens for launch will not be ready in time, and the Leashgate console screens in the library carry the early access pill, which is not to be cropped off. Keep them off every asset in this campaign. The landing page hero is a working room.", "heading": "Code and image requirements"}, {"content": "Maren's post. It is a draft for her to rewrite. Do not schedule it, and do not assume a yes. Questions come to me. Anything that touches the claims goes to Priit first.", "heading": "Draft handling and routing"}], "unknowns": []}}

{"passages": [{"content": "### Our three pillars

**Pillar 1: Every Workload.**
Complete coverage. Every pod, every node, every cluster, every cloud account. There are no blind spots on the Wickhold Security platform.

Supporting language: *full coverage*, *no blind spots*, *one single pane of glass for runtime and posture*.

**Pillar 2: Always Watched.**
Security that never sleeps! Our eBPF agent and continuous scanning mean you find out in seconds, not in next quarter's audit.

Supporting language: *always on*, *continuous*, *real time*, *24/7 visibility*.

**Pillar 3: Built by Operators.**
Maren and Dov carried the pager. Our product respects the people who run production, with lightweight deployment, sensible defaults and robust integrations that fit how platform teams already work.

Supporting language: *by operators, for operators*, *lightweight*, *fast to deploy*.

", "end_line": 129, "heading_path": ["WICKHOLD SECURITY BRAND GUIDELINES", "4. Our Messaging", "Our three pillars"], "ref": "source_0", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_v3_FINAL.md", "start_line": 113}, {"content": "## Size

16:9, 1600x900. Keep the focal point in the middle, as the timeline crops and phone previews trim the edges. Long screenshots of text get a "show more" crop, so do not post them. Write a thread.

", "end_line": 19, "heading_path": ["X images", "Size"], "ref": "source_1", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/x-image.md", "start_line": 16}, {"content": "---
title: Content style guide
version: 4
owner: Noor Eskelund
updated: 2026-07-09
---

", "end_line": 7, "heading_path": [], "ref": "source_2", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "start_line": 1}, {"content": "### A worked hierarchy

A typical landing section might read:

- Page headline, Bricolage Grotesque Bold: "Small fires stay small."
- Subhead, Plex Sans SemiBold: "Wickhold Quenchline contains runtime failures on your Kubernetes nodes, within limits your team sets."
- Body, Plex Sans Regular: one short paragraph.
- Inline literal, Plex Mono: `kubectl get containmentpolicy`.

Four levels is plenty. If a layout seems to need a fifth, the content usually needs editing.

", "end_line": 380, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "8. Typography", "A worked hierarchy"], "ref": "source_3", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 370}, {"content": "# LinkedIn images

Social lead's notes, updated August 2026.

", "end_line": 4, "heading_path": ["LinkedIn images"], "ref": "source_4", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/linkedin-image.md", "start_line": 1}, {"content": "## Who signs off

Product marketing checks accuracy. Brand checks the crop and annotations. If a screenshot shows a feature that engineering has not shipped to all customers, the product manager for that area also signs off. Allow two working days.
", "end_line": 115, "heading_path": ["Product UI screenshots", "Who signs off"], "ref": "source_5", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/product-ui-screenshots.md", "start_line": 113}, {"content": "### File Names

Name working files clearly so that everyone can find them: project, piece, version. For example, `summit_booth_backwall_v2`. When a file is done, add `FINAL` to the name and move it to the shared drive so that nobody has to guess which one is approved.

---

", "end_line": 448, "heading_path": ["WICKHOLD SECURITY BRAND GUIDELINES", "9. Putting It All Together", "File Names"], "ref": "source_6", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_v3_FINAL.md", "start_line": 443}, {"content": "### The primary logo

Our logo combines two elements: the **shield**, which stands for protection, and the **flame** rising from inside it, which stands for the constant, watchful light of runtime visibility. Beside the shield sits the **Wickhold Security wordmark**, set in Inter Bold with a custom tight fit.

The shield and the wordmark are a single unit. In nearly all cases, use them together.

", "end_line": 203, "heading_path": ["WICKHOLD SECURITY BRAND GUIDELINES", "5. Our Logo", "The primary logo"], "ref": "source_7", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_v3_FINAL.md", "start_line": 198}, {"content": "## Copy on cards

Cards follow the voice rules with no special allowance for being short. Good:

- Small fires stay small.
- 11 minutes to contain, down from 4 hours.
- Contain mode, explained.

Bad:

- Hackers never sleep. Neither do we.
- The future of cloud security is HERE!
- Is your cluster on fire right now?

The 11-minute line needs Lowmoor named in the post or on the card, so that the number has a source.

A card should not repeat the post word for word. Use the post to expand on the card.

", "end_line": 52, "heading_path": ["Social graphics", "Copy on cards"], "ref": "source_8", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/social-graphics.md", "start_line": 35}, {"content": "### Claims made in a hurry

Launches and field events are when unapproved language tends to appear, usually from someone trying to help. If you see a claim in circulation that isn't on the approved list, tell Priit the same day, including where you saw it. There is no blame in reporting one. The aim is to get it corrected before it's copied into something else.

", "end_line": 532, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "11. Governance", "Claims made in a hurry"], "ref": "source_9", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 529}, {"content": "## 9. People and companies

- Full name and title on first mention, in this order: Hana Brandvold, CISO, Lowmoor Credit Union.
- After that, surname for external people, in the press-release style: Brandvold said. First name for our founders only where they signed the piece.
- Job titles are capitalized in a byline or attribution line and lowercase in a sentence: "the company's head of developer relations".
- Companies are singular. "Wickhold is", "Ostler Grocers has".
- Use "they" for an unnamed person. "On-call lead", not "on-call guy". "Staffed", not "manned".
- Teams are lowercase: the platform team, the brand team.

", "end_line": 186, "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "9. People and companies"], "ref": "source_10", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "start_line": 178}, {"content": "### Product behavior

Wickhold Quenchline takes a containment action only in contain mode. In observe mode it records what it would have done. Copy describing automatic containment must therefore be true of contain mode and should say so where a reader could assume otherwise. Containment actions are isolating a pod's network, freezing a process and draining a node. Do not add to the list without product confirmation.

Wickhold Evenburn reports drift, exposure paths and a fix order. It does not change a customer's environment by itself, and copy should not imply that it does.

", "end_line": 72, "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "2. Claims that need a qualifier", "Product behavior"], "ref": "source_11", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md", "start_line": 67}, {"content": "## Things we tried

Polls brought a lot of votes from people outside our audience and no replies worth reading. Dropped in late 2025.

Document posts and carousels are off the plan. Swipes fell away after the third page.

Paid boosting is decided per post by demand gen. A boosted post goes through the same review as paid copy, even when it started life as an organic one.
", "end_line": 110, "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Things we tried"], "ref": "source_12", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md", "start_line": 104}, {"content": "## What works

- A code or YAML card on Soot, from the engineering post format
- A tight product crop of one containment action
- One chart with its title
- A spot illustration, flattened on Tallow or Soot, for a light post

This is narrower than the social graphics rules in two ways. No overlay text on photos here, since the feed crop is unpredictable. And no quote cards: on X, type the quote into the post with the customer's name.

", "end_line": 15, "heading_path": ["X images", "What works"], "ref": "source_13", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/x-image.md", "start_line": 7}, {"content": "# Wickhold Leashgate

*Product marketing overview for the May 2026 early access. First draft for field and web teams, May 4, updated September 2026.*

", "end_line": 4, "heading_path": ["Wickhold Leashgate"], "ref": "source_14", "relative_path": "brand/products/leashgate-overview.md", "start_line": 1}, {"content": "## June 23, 2026: Leashgate early access build 0.4

First schema migration. Argument constraints moved under `rules[].arguments`. Policies need rewriting by hand in this one case, and partners have a migration note from their engineering contact.

- MCP proxy mode now supports multiple upstream servers per gateway
- Human-user identity can be passed through to policy evaluation
- Agent credential lifetime is configurable, default 15 minutes

", "end_line": 100, "heading_path": ["Release notes 2026", "June 23, 2026: Leashgate early access build 0.4"], "ref": "source_15", "relative_path": "brand/products/release-notes-2026.md", "start_line": 93}, {"content": "# LinkedIn playbook

Noor Eskelund. Last edit 12 August 2026, after the Leashgate early access posts. Ask in the brand channel before you ask me by email.

LinkedIn is the one channel where CISOs, platform leads and our own hiring pipeline all look at the same feed. Most of what we post there is read on a phone, between meetings, by someone who has never heard of us. Write for that person.

", "end_line": 6, "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook"], "ref": "source_16", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md", "start_line": 1}, {"content": "### Data location and processing

Do not state where customer data is stored, or use "EU-hosted", "data residency" or "sovereign", unless the sentence has been cleared for that specific asset. Questions on data location go to the account team and then to me. The answers depend on the deployment, and marketing copy should not try to summarize them.

Sub-processor lists and the data processing agreement are shared on request. They are not marketing assets. Do not screenshot them into a deck.

", "end_line": 40, "heading_path": ["Regional rules: EU and UK copy", "Data location and processing"], "ref": "source_17", "relative_path": "brand/legal/regional-rules-eu-uk.md", "start_line": 35}, {"content": "### Swag

Quality over quantity. Pick items people keep, such as good bottles, thick socks and well-cut T-shirts. Navy or Cobalt base with the reversed shield. Any vendor needs the vector logo files from Marketing, and we check a sample before we approve a run.

", "end_line": 378, "heading_path": ["WICKHOLD SECURITY BRAND GUIDELINES", "9. Putting It All Together", "Swag"], "ref": "source_18", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_v3_FINAL.md", "start_line": 375}, {"content": "## March 2026: pricing

New Core and Team prices took effect this month. No product entitlement changed for existing contracts until renewal.

", "end_line": 165, "heading_path": ["Release notes 2026", "March 2026: pricing"], "ref": "source_19", "relative_path": "brand/products/release-notes-2026.md", "start_line": 162}, {"content": "# Data visualization

Charts are built from data by a person, in code or the design tool. They are never drawn by an image model and never traced from somebody else's report. Written for the 2026 Containment Report and kept for everything since.

", "end_line": 4, "heading_path": ["Data visualization"], "ref": "source_20", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/data-viz.md", "start_line": 1}, {"content": "# Wickhold brand guidelines 2026

Noor Eskelund, Head of Brand. Issued February 10, 2026, with the rebrand. Revised September 2026.

These guidelines replace the 2024 guidelines in full. They cover what the brand is, what it stands for and how it looks at the level a writer, designer or marketer needs to make decisions. The detailed working rules for words, claims, channels and images sit in their own documents, and this one does not repeat them.

", "end_line": 6, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026"], "ref": "source_21", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 1}, {"content": "### Co-marketing

Partners write their own claims about their own products. When a joint asset says anything about Wickhold and data protection, the approved sentence is used, and the partner's version is not. If a partner insists on the banned phrase about itself, the phrase stays in the part of the asset that is clearly theirs, and it comes to me first.

", "end_line": 55, "heading_path": ["Regional rules: EU and UK copy", "Co-marketing"], "ref": "source_22", "relative_path": "brand/legal/regional-rules-eu-uk.md", "start_line": 52}, {"content": "## Narrower than the category pages

Not everything in the illustration category qualifies here:

- **Hero illustrations only.** A spot illustration is transparent and square, and it sits inside body copy. Set as a hero, it leaves a small object floating in a wide band, so it is out.
- **No abstract backgrounds.** They have no focal point on their own, and a hero has no type set over it.
- **Tallow or Soot, matched to the post.** Illustration category rules allow either. For blog heroes, default to Tallow. Use Soot for incident retrospectives and long technical posts, so that the list page has some rhythm.

And from photography:

- **Landscape only.** Portrait photos in the library cannot become 16:9 without losing most of the frame.
- **A person is allowed as the subject, but the post has to be about the work** and not a staff profile.

No text on the hero at all, including the post title. The blog template sets the title in live type below the image. Older posts had titles burned into the image, and they looked wrong in every preview card that also printed the title.

", "end_line": 23, "heading_path": ["Blog hero images", "Narrower than the category pages"], "ref": "source_23", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/blog-hero.md", "start_line": 9}, {"content": "## May 2026: Leashgate early access build 0.3

Fix release for the first partners. Corrects sidecar injection on namespaces with restrictive pod security settings and adds a readiness gate so an agent pod does not start before its gateway.

", "end_line": 116, "heading_path": ["Release notes 2026", "May 2026: Leashgate early access build 0.3"], "ref": "source_24", "relative_path": "brand/products/release-notes-2026.md", "start_line": 113}, {"content": "## Templates first

The library holds a small set of social templates, built in HTML and rendered with Playwright so the type is live and the layout stays exact. Start from one. Copy it, change the content, render it. A file marked as a template is a master and should not be posted unfilled.

Do not rebuild a template in a slide app. That is where off-size margins and the wrong weight of Bricolage Grotesque come from.

If you need a layout the templates do not cover, ask a designer. Do not stretch the stat card to hold a quote.

", "end_line": 14, "heading_path": ["Social graphics", "Templates first"], "ref": "source_25", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/social-graphics.md", "start_line": 7}, {"content": "## The problem with agents in production

An agent in a production cluster is a workload that makes its own decisions about what to call next. Platform teams are being asked to run these agents, often with credentials that were copied from a developer's laptop during a pilot. The agent can reach a database, a ticketing system and a deployment pipeline, because during the pilot that was convenient.

Most of the time this works fine. When it does not, the failure is hard to reason about. A model may be manipulated by content it read, or it may simply make a poor decision. Either way, the question for the on-call engineer is the same as for any other incident: how far can this get?

The term we use for that is the blast radius of an agent. It is set by what the agent is allowed to do at runtime, and that is what Leashgate controls.

", "end_line": 21, "heading_path": ["Wickhold Leashgate enters early access", "The problem with agents in production"], "ref": "source_26", "relative_path": "brand/archive/blog/leashgate_early_access_notes.md", "start_line": 14}, {"content": "Leashgate joins Wickhold's two other products: Wickhold Quenchline for runtime detection and containment in Kubernetes, and Wickhold Evenburn for cloud and cluster posture management. Early access is intended for teams running agents against real infrastructure who are willing to give direct feedback to the product team. Features and behavior will change during early access, and policy written today may need revisiting. Support during early access runs through a shared channel with the product team.

Wickhold will review each application with the applicant's platform and security teams, since a tool-call policy usually needs both to agree on it. Customers who are not on the Enterprise tier can register interest through their account contact.

Some topics drag writers back toward the register the rebrand left behind. These are the ones reviewers see most.

**AI agents.** Wickhold Leashgate, in early access, attracts the worst habits in the building, because the whole market is shouting about agents. Treat an agent as a workload with credentials and questionable judgment. Talk about tool calls, agent identity and the blast radius of an agent. Leave the future of work to other people. Anyone who has run production will recognize the problem from there, and that recognition is worth more than any amount of excitement.

**Compliance.** Dull on purpose. Certification status is a fact with one correct wording, and legal owns that wording. Copy the approved sentence and do not improve it. A nicer phrasing here is how a company ends up saying something untrue.

**Money.** Prices are stated flatly, with no "just", "only" or "starting from". Core is $18 per node per month. The reader can decide how they feel about that.

**Company news.** Funding, awards, headcount. Nobody is thrilled, excited or proud. The Series B was $46M in June 2024; that is a date and a number, and the sentence after it should say what changed for customers. If nothing changed for customers, ask whether the post needs to exist.

**Customers.** They did the work. Lowmoor Credit Union's on-call team runs its own incidents, and the product took one job off their list. Avoid "partnered with", "journey" and anything that casts us as the guide who showed them the way.
