From the lifecycle marketing manager, March-May 2026 tests, tidied in June.

", "heading_path": ["Email header images"], "ref": "s156", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/email-header.md"}, {"chunk_id": "7bb0cf4a-110d-4e05-bfce-10b7ed8ed4bf", "content": "## Photos by setting

**Team and office.** Real desks, real clutter. Aim for moments between people, with one person clearly the focus of the frame. Conference-room shots work when something is happening on the table. The office kitchen works better than the boardroom.

**Infrastructure.** Shoot close. A patch panel with handwritten labels says more than a long aisle. Cables, breakers, fans, a rack door left open. Whatever the room's own lighting does, keep it warm in the edit, and if the room is lit cold and cannot be corrected, get closer to a warm lamp or drop the shot.

**Customer scenes.** The grocery distribution office, the credit union's back room, a store's network closet. These are the most valuable photos we have, since they show Kubernetes and its operators somewhere other than a startup. They also have the most paperwork behind them. A customer scene looks ordinary and that is the point: no hero angles.

**Remote on-call.** Kitchen tables and spare rooms, a laptop at dusk, a phone face-up beside it. On-call happens at home and most stock libraries do not show it. Keep faces turned away unless the person is a signed volunteer.

", "heading_path": ["Photography", "Photos by setting"], "ref": "s157", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/photography.md"}, {"chunk_id": "7bd9df56-982b-4dd6-b3f7-e2c369f80b23", "content": "### `variant_of`

If the record points to a parent, or other records point at this one, you have siblings. Look at them before you decide the image does not work. The version for your ground often already exists.

", "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "The image library and its metadata", "variant_of"], "ref": "s158", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md"}, {"chunk_id": "7ce46d76-f11e-471f-970d-76095f72b3d6", "content": "# Content style guide

The house rules for how Wickhold copy is set on the page. Voice lives elsewhere. This is commas, numbers and headlines. Where a rule here seems fussy, it is usually because somebody spent an afternoon arguing about it and the team would rather not repeat that.

The first three sections are the ones reviewers send back most often.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide"], "ref": "s159", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "7d259d8a-77a1-4bfb-9b28-e6d654860e26", "content": "## Type and labels

Chart titles in Bricolage Grotesque. Axis labels and data labels in IBM Plex Sans. Commands and metric names, where they appear, in IBM Plex Mono.

Label units every time, and spell out units in axis titles ("hours to contain"). Round to the precision of the source: 7.4 hours stays 7.4, and it does not become "about 7" or "7.40".

Gridlines are thin, Whetstone at a low weight, and only where they help a reader estimate a value. If each bar has a data label, delete the gridlines and the axis.

", "heading_path": ["Data visualization", "Type and labels"], "ref": "s160", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/data-viz.md"}, {"chunk_id": "7e64f43e-9873-4a02-b501-519e513b5dc0", "content": "## 4. Positioning

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning"], "ref": "s161", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "7ebb4833-c358-4e50-aa82-4fa58d196656", "content": "# Capitalization + product names (quick sheet)

Pinned for the web team after three separate spellings turned up on one page.

Full form on first mention, short form after. First mention means the first place the name appears in a piece, and a headline counts.

| First mention | After that |
|---|---|
| Wickhold Quenchline | Quenchline |
| Wickhold Evenburn | Evenburn |
| Wickhold Leashgate | Leashgate |

One capital each. Never QuenchLine, EvenBurn or LeashGate. No internal caps, no hyphens, no all-caps in slides or nav.

Each piece starts over. A blog post that says Wickhold Quenchline does not earn the short form in the email promoting it.

Evenburn took its name on March 2, 2026. Don't write the former name in current copy, including "formerly" lines. Support handles customers who still ask for it.

Right: "Wickhold Evenburn ranks drift by exposure path. Evenburn does not contain anything at runtime."

Wrong: "Evenburn ranks drift" as the opening line, with the full name saved for the footer.

Nav labels and pricing table rows can use the short form. The page's first heading or sentence still uses the full one.

Never combine products into one name ("Quenchline-Evenburn suite"). There is no suite. If you mean more than one, name them.

**Company:** Wickhold. "Wickhold Security" retired with the rebrand on February 10, 2026. Wickhold, Inc. appears in contracts and legal footers and nowhere else.

**Lowercase, always:** contain mode, observe mode, containment action, default containment policy, drift, exposure path, fix order, tool-call policy, agent identity. These are concepts, not features with a logo.

**Capitalized:** tiers (Core, Team, Enterprise), Slow Burn Summit, Field Day, Wickhold Containment Report. "The report" on second reference, lowercase. Series A and Series B take capitals; SOC 2 Type II is set as shown.

Possessives are fine (Quenchline's agent). Skip the article: "Quenchline contains", never "the Quenchline".

The report had a different name before 2025: Wickhold Field Report. Keep that name when citing an edition that carried it. Don't rename old editions.

Feature names don't get "Wickhold" in front of them, and they don't get a trademark symbol. Neither do the products in running copy.

Lowercase product names only in code, where the tool demands it.
", "heading_path": ["Capitalization + product names (quick sheet)"], "ref": "s162", "relative_path": "brand/style/capitalization-product-names.md"}, {"chunk_id": "7f1c6115-d13c-4954-b8dc-d9d71ce61d60", "content": "## One rewrite, start to finish

A draft that came through in May, lightly disguised:

> We're excited to announce that we think our powerful new drift capabilities will transform how modern teams approach cloud risk, giving you the confidence you need in an increasingly dangerous world.

The edit went like this.

"We're excited to announce" went first. The reader's interest in our excitement is zero.

"We think" is out, because this is brand voice.

"Powerful", "new" and "modern" were doing nothing. Remove them and the sentence gets more honest and no less informative.

"Increasingly dangerous world" is the fear habit, and it also isn't something we can source.

That left "drift capabilities will transform how teams approach cloud risk", which on inspection means nothing. So the reviewer asked the only useful question: what does a person see on the screen? The product manager's answer became the copy.

> Wickhold Evenburn lists the drift in a cluster and ranks it by exposure path, so the fix order is on one page. It does not contain anything at runtime.

That is shorter, it can be checked, and it names an edge. Nobody involved felt that it was a loss.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "One rewrite, start to finish"], "ref": "s163", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "7f64603f-ccc1-4ba3-b729-e595e2b4b371", "content": "## 8. Typography

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "8. Typography"], "ref": "s164", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "80b784b5-ed7e-43ee-b94b-c4b9f387f3b3", "content": "### GDPR wording

Never say "GDPR compliant". Not about Wickhold, its products, its customers' deployments or any feature. The ban began with EU and UK copy and it now applies everywhere, including US pages that a European buyer can obviously read.

The approved wording is:

> Wickhold supports customers' GDPR obligations.

Use it as written. GDPR obligations belong to the controller and the processor and depend on what they do with the data. No vendor product can make a customer compliant, and a regulator or a procurement lawyer will read the phrase as a promise.

Variants that have turned up in drafts, all refused:

- "GDPR-ready"
- "fully GDPR aligned"
- "compliant with EU privacy law"
- "UK GDPR certified"

If a UK reader needs the point spelled out, the approved sentence covers UK GDPR. Do not add a second claim.

Examples:

| Bad | Good |
|---|---|
| Our GDPR compliant platform keeps EU workloads safe. | Wickhold supports customers' GDPR obligations. |
| Quenchline makes your clusters GDPR compliant. | Wickhold Quenchline records each containment action with a timestamp. Wickhold supports customers' GDPR obligations. |

A word on tone. European security buyers we've met through Field Day meetups tend to ask for the document and not the promise, so a short, flat statement does better than a paragraph about how seriously we take privacy. If a page has one line on GDPR, the approved sentence is that line. Don't surround it with "privacy-first" or "by design", which raise the same problem in softer words.

", "heading_path": ["Regional rules: EU and UK copy", "GDPR wording"], "ref": "s165", "relative_path": "brand/legal/regional-rules-eu-uk.md"}, {"chunk_id": "80bb122e-2883-4f39-b76e-9e8655ac896f", "content": "## Terminals and CLI output

Engineers often trust a terminal capture over a dashboard. Use a plain terminal at a normal size with IBM Plex Mono, on a Soot background, with the prompt trimmed to `$`. The command has to be real and its output has to be pasted from a real run in the demo environment. Do not edit output to shorten it. Use `...` on its own line if you must cut something, and do so only where the cut changes nothing. Remove usernames, internal hostnames and tokens by fixing the environment and running it again.

", "heading_path": ["Product UI screenshots", "Terminals and CLI output"], "ref": "s166", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/product-ui-screenshots.md"}, {"chunk_id": "819d53ad-e32a-41b3-94ae-7ccd3f1cc7d5", "content": "### Everything else

- **Measurements take digits, always.** Anything with a unit: 220 nodes, 11 minutes, 7.4 hours, 90 days, 38 seconds, 1,900 nodes.
- **Counts of ordinary things** spell out one to nine and use digits from 10: "three clusters", "12 namespaces". Mixed in one sentence, go with digits.
- **Commas from 1,000 up.** No "1.9k nodes", not even on social.
- **Keep the decimal the source gave you.** 7.4 hours stays 7.4 hours. Don't round to "about seven hours", and don't add precision the source lacks.
- **Approved sentences stay as approved.** The report line says "more than six hours", spelled out, and that's how it runs in every piece. The same goes for "more than 140 customers", which never becomes "140+". Legal approved the sentence, and this guide doesn't get to tidy it.
- **Don't do arithmetic on claims.** Lowmoor went from 4 hours to 11 minutes. Do not convert that into a percentage or an "x times faster". The figures we can stand behind are the two figures we were given. Same for adding results from different customers together.
- **No "up to".** "Up to" numbers are a best case wearing a fact's clothes. Give the median, or say which run you mean.
- **No tildes or "approx."** in published copy. If a figure is an estimate, say "about".

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "4. Numbers", "Everything else"], "ref": "s167", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "82d8c439-6354-40ca-bb8c-af8c8d4b11a3", "content": "## What to use

- A hero illustration crop, on Tallow, with one Ember focal element in the center third
- A photo crop with a calm, simple subject

600 wide by 200 tall is a thin strip from a 3:2 source. Pick images whose focal point fits in a band, such as a row of tiles or a cable tray. A person's face at this crop rarely works, because it either fills the strip or gets cut off.

", "heading_path": ["Email header images", "What to use"], "ref": "s168", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/email-header.md"}, {"chunk_id": "849c4a03-5ccb-4481-baf9-1a0a8bee9d61", "content": "## The two rules that come up every week

", "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "The two rules that come up every week"], "ref": "s169", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md"}, {"chunk_id": "84b8a0dc-e59a-4111-a6c8-65e03b1aea37", "content": "## Older notes

From the nurture rebuild, September 2025:

- Emails can run to 250 words when there's a code sample or a step list, since those read faster than prose.
- Keep the button above the fold on desktop. On long sends, repeat it at the end.
- Don't send anything from a `noreply` address. Replies are how we find out about bad lists.

---

", "heading_path": ["Email templates", "Older notes"], "ref": "s170", "relative_path": "brand/templates/email-templates.md"}, {"chunk_id": "85f52c31-27b5-4fe5-921a-ea411fb55932", "content": "## The image library and its metadata

Every approved image lives in the image library, and every image in it has a metadata record. Do not pick from the thumbnail grid and stop there. The thumbnail does not show you the limits on the image.

| Field | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| `id`, `filename` | Identity. Filenames were set by different people across several years and tell you little. |
| `type`, `title` | Rough category and a human label. |
| `description` | What is in the picture. Often thin, sometimes empty. |
| `tags` | Search help. Inconsistent, so never treat a missing tag as meaning anything. |
| `usage_rights` | The grant we hold for the file. |
| `restrictions` | The limits on this particular image. See below. |
| `added_date` | When it entered the library, which is not when it was made. |
| `source`, `attribution` | Where it came from. In-house work reads `internal-production`, and `attribution` is usually empty or names the in-house team. Empty attribution means no credit line is needed. |
| `width`, `height` | Pixel size. Check before you plan a crop. |
| `background` | How the image relates to what sits behind it. See below. |
| `safe_on` | Which grounds it can sit on. See below. |
| `variant_of` | Points at the parent when the image is one version of another. |

", "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "The image library and its metadata"], "ref": "s171", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md"}, {"chunk_id": "86969aea-4633-4607-bc0c-60994231516b", "content": "## 11. Governance

The folder contains documents from seven years, written by different people for different deadlines, and sometimes two of them disagree. This section says which one wins, who owns what, and how a piece of work gets approved. It takes precedence over any statement elsewhere about what is "final" or "current", including a file name.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "11. Governance"], "ref": "s172", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "86b7451f-baa7-4f78-b543-2cd8ad677052", "content": "### The values at work

| Value | What it looks like in marketing | What it rules out |
|---|---|---|
| Say what happened | A release note that names the bug | "Various improvements" |
| Contain first | The useful thing in the first line | A long wind-up about the threat landscape |
| Admit limits | A page that says which environments are unsupported | A feature table with a check in every box |
| Leave it better for the next on-call | A source file with a clear name and a note on why | A final deck that only one person can edit |

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "3. Values", "The values at work"], "ref": "s173", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "88232ed2-141f-4266-ba36-e451ef0a3866", "content": "### What fits and what doesn't

| Subject | Fits | Doesn't fit |
|---|---|---|
| A person at work | An engineer at a desk at dusk, reading a log | A team high-fiving around a laptop |
| Infrastructure | A real rack with labels and a worn floor | A computer-generated tunnel of light |
| The idea of containment | A single paper flame inside a paper ring | A digital barrier across a globe |
| AI agents | A simple cut-paper figure on a short lead | A glowing robot face |

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "9. Photography and illustration direction", "What fits and what doesn't"], "ref": "s174", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "8873c663-3967-4a15-92f2-c5e65fde3b3c", "content": "### Comparisons

"Faster than" needs a "than what". If the sentence compares to a named thing, that thing must be in the sentence. If it compares to a previous version of our own product, say which version.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "4. Numbers", "Comparisons"], "ref": "s175", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "89a4ae21-b22e-434f-b3f5-1a976c050d1c", "content": "## Data you can chart

Only approved figures go into public charts. A chart does not launder a number: the rules on claims, ages of statistics and lab figures apply to the chart the same way they apply to a sentence.

- Survey data carries its report name and year, and the sample where there is space. The 2026 report surveyed 412 platform and security leaders.
- Customer results appear only with approved customers, with node counts: Lowmoor at 220 nodes, Ostler at 1,900 nodes.
- A lab figure keeps its label on the chart itself: "in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026". Do not move it to a footnote on another page.

No invented or "illustrative" numbers in published charts, even on an unlabeled axis. A rising line with no scale is a claim with nothing behind it.

Every chart carries a source line at the bottom, in the citation format from the style guide, small and in Whetstone on Tallow.

", "heading_path": ["Data visualization", "Data you can chart"], "ref": "s176", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/data-viz.md"}, {"chunk_id": "8b8313bb-1412-4f76-8648-3f15a52d142a", "content": "### Exceptions

Exceptions are allowed and they are written down. Ask Noor by email with the piece, the rule, and the reason. If she agrees, the exception goes in the log she keeps, with an end date. Verbal approvals from a hallway don't count. Legal rules have no exception process through Brand. Those go to Priit.

Two exceptions from this year are typical. The Slow Burn Summit stage used a Soot and Ember backdrop well past the usual Ember proportion, because a stage is seen from 40 meters away. The Evenburn rename notice ran for 60 days using the previous product name in customer communications, so that people could find it.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "11. Governance", "Exceptions"], "ref": "s177", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "8cb0b048-4d9d-4fbb-aae3-79c022f6f5ad", "content": "## The hero

**A landing page hero shows product UI or a working room.** Those two options only.

That excludes illustration from the hero slot, even though we use it heavily elsewhere. Visitors on a landing page are deciding whether Wickhold is real. A screen from the product, or a real room where this work happens, answers that faster than a metaphor.

Use product UI when the page is about a product or a capability. Use a working room when the page speaks to a role or a problem and there is no single screen to show.

| Page | Hero |
|---|---|
| Quenchline product page | Product UI: one containment action |
| Evenburn product page | Product UI: exposure path or fix order |
| Leashgate early access page | Product UI: a tool-call policy, with the early access pill in frame |
| Platform engineering solutions page | Working room, or a terminal-adjacent product view |
| CISO or board-facing page | Working room. No people posing |
| Campaign page for the Containment Report | Working room |
| Event registration | A working session photographed at a past Slow Burn Summit, cleared for this use |

", "heading_path": ["Landing page imagery", "The hero"], "ref": "s178", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/landing-page-imagery.md"}, {"chunk_id": "8d7d04a2-dd22-458e-a916-86d6366a7a56", "content": "# Social graphics

For anything designed for a feed: stat cards, quote cards, announcement cards, event cards. A plain photo or a plain chart uploaded to a post is covered by its own category. This page is about designed layouts.

Last touched by the social lead, May 2026. Kofi's team added the engineering post notes.

", "heading_path": ["Social graphics"], "ref": "s179", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/social-graphics.md"}, {"chunk_id": "8dd6c955-a13b-4185-a4fd-f44638a66137", "content": "# Image accessibility

Web lead's notes, cleaned up by Brand in May 2026 after the customer procurement questionnaire asked us about this and we had no document to point to.

", "heading_path": ["Image accessibility"], "ref": "s180", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/accessibility.md"}, {"chunk_id": "8e229f98-1ea5-4a28-8b10-5f4b455449ff", "content": "## Email preheader

Every email has a preheader of at most 90 characters. It shows beside or under the subject line in most inboxes, so treat it as the second half of the subject. It must add something. Don't repeat the subject, and don't leave the field empty, or the client will fill it with the first text in the email, which for us is often the "view in browser" line.

Good: `Survey of 412 platform and security leaders on what happens after detection.`

Bad: `Containment Report 2026 is out. Read the Containment Report 2026 today.`

", "heading_path": ["Email templates", "Email preheader"], "ref": "s181", "relative_path": "brand/templates/email-templates.md"}, {"chunk_id": "92dc165a-1d79-4286-bdce-d5323f42f779", "content": "### Commissioning imagery

A good image brief names the idea, where the image will run and its one focal point, and it leaves the style to the visual guidance. "A wick in a ring of cut paper, for a blog on containment policy" is a usable brief. "Something cool about AI security" is not.

Freelancers and agencies should get the visual guidance before their first sketch. On the launch film, the first round of location photos came back blue and spotless, because the agency had worked from a mood board built on the old identity. Reshooting took a week.

Any generated or composited image gets the same review as a commissioned one. It is held to the same direction, and a person looks at it at full size before it goes anywhere.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "9. Photography and illustration direction", "Commissioning imagery"], "ref": "s182", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "930be8e8-ae39-4b4c-92f1-fb0b444f55be", "content": "## How the visual rules are layered

Three layers, read in this order.

1. **This page.** Applies to everything.
2. **The category.** What kind of image is it? Photo, illustration, icon, logo, product screenshot, chart, social graphic, event graphic, legal and trust imagery, anything showing a person.
3. **The content type.** Where is it going? Blog hero, LinkedIn, X, email header, landing page.

Most images touch one rule from each layer, and some touch two categories. A photo of a staff member at a customer site is photography and consent at once, and it has to pass both.

A lower layer can narrow a higher one. The illustration category accepts several formats, for example, and the blog hero page accepts fewer of them. In that case follow the narrower rule for that placement, and the broader rule stays true everywhere else. A lower layer cannot loosen this page. If a content-type page seems to let you do something this page forbids, bring it to Brand, because one of the two pages is wrong and we want to fix it.

Per-campaign exceptions go through Noor's exception log. Without an entry there, if a campaign needs something new, the rule changes for everybody or the campaign changes.

", "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "How the visual rules are layered"], "ref": "s183", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md"}, {"chunk_id": "9336bbf6-9e63-48a3-bf85-2a189d802297", "content": "## The style

**Flat cut-paper shapes.** Crisp edges with a slight hand-cut irregularity. Layers can overlap. Depth comes from stacking, and the only shadow allowed is a hard offset shape in one flat, darker tone.

**One Ember focal element.** Exactly one thing in the picture is Ember. That is where the eye goes. Everything else is Soot, Tallow, or a small amount of Whetstone or Verdigris.

**On Tallow or Soot.** Those are the only two grounds for finished illustration. An Ember ground removes the focal element, because nothing can stand out from it. Whetstone and Verdigris grounds look muddy.

**No gradients.** None, anywhere: no soft shadows, glows, blurs, mesh fills or textured airbrush. If a shape needs to look lit, cut a second shape. In review, this is the rule most often broken by accident, usually by a shadow effect left on by default in the design tool or by an export that adds banding.

Also out: outlines around shapes, 3D, isometric projection, photographic textures pasted on shapes, and stock vector packs. We tried isometric cluster diagrams in January. They looked like every infrastructure startup's site, and they required a depth that flat paper cannot give.

", "heading_path": ["Illustration", "The style"], "ref": "s184", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/illustration.md"}, {"chunk_id": "9444a373-5e1b-44c8-b229-396932ea45d4", "content": "## Body

Most of our email has three parts.

1. **What happened or what's new.** One or two sentences.
2. **Why it matters to this reader.** Two to four sentences. Different for a CISO list and a platform list, which is why the tracks are separate.
3. **What to do.** One button or link. Then the sign-off.

The working drafts are in the email templates, and the merge fields there match the sending platform. Start from a template. A blank page tends to produce an email that's 400 words long.

Good body copy, platform track:

> You downloaded the Containment Report, so here's the practical follow-up. Our rollout guide starts with Wickhold Quenchline in observe mode on one namespace, then moves to contain mode once you've read two to four weeks of would-have-acted events.
>
> It takes about an hour, and the failure modes are listed at the end.

Good body copy, CISO track:

> Decide whether your team tracks time to contain today. Your board will ask how long a runtime incident takes to contain. In our survey of 412 platform and security leaders, the median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].
>
> The report sets out how teams measure that number and what they report upward. If your team doesn't track it, section two is a place to start.

Bad body copy:

> Hope you're having a great week! As a valued member of our community, we wanted to reach out and share some exciting content we think you'll love. In today's rapidly evolving threat landscape, security has never been more important.

Four sentences in and the reader has learned nothing. Cut until the first sentence is the news.

Personalization: first name in the greeting when we have it, and role-based copy through segments. Anything else, like company size, industry or recent page views, stays out of the visible copy. Being told what you browsed by a security company is unsettling.

", "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "Body"], "ref": "s185", "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "94ad855d-2378-47b1-ba68-3bb6f5752827", "content": "## Withdrawal

A customer may withdraw at any time. Legal tells Noor, and owned assets are changed within five working days. Logo walls in decks are updated the same week. Events that have already printed are the only exception.
", "heading_path": ["Customer logo and quote policy", "Withdrawal"], "ref": "s186", "relative_path": "brand/legal/customer-logo-and-quote-policy.md"}, {"chunk_id": "95351c5f-43bc-488f-adc7-ddbebe98571a", "content": "# Wickhold voice and tone

Noor Eskelund, Head of Brand. Written for the February 2026 rebrand, rewritten in April after the Containment Report went out, last edited in June. Comments go to #brand-review in Slack.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone"], "ref": "s187", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "95a3bc17-3a62-42aa-bb1c-70545612062c", "content": "## 5. Code and commands

- Every code block must run. An engineer other than the author pastes it into a test cluster before publishing. Kofi keeps a throwaway cluster for this and will give you access.
- State versions at the top of the block or in the sentence before it: Kubernetes, Helm chart, kernel where it matters.
- Show the output when the output is the point, and trim it with a visible `...`.
- Use real-looking names like `payments-api` and `checkout`. Avoid `foo` and `my-app`, and don't use a customer's actual namespace names, even with permission.
- Say what fails. If `helm upgrade` can leave the agent in `CrashLoopBackOff` on an old kernel, put that in the post.

```bash
# Good: what you ran, and what to look for
kubectl get pods -n payments-api -o wide
# ...
# payments-api-6f9c7d   0/1   Terminating   0   3m   10.2.4.17   node-a
# A pod stuck here after a drain usually has a finalizer. Check that first.
```

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "5. Code and commands"], "ref": "s188", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "96ddc51c-fae4-4130-b3cc-2deb903e70d4", "content": "# Word list

Everything here applies to anything a customer, prospect, journalist or candidate can read. Slack can say what it likes.

", "heading_path": ["Word list"], "ref": "s189", "relative_path": "brand/voice/word-list.md"}, {"chunk_id": "974c9dd1-f990-47ba-bc47-a49f901d010c", "content": "## Other rules for all images

**Current identity only.** Ember `#C2501F`, Soot `#15181C`, Tallow `#F4EFE6`, with Whetstone `#5E6B73` and Verdigris `#2F8F83` as secondary colors. Bricolage Grotesque, IBM Plex Sans and IBM Plex Mono for any type on an image. Anything leaning on the 2024 blue palette or the 2024 logo is out, however good it looks. Some of those images are still in the library with no flag on them, so your eye is part of this check.

**No third-party marks.** No real product logos on laptop lids, no cloud provider marks on diagrams, no conference logos in a crop unless the agreement with that organizer allows it. Customer marks are a legal matter and go through Legal first.

**No watermarks,** no preview overlays, no leftover crop marks. If an image arrived with a watermark, its rights are not what you think they are.

**Do not stretch, tint or recolor library files.** Crop freely within the category's limits. Stretching breaks the proportions of the art and recoloring breaks the palette. Filters are out too: the warm look comes from the source image, and a filter laid on a cool image only makes it look cool and filtered. If an image needs a color change to fit, it is the wrong image.

**Export for the placement.** WebP or PNG for web, PNG where transparency matters, SVG for logos and icons when the placement accepts it. Keep web images under 400 KB unless the content-type page says otherwise. JPEG artifacts around Ember shapes are very visible, so check flat illustration at full size after compressing.

**Nothing that frightens.** Images follow the same stance as the copy. Show the small fire or the calm room, and skip the alarm. Red alert screens, countdown timers, sirens and skulls have no place here, even as a joke in an engineering post.

", "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "Other rules for all images"], "ref": "s190", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md"}, {"chunk_id": "9792dec6-922e-42ef-aded-9a7b0bc70f03", "content": "## 2. The intro

A blog intro must cite a market statistic. Put it in the first two sentences, in the citation format from the style guide, and follow it with one sentence that says why this post exists. The rule is there because engineers are more willing to keep reading once they know the problem is measured and someone has measured it honestly.

Statistics are subject to the age limit in the approved claims, so check the date before you reuse an intro from an older post.

Market statistics are figures about the market or a surveyed population. Our own customer results and benchmark numbers belong further down the post, and they don't satisfy this requirement.

Good:

> The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. Most of the teams we talk to can tell you how long detection took. Far fewer can tell you what happened in the hours after. This post is about those hours.

Good:

> 41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. A lot of that time goes to one question: who is allowed to touch the workload? Here is how to settle that question before the page goes off.

Bad, because it has no statistic and no reason to read on:

> Kubernetes has changed how modern teams ship software, and with that change come new security challenges.

Bad, because a customer result is doing the job of a market statistic:

> Lowmoor Credit Union cut time to contain from 4 hours to 11 minutes. Here's how your team can get the same results.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "2. The intro"], "ref": "s191", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "981ba9d5-3b99-42f9-af09-28500c013f09", "content": "## Cropping

Crops are allowed and usually needed, because different placements want different shapes. Keep the focal point inside the middle two-thirds of the frame, so a further crop by a platform does not cut it off. Do not crop a person at the neck or the wrist. Rotation is limited to straightening a horizon by a degree or two.

", "heading_path": ["Photography", "Cropping"], "ref": "s192", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/photography.md"}, {"chunk_id": "98588c52-bb4f-4b97-8b2e-da0afede6983", "content": "## 15. Usage notes

- **a/an:** go by sound. An eBPF agent, a SOC 2 report, an SRE.
- **back end** (noun), **back-end** (adjective).
- **cyber:** avoid as a prefix. Say what kind of security you mean.
- **data** is singular in our copy: "the data is".
- **drain:** a verb in Kubernetes and in our copy. "Drained the node."
- **e.g., i.e., etc.:** write "for example", "that is", or finish the list.
- **email:** no hyphen.
- **failover** (noun), **fail over** (verb).
- **in order to:** "to".
- **log in** (verb), **login** (noun). Same pattern for **set up / setup**, **roll out / rollout**, **shut down / shutdown**.
- **real time** (noun), **real-time** (adjective).
- **sidecar, service mesh:** lowercase, one and two words.
- **startup:** one word.
- **third party** (noun), **third-party** (adjective).
- **trade-off:** hyphenated.
- **utilize:** "use".
- **very, really, extremely:** delete and reread.
- **via:** "through", unless it's a technical path.
- **zero-day:** hyphenated, and only for an actual zero-day.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "15. Usage notes"], "ref": "s193", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "987d025c-85c7-409f-af90-692ae691340a", "content": "## Review

Data checked by whoever owns the source: product marketing for the Containment Report, Legal for customer results. Brand checks form and color. Do not skip the first of these because the chart "only reuses" a number from an earlier piece.
", "heading_path": ["Data visualization", "Review"], "ref": "s194", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/data-viz.md"}, {"chunk_id": "9942e960-ecb2-4c7b-8a55-e84683c37ee4", "content": "## Common rejections

| What came in | What we said |
|---|---|
| Stat with no source anywhere | Add the source in the post or the card, or drop it |
| Ember headline on Tallow | Fails contrast. Use Soot, and keep Ember for the rule |
| Three stats on one card | Pick one. Post the others another day |
| Portrait, quote, logo and a screenshot together | Four focal points. Keep the quote |
| Card reused from before the rebrand | Rebuild it from the current template |
| Customer logo added to a stat card | Needs Legal first. Usually the answer is to name them in the post |

", "heading_path": ["Social graphics", "Common rejections"], "ref": "s195", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/social-graphics.md"}, {"chunk_id": "99b64151-dd64-4f1d-afb3-b4f3e8dbee05", "content": "## FAQ

Pull questions from sales calls, not from what we wish people asked. Answer in two sentences or fewer. A good FAQ answers the objection that would otherwise stop the form.

> **Will this take down production?**
> In observe mode, Wickhold Quenchline takes no action. You choose when and where contain mode starts.

> **How much overhead does the agent add?**
> Under 2% CPU overhead on a typical node in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026.

", "heading_path": ["Landing pages", "FAQ"], "ref": "s196", "relative_path": "brand/channels/landing-page-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "9b333c21-ba1c-413a-bd7a-144ac492a1b9", "content": "### The brand idea

A wick is where a fire is allowed to exist. It gives the flame a place to be, and it keeps the flame there. That is the idea behind the name, the mark and the tagline. Wickhold accepts that production systems have heat in them. The job is to hold it to a small, known place.

This idea should explain design and copy decisions when a rule doesn't. When two options are both on brand, pick the one that feels calmer and more contained.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning", "The brand idea"], "ref": "s197", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "9c9c499f-95af-44df-aa6b-d95254aa4570", "content": "## The look

Wickhold photography looks like it was taken by someone who was already in the room.

**Available light.** Windows, overhead tubes, the glow of a laptop, a desk lamp. No strobes, ring lights or colored gels. If a room is too dark for the shot, use a longer exposure or find a better room.

**Warm and slightly underexposed.** Think of the last hour of a working day. Skin tones stay warm and natural. Shadows may go deep, though they should not go black across half the frame. If the image histogram crowds the right side, it is too bright for us.

**Working rooms and real infrastructure.** Equipment rooms, cable trays, network closets, a shared office with coffee rings on the table, a laptop open at a kitchen counter during an on-call shift. Places where the work of running Kubernetes actually happens. The subject of a security company's photo library is the people on call and the things they keep running.

**Honest mess.** Leave the cables. Leave the sticky notes (after reading them). A tidied room reads as staged, and staged reads as an advertisement.

", "heading_path": ["Photography", "The look"], "ref": "s198", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/photography.md"}, {"chunk_id": "9d594429-aec3-41bb-bf14-e0c498d102f8", "content": "### Owners

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "11. Governance", "Owners"], "ref": "s199", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "9d7a7c9b-1638-436b-b0fe-ef2ae3a5d21a", "content": "## Before you send it for review

Read it out loud as a handover to the next on-call. If you stumble, or feel you are selling to a colleague, rewrite that part.

Then a few checks that catch most problems:

- Can a stranger tell what happened, what is contained and what is next?
- Does each claim have a figure and a source, or is it a plain description of what the product does?
- Is there an "I" or "we think" outside a signed founder piece?
- Does anything rely on the reader being scared?
- What's the last line doing there?

Copy review goes through #brand-review, and Noor or one of the brand team turns it around in two working days. Claims go to Priit Salonen's team and take the time the approved claims set. If a deadline leans on either of those, say so early.
", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "Before you send it for review"], "ref": "s200", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "9eeb0cca-0fab-4d0b-aba9-a395e700120f", "content": "# Blog hero images

Content team working rules, June 2026.

**Every blog post has one hero. It is a 16:9 illustration or photo. It is never a dashboard.**

Product UI in the hero looks like an ad on top of an article, and the detail goes illegible at the size most people see it, which is the preview card. If a post is about a product screen, put the screenshot in the body, at a size where it can be read.

", "heading_path": ["Blog hero images"], "ref": "s201", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/blog-hero.md"}, {"chunk_id": "9fa331ad-cbeb-4c25-ab4f-ffc8fb3d18ec", "content": "### Choosing between them

| If the piece is about | Lean toward |
|---|---|
| People, customers, the company | Photography |
| An idea or a risk | Illustration |
| What the product does | Product imagery |

Security imagery has a set of tired visual habits, and the brand stays well clear of them. Fear is not part of the visual language, for the same reason it is not part of the verbal one.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "9. Photography and illustration direction", "Choosing between them"], "ref": "s202", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "a1cb5f0e-a0a0-4e46-9bcf-3ae99202023b", "content": "## Hero copy

The hero says what the product does and who it's for, in that order. Lead with what happens to the reader's workload. Our tagline can sit in the hero of the brand page, but it doesn't describe a product, so product pages shouldn't rely on it.

Good, product page:

> **Contain runtime failures before they spread**
> Wickhold Quenchline detects bad behavior in Kubernetes and isolates a pod, freezes a process or drains a node, under the policy you set.
> [Book a demo]

Good, posture page:

> **Know which misconfiguration to fix first**
> Wickhold Evenburn tracks drift across cloud and cluster, finds each exposure path and gives your team a fix order.
> [See a sample report]

Good, early access page:

> **Set policy for what AI agents can call**
> Wickhold Leashgate, in early access, applies tool-call policy at runtime and limits what a compromised agent can do.
> [Request early access]

Good, report page:

> **The Wickhold Containment Report 2026**
> A survey of 412 platform and security leaders on how long containment takes, and where the hours go.
> [Read the report]

Good, brand page:

> **Small fires stay small.**
> Wickhold is the runtime security company for teams that run Kubernetes.
> [See how it works]

Bad, from a 2025 agency concept:

> **Next-level cloud security for the modern enterprise**
> One powerful platform. Total confidence. Peace of mind at every layer of your stack.

Nothing in that hero says what the software does. It would fit a mattress company if you swapped "stack" for "bed".

", "heading_path": ["Landing pages", "Hero copy"], "ref": "s203", "relative_path": "brand/channels/landing-page-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "a46a0775-894e-42be-977d-0610b7c892ae", "content": "## Deliverability

A security vendor's mail gets scanned hard, and a lot of it lands in quarantine. Keep the sending domain authenticated, and check with IT before anyone adds a new sending tool. Avoid link shorteners. Don't attach files. Link to the page instead, as PDFs from vendors are often stripped at the gateway. Contacts with no opens in a year go to the re-engagement note, and if they don't respond, off the list.

", "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "Deliverability"], "ref": "s204", "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "a55aa74f-5cd7-4ad5-b930-7c95b442740a", "content": "## Old pages

Any page without traffic for six months gets redirected. Campaign pages get an end date at launch. In the 2026 rebrand cleanup, the web team found pages from 2023 still live and indexed, which is how you end up with a stale claim ranking above the current one. Put the end date in the brief.
", "heading_path": ["Landing pages", "Old pages"], "ref": "s205", "relative_path": "brand/channels/landing-page-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "a5eca255-6e97-40a8-be37-f50288aba296", "content": "### Money

- Dollars with the symbol: $18, $29. No ".00".
- Node pricing is written in full: "$18 per node per month". Not "/node/mo", not "per-node", not "$18 pnpm", which someone did actually write in a deck.
- Funding and other large sums use a capital M and no space: $46M. Don't write "$46 million" in one place and "$46M" in another; pick the M.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "4. Numbers", "Money"], "ref": "s206", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "a9d334b2-f0f5-434d-abf2-0a43a5379762", "content": "## Checks before publishing

- Alt text present and written for this placement
- Text on image measured, with the worst spot checked
- Image still makes sense at 320px wide
- Meaning does not depend on color alone
", "heading_path": ["Image accessibility", "Checks before publishing"], "ref": "s207", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/accessibility.md"}, {"chunk_id": "aaf2972c-7d1e-457d-8af8-632e772bef8b", "content": "### Company

The legal name is Wickhold, Inc., which appears in legal notices, contracts and the copyright line. The brand name is Wickhold, pronounced WICK-hold. "Wickhold Security" is the former brand name, and it survives only in historical references such as a press archive.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "5. Brand architecture", "Company"], "ref": "s208", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "abdccafa-35be-4ed9-a7fc-57720e907977", "content": "## T8b. Field Day follow-up

Owner: the Field Day host. Plain text, within two days of the event.

**Subject:** What we showed at Field Day {{city}}
**Preheader:** The commands from the live session, and the answer to the question we ran out of time on.

Hi {{first_name}},

Thanks for coming on {{date}}. The commands from the live session are on the page below, with the seeded incident if you want to run it yourself.

We ran out of time on {{open_question}}. {{short_answer}}

**[See the session notes]**

{{host_first_name}}, Wickhold

", "heading_path": ["Email templates", "T8b. Field Day follow-up"], "ref": "s209", "relative_path": "brand/templates/email-templates.md"}, {"chunk_id": "abf52a1c-e75d-4337-8a09-6ceaa48a588c", "content": "## Reuse across pages

A/B test variants use the same hero rule. If you test a hero, both arms must pass. An illustration "just for the test" still fails, and test pages have a way of becoming permanent.

Do not use the same working-room photo on two product pages. Visitors move between them, and a repeated picture makes the site look small.

", "heading_path": ["Landing page imagery", "Reuse across pages"], "ref": "s210", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/landing-page-imagery.md"}, {"chunk_id": "abfc6c9b-fa74-4690-92be-fe600f22909f", "content": "### Translation

Legal wording is not translated freely. If an asset is localized, the translated version of the approved GDPR sentence comes to me first, and a claim that was fine in English does not stay fine because a translator softened or sharpened it.

", "heading_path": ["Regional rules: EU and UK copy", "Translation"], "ref": "s211", "relative_path": "brand/legal/regional-rules-eu-uk.md"}, {"chunk_id": "ac2ef319-64a9-42c8-b403-4fe159097fc2", "content": "## Timing

Tuesday to Thursday, 9 to 11am in the recipient's time zone where the platform knows it. Customer notices go when they're ready, at any hour. Avoid the last week of a quarter for prospect sends, because sales wants clean inboxes for their own outreach, and avoid the week of the big cloud-native conference in November unless the send is about the conference.

If a customer notice is going out, hold marketing sends to the affected accounts for 48 hours. Nobody wants a newsletter in the same hour as a CVE note. Lifecycle owns the pause, and the on-call engineer writing the notice tells them in the channel.

", "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "Timing"], "ref": "s212", "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "ae9dabc4-57ef-4af0-88b2-208f490ba284", "content": "## Metadata for new captures

Every new capture gets a record with `background` set, `source: internal-production`, the product name in `tags`, the release in `description`, and any limits in `restrictions`. If a capture shows a beta feature, say so in `restrictions`, with the date it should be reviewed.

", "heading_path": ["Product UI screenshots", "Metadata for new captures"], "ref": "s213", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/product-ui-screenshots.md"}, {"chunk_id": "b0b53749-5be6-4308-8b5a-8b34e65f5020", "content": "## 10. Tried and dropped

Guest posts from partners took more editing than writing one ourselves, and the partners wanted a link in every paragraph. Weekly "news roundups" lasted nine weeks in 2025 and nobody missed them. Keyword-led briefs from an agency produced the "Everything You Need To Know" titles above, and we stopped that contract in the spring.
", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "10. Tried and dropped"], "ref": "s214", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "b1963df5-8f44-4062-a767-6c822e7f71e4", "content": "### Regulators and public bodies

Do not name a regulator, or imply that a regulator has reviewed Wickhold. Do not use a guidance document as a sales hook while it is in consultation.

", "heading_path": ["Regional rules: EU and UK copy", "Regulators and public bodies"], "ref": "s215", "relative_path": "brand/legal/regional-rules-eu-uk.md"}, {"chunk_id": "b2af5123-9ec1-4562-8c1d-22ea9532be1c", "content": "### The three families

| Family | Role | Why it was chosen |
|---|---|---|
| Bricolage Grotesque | Headlines | Slightly irregular, with some personality at large sizes. It looks made by a person |
| IBM Plex Sans | Body | Plain and sturdy, and easy to read over long documents |
| IBM Plex Mono | Code | Pairs with Plex Sans and has clear distinctions between similar characters such as 0 and O |

All three are open-licensed, so anyone at the company, any agency and any build pipeline can use them without a license request. Inter was retired with the 2024 identity.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "8. Typography", "The three families"], "ref": "s216", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "b39ffdf9-91aa-4c47-a19d-da6e58b90e6e", "content": "## 12. Social and email formatting

- No emoji in brand posts or email. Founders can do as they like on their own accounts within reason.
- One link per post. Put it where it reads naturally; shortened links are for tracking and shouldn't appear as bare text where the full domain would fit.
- Line breaks on LinkedIn mark real paragraph breaks. No one-sentence-per-line posts.
- Greeting in email: "Hi Sam," with the first name and a comma, or no greeting for a broadcast. No "Dear". No "Hey there".
- Plain sign-off: name, job, company, or the team name on a broadcast. Nobody signs "Cheers" on a customer notice.
- In email, check that the piece reads correctly with images off.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "12. Social and email formatting"], "ref": "s217", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "b463cb57-17ad-45be-a529-05c9e37501e7", "content": "X playbook
==========

Kofi Anselm / DevRel. Written June 2026 when marketing handed the account over to us. Short on purpose.

The audience on X is platform engineers, SREs and the people who maintain the projects we depend on. Nobody on there is shopping. They follow accounts that post useful things and are funny about once a week.

**Length.** An X post from any Wickhold account is 240 characters at most. The platform allows more. We stop at 240 so a post can be quoted with a comment and still read whole, and because anything longer is usually two thoughts. Count the raw text, including the link as typed.

**Who has the password.** DevRel owns the main account. Marketing queues launch posts and report posts; DevRel reviews them. Noor can pull anything at any time. Two-factor is on the shared vault, and nobody posts from a personal phone without it.

**What goes out**

- Release notes in one line, with a link
- Findings from the Containment Report, one figure per post
- Practical tips: an eBPF gotcha, a kubectl one-liner, something odd about containerd
- Clips from Slow Burn Summit talks and Field Day
- CVE notes when a CVE touches something we ship or something our customers run a lot of, with facts and the fix

About three to five posts a week. More during Summit, fewer in December. Nothing goes out just to fill a slot in the calendar.

**What a good post looks like**

One thought. A concrete noun in the first few words. If there is a link, it comes last.

Good:

> Wickhold Quenchline can drain a node for you if your policy says so. It will not write the postmortem.

> 41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].

> Tip: run contain mode on one namespace first. Observe mode tells you what would have happened. Contain mode tells you who in that namespace forgot to mention a sidecar.

> The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. That is one whole on-call shift, plus a sandwich.

> Wickhold Evenburn's fix order will not make the list shorter. It will tell you which line to start on.

", "heading_path": ["X playbook"], "ref": "s218", "relative_path": "brand/channels/x-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "b47549a2-fea7-42ba-bec7-3acb024770f4", "content": "## Demo data

The demo environment is seeded with fictional clusters, namespaces and workloads. Keep it believable:

- Cluster and namespace names that look like real engineers wrote them: `payments-prod`, `batch-eu`, `ingest`. No `foo`, no `test123`, and nothing funny at a customer's expense
- Container images under `registry.wickhold.example`, so no real image names or registries appear
- People's names, where the screen shows an assignee, from the fictional demo roster. Do not use real staff, because staff leave. No names of customers, approved or otherwise
- Timestamps that agree with each other. An alert cannot be contained before it fired
- CVE IDs only when they are real, public and old. Do not imply a live incident

**Numbers on screen are claims.** A tile that shows a time to contain, a CPU figure or a count of findings fixed will be read as a result. Demo values must not look like a customer result or undercut an approved figure. If a tile reads like a brag, change the seed data, or crop it out. If you want to make a performance point, use an approved claim in the copy and keep it out of the picture.

Pricing and contract screens are never captured. Discount fields, billing pages and node counts tied to a plan stay out of marketing images.

", "heading_path": ["Product UI screenshots", "Demo data"], "ref": "s219", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/product-ui-screenshots.md"}, {"chunk_id": "b7195205-6479-423b-bbc7-d14ba956b98e", "content": "## What didn't work

- Fortnightly newsletter. Unsubscribes rose and we had nothing to say on the off weeks.
- "Webinar replay" emails after every webinar. Replaced by one line in the newsletter.
- A six-email welcome series. Most people stopped opening at the third. Now three emails.
", "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "What didn't work"], "ref": "s220", "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "b7b87728-b779-4387-aded-a12e59f856d7", "content": "## 1. Headlines

**Headlines are in sentence case.** Capitalize the first word and any proper noun. Everything else is lowercase.

This covers page titles, blog titles, section headings, email subject lines, slide titles, buttons, nav labels, form labels, table headers and any text set over an image. If it looks like a heading, it is one.

| Right | Wrong |
|---|---|
| What contain mode does to a running pod | What Contain Mode Does To A Running Pod |
| Wickhold Containment Report 2026 | WICKHOLD CONTAINMENT REPORT 2026 |
| How Ostler Grocers cut its open critical misconfigurations | How Ostler Grocers Cut Its Open Critical Misconfigurations |

Details:

- Product names, event names and the report title keep their capitals, as do Kubernetes, Helm, CVE and the rest of the proper vocabulary. `containerd` and `eBPF` keep their lowercase starts even as the first word, though it's nicer to rewrite so that neither opens a headline.
- The word after a colon is lowercase: "Drift: what it is and how to read it".
- No full stop on headlines. The tagline is the one exception, and it keeps its full stop everywhere.
- No code formatting in headlines. They break in email clients and in link previews.
- Keep a headline to one idea. If it needs a colon and a dash, it's two headlines.

The old sheet used Title Case for everything over 24px. That went in the rebrand, and pages still carrying it get fixed when someone next touches them.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "1. Headlines"], "ref": "s221", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "ba11321a-3c46-44c9-b56c-ba0b84503c24", "content": "### Writing the company name

Write Wickhold, with one capital. The possessive is Wickhold's. The name is singular in American English, so "Wickhold is", and it never takes "the" in front of it. In a logo-free context such as a plain-text email or a form field, the name is simply typed out. Internal team names like "Wickhold Marketing" are descriptions and do not need any special treatment.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "5. Brand architecture", "Writing the company name"], "ref": "s222", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "bab04564-38bc-4e96-ba78-9bb00fa98da6", "content": "### Email and event lists

- Do not import badge scans or partner lists into a send until field marketing confirms the lawful basis for that list.
- Every EU and UK send carries an unsubscribe link and the Wickhold, Inc. postal address.
- Bought lists are not used in these regions. This was tried once in 2025 for a German webinar and dropped after the complaints.
- Event pages say who receives attendee data before the attendee registers.

", "heading_path": ["Regional rules: EU and UK copy", "Email and event lists"], "ref": "s223", "relative_path": "brand/legal/regional-rules-eu-uk.md"}, {"chunk_id": "bc78b090-211c-4c83-92b8-ef866c9adc03", "content": "### Say the number, then stop

Claims carry a figure and a source. No adjective stacks.

"Fast" is not a claim. "A fast, powerful, highly scalable runtime platform" is three non-claims in a row. Write the number, say where it came from, and end the sentence. The urge to add a second sentence explaining why the number is impressive is the urge to resist. A reader who needs that sentence is the wrong reader; a reader who doesn't will think less of us for it.

Bad: "Lowmoor Credit Union saw an incredible, game-changing reduction in response times."

Good: "Lowmoor Credit Union cut time to contain from 4 hours to 11 minutes across 220 nodes."

Bad: "Quenchline is extremely lightweight and blazingly quick."

Good: "Wickhold Quenchline contains a known-bad process in a median of 38 seconds in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026."

If there is no figure, there is usually no claim, and the honest move is to describe what the product does in plain mechanical terms. "Isolates a pod's network" needs no number and no source. It's a description. "Industry-leading isolation" needs both and has neither.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "What Wickhold believes", "Say the number, then stop"], "ref": "s224", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "bd7ba1fe-13b7-4692-afd2-ef01d0dc122b", "content": "## Review

Check the last ten posts on the blog before you commit. The same image twice in a month makes the blog look thin, and readers on the index page see them side by side. Since a hero image goes out in the social card by default, check the record's `restrictions` as you would for social use.

| Product | Job | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Wickhold Quenchline | Runtime detection and containment for Kubernetes, using an eBPF agent | Available since September 2020 |
| Wickhold Evenburn | Cloud and cluster posture management | Available. Took this name on March 2, 2026 |

A leash gate is a control point an animal has to pass through on a lead. When someone asks where the names came from, those are the answers, and they make a decent line in a founder talk. They do not belong in product copy.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "5. Brand architecture", "Products"], "ref": "s227", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "be3c1859-7e07-406e-95dc-7c736c76f1db", "content": "## What the metadata means for photos

All photographs carry `background: scene`. A photograph keeps its environment: we do not cut people or objects out of their rooms, and we do not swap the sky through an office window. If you need a subject on a plain ground, you need an illustration.

Most photos are 1536x1024 landscape, with a few 1024x1536 portrait. Check `width` and `height` before you plan a layout around one. Upscaling a photo by more than about 20% shows.

`safe_on` is mostly `any` for photos, since a scene brings its own ground. A photo edge can still fight the layout. A dark, underexposed photo set straight on Soot loses its edges entirely, so give it margin or move it to a Tallow section.

`source` will read `internal-production` for in-house work, and `attribution` is often empty. We do not run photographer credits.

", "heading_path": ["Photography", "What the metadata means for photos"], "ref": "s228", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/photography.md"}, {"chunk_id": "bfb82499-dbaa-4829-975f-6158d7cdb131", "content": "## Who picks

When a table is the right call, keep it plain: horizontal rules only, Soot text on Tallow, numbers right-aligned in IBM Plex Mono so that digits line up. Highlight one row with an Ember rule at its left edge. Do not zebra-stripe.

", "heading_path": ["Data visualization", "Tables"], "ref": "s231", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/categories/data-viz.md"}, {"chunk_id": "c0c60096-8668-4c20-87fe-10c000e9f1d1", "content": "## By email type

| Email | Header |
|---|---|
| Monthly newsletter | One hero illustration crop, changed each issue |
| Report announcement | Illustration taken from the report cover art, with its title removed |
| Event invitation | Photo crop or illustration, cleared for event use |
| Product update | Usually none. A small product crop in the body does more |
| Sales follow-up | None |
| Renewal or billing notice | None |

Do not animate headers. Some mail apps only show the first frame, which then has to work alone. Do not slice a header into several image cells. That technique causes hairline gaps in the same older apps that dislike large images.

Keep one crop per campaign and reuse it across the sequence, so that the second and third sends read as a set. Each one still gets its image record checked, because `restrictions` can change between sends.

", "heading_path": ["Email header images", "By email type"], "ref": "s232", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/email-header.md"}, {"chunk_id": "c1079d42-ff19-496b-9bbf-e72c382dc03d", "content": "## Page skeleton and word budget

| Section | Budget (words) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Hero: headline, one sentence, CTA | 40 | Must make sense with no scrolling |
| Proof strip: customer logos or one number | 25 | One row, no carousel |
| What it does: three blocks at most | 150 | Concrete actions, not themes |
| How it works or how you roll it out | 100 | Steps. Commands if the audience is technical |
| Customer proof: one result, one quote | 70 | A full sentence with the number and the source |
| FAQ: three questions at most | 80 | Real questions from sales calls |
| Closing CTA | 15 | Same action as the hero |
| **Total** | **480** | Leaves 20 words of slack |

CTAs follow the shared CTA format in the email templates. Use one primary CTA per page, repeated at the top and bottom with the same wording. A secondary link is allowed for a technical reader who is not ready for a form, like the docs or the rollout guide.

", "heading_path": ["Landing pages", "Page skeleton and word budget"], "ref": "s233", "relative_path": "brand/channels/landing-page-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "c1483026-3308-4a52-8cf9-e6314d11b35f", "content": "## 6. Grammar and punctuation

- **American spelling** in all copy, including copy going to UK and EU readers. Containerize, not containerise.
- **Oxford comma**, always. It has settled more than one argument in Kubernetes prose, where lists of nouns can double as lists of objects.
- **Active voice** with a named actor, wherever the actor is known. "Wickhold Quenchline drained the node." If the passive is hiding who did it and that person is us, it goes.
- **Tense.** Past for what happened, present for what the product does, and nothing in the future except where a date is public.
- **Contractions** are fine in the blog, on social and in email. Skip them on legal pages and in anything aimed at a board.
- **Colons** are our favorite punctuation mark and they're doing fine. Use them to introduce the fact.
- **Semicolons** at most once a page. If there are two, one wants to be a full stop.
- **Em dashes** rarely in body copy. Most are a full stop that lost its nerve. Spaced en dashes are not a substitute.
- **Parentheses** for the short aside only. If the aside matters, promote it to a sentence.
- **Quotation marks:** double, with commas and full stops inside, American style, except for literal strings in technical writing where the punctuation would change the meaning. Single quotes only inside double.
- **Italics:** titles of reports and the occasional stress only. They disappear on Soot grounds and in email.
- **Bold:** for scanning in long documents, once or twice per section. Bold on a landing page means the design isn't working.
- **Ampersands:** only in proper names. Plain "and" in headlines too.
- **"And/or"** is a legal term. Pick one.
- **Slashes** as a shortcut ("platform/security teams") get rewritten: "platform and security teams".

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "6. Grammar and punctuation"], "ref": "s234", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "c1865b41-5cea-419f-8a42-5a9096193a21", "content": "### Positioning statement

For teams that run Kubernetes in production, Wickhold is the runtime security company that contains failures early. Other tools report what they saw. Wickhold products act on it, within limits the customer's team has set, and tell the team what was done.

This statement is internal. It tells writers where the company stands, and it is not customer copy. The approved public description of the company is the current boilerplate, which is kept and owned separately.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning", "Positioning statement"], "ref": "s235", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "c28e7438-46d7-471e-b55d-ea5418751c6c", "content": "## Document posts and video

PDF document posts are off the plan, for the same reasons as carousels. Native video follows the screenshot rules for captures. A title frame counts as an image and falls under the seven-word cap.

", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn images", "Document posts and video"], "ref": "s236", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/linkedin-image.md"}, {"chunk_id": "c37df191-6216-45a0-a492-50686e14a2e5", "content": "### One focal point

Every image has one focal point. A reader should be able to say what the image is of after a second's look. If two things compete, crop or pick another image.

Tests we use in review:

- Squint at it. One shape or area should hold.
- Shrink it to a thumbnail. Something should still be identifiable.
- Describe it in one short sentence without "and". "An engineer reading a terminal in a dark room" passes. "A team at a table and a wall of monitors and a logo on the door" does not.

Collages, split screens and before-and-after pairs fail this unless they are charts, where the comparison is the single point.

", "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "The two rules that come up every week", "One focal point"], "ref": "s237", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md"}, {"chunk_id": "c555aa43-f86c-4b00-af8f-ab621338c84f", "content": "## 4. Certification status

SOC 2 Type II: held. Renewed January 2026. The report is shared under NDA through the account team.

FedRAMP Moderate: in process. The approved sentence is "Wickhold is pursuing FedRAMP Moderate authorization." Never state or imply FedRAMP authorization or certification. The status sheet has the detail and is the first thing to check.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "4. Certification status"], "ref": "s238", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "c6394c1c-58a9-4ee0-8f7e-d115ca33d2d6", "content": "## Alt text on every image

Every image has alt text. This covers blog images, email images, landing pages, social uploads where the platform offers the field, and images in PDFs. The author of the piece writes it, because the designer usually does not know why the image is there.

Write what the reader would lose if the image failed to load. One or two plain sentences, under about 125 characters when you can manage it. Skip "image of" and "picture of". Do not stuff keywords. Do not paste the `description` field from the library: that describes the file, and alt text describes what the image is doing in this piece.

| Image | Bad | Good |
|---|---|---|
| Photo | "Engineer, Kubernetes, security, on-call, data center" | "An engineer reads a terminal in a dim equipment room." |
| Product screenshot | "Screenshot of dashboard" | "Quenchline shows one pod isolated, with network access removed and the process frozen." |
| Chart | "Bar chart" | "Median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours. Wickhold Containment Report 2026." |
| Logo | "logo.png" | "Wickhold logo" |
| Illustration | "Decorative graphic" | "A cut-paper wick with a single small Ember flame." |

Charts and screenshots carry the finding in the alt text, and the reader should not need the picture to get the number. If the chart has more than about four values, put the values in a table or the body copy under it and let the alt text state the point.

Any text set on an image must also appear in the alt text or the surrounding copy. Screen readers cannot read a stat card.

The "every image" part holds for decorative images too. If an image truly adds nothing, the first question is why it is in the piece. Background textures set in CSS are not images for this purpose and need no alt.

", "heading_path": ["Image accessibility", "Alt text on every image"], "ref": "s239", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/accessibility.md"}, {"chunk_id": "c6a52d68-5c35-45b0-aceb-b1a1e1b7e799", "content": "## 17. Accepted shortcuts and exceptions

- Internal documents (including this one) don't need to meet the citation form. They do need to be right.
- Slide speaker notes follow the same rules once they go into a shared deck, since decks get forwarded.
- Quoted customer language stays as approved, including its capitalization. If a quote has a problem, go back to the customer through the customer marketing owner; don't fix it in place.
- Text inside a screenshot is not edited. If a screenshot shows something out of date, take a new one.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "17. Accepted shortcuts and exceptions"], "ref": "s240", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "c7346580-863d-4b26-aa24-4419525276a3", "content": "## T4. Field Day invite
